options.rationale: The kidneys clear magnesium. With low output the drug builds up and toxicity follows.

questions.takeaway: Magnesium leaves through the kidneys. Normal reflexes and breathing are reassuring now, and low urine output warns of what is coming.
questions.strategy: The reflexes and breathing are the usual toxicity checks and both are fine. Look for the finding that predicts trouble.

steps.detail: Reflexes present and respirations 16. No toxicity yet.
Warmth is common with the infusion.
Output below 30 mL per hour means magnesium is not being cleared.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 22 mL per hour.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old with heart failure ate a salty holiday dinner yesterday. Today his weight is up 2.3 kg. He is short of breath lying flat and has new crackles in both lung bases.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: He is short of breath lying flat. Sitting him up eases breathing right away.

options.text: Give furosemide as prescribed
options.rationale: A loop diuretic removes the extra fluid before it becomes pulmonary edema.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids
options.rationale: He already has too much fluid.

options.text: Start 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and adds to the overload.

options.text: Fluid overload with early pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Sudden weight gain, orthopnea and new crackles after a sodium load.

options.text: Isotonic dehydration
options.rationale: Dehydration brings weight loss and clear lungs.

options.text: Hyponatremia from sodium loss
options.rationale: He took in extra sodium, and nothing in the scenario shows a loss.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: May follow the diuretic later. It does not explain today's findings.

options.text: Lung sounds
options.rationale: Crackles clearing or spreading tells you which way the lungs are going.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: The best indicator of fluid status, measured at the same time on the same scale.

options.text: Chvostek sign
options.rationale: A calcium and magnesium check.

options.text: Skin turgor over the sternum
options.rationale: A dehydration check, and he has the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: A sudden weight gain with new crackles is overload heading toward pulmonary edema. Sit him up, remove fluid, then track lungs and weight.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction first. Every wrong option belongs to a patient who is dry.

steps.detail: Weight up 2.3 kg overnight with crackles means too much fluid.

steps.action: Choose actions that help breathing and remove fluid
steps.detail: Head of bed up, then the diuretic.
Lung sounds and daily weight.

elimination.verdict: Fluid overload; raise the head of the bed and give furosemide; lung sounds and daily weight.

questions.stem: A patient taking lisinopril and spironolactone has a potassium of 5.4 mEq/L and receives diet teaching. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll have orange juice and a banana with breakfast every morning."
options.rationale: Both are high in potassium, which he needs to limit.

options.text: "I'll read the label on my salt substitute before I use it."
options.rationale: Many salt substitutes are potassium chloride. Checking the label shows he knows the hidden source.

options.text: "I'll skip the spironolactone on days I feel weak."
options.rationale: He should report weakness, not change his own doses.

options.text: "I'll switch to baked potatoes instead of fries."
options.rationale: Sounds healthier, and potatoes are a high potassium food either way.

questions.takeaway: Both of his drugs hold on to potassium. Salt substitutes are the source patients do not suspect.
questions.strategy: Three statements either add potassium or change a prescription. One shows he can find potassium that is not obvious.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Juice, bananas and potatoes all add potassium.
Stopping a drug on his own is not safe self care.
It targets a hidden potassium source.

elimination.verdict: Reading the salt substitute label.

questions.stem: A patient with a calcium of 7.2 mg/dL had hand spasms when the blood pressure cuff inflated. After IV calcium, which finding indicates the treatment was effective?

options.text: No hand spasm occurs when the cuff is inflated
options.rationale: The Trousseau sign is gone, so the nerves are no longer overexcitable.

options.text: Tingling has moved from the fingers to the mouth
options.rationale: Tingling that is still present, and now around the mouth, means the calcium is still low.

options.text: Patellar reflexes are absent
options.rationale: Absent reflexes point past normal toward too much calcium.

options.text: Bowel sounds are hypoactive
options.rationale: A slowed gut is a high calcium finding, not a sign of recovery.

questions.takeaway: Judge the treatment by the sign that showed the problem. A negative Trousseau means the calcium is doing its job.
questions.strategy: Less tingling and no spasm both sound like improvement. Only one of them is a finding that has fully resolved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Absent reflexes and a slow gut belong to high calcium.
Tingling that remains is still a symptom.
The cuff no longer triggers a spasm.

elimination.verdict: No hand spasm with cuff inflation.

questions.stem: An alert 86-year-old resident who swallows safely has a sodium of 149 mEq/L and says she is never thirsty. Which intervention does the nurse add to her plan?

options.text: Remind her to ask for water when she is thirsty
options.rationale: Her thirst signal is weak, so she will not ask.

options.text: Limit high sodium foods at meals
options.rationale: Tempting, since restricting sodium is a real treatment. Her problem is too little water, and this adds none.

options.text: Offer fluids every hour while she is awake
options.rationale: Older adults lose the thirst drive. Scheduled fluids replace the water she is not asking for.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: She is alert, swallows safely and is only mildly high, so the oral route comes first.

questions.takeaway: When thirst cannot be trusted, put water on a schedule. Use the least invasive route that works.
questions.strategy: Her own words are the cue. A plan that depends on her thirst will fail.

steps.detail: She is never thirsty, so waiting for thirst is out.
The sodium is high because water intake is low.
She can drink, so oral fluids come before IV.

elimination.verdict: Offer fluids every hour while awake.

questions.stem: A patient with a sodium of 116 mEq/L had a seizure and is receiving 3% sodium chloride. Two hours later, which finding best indicates the therapy is working as intended?

options.text: Sodium is 134 mEq/L
options.rationale: Tempting because it is nearly normal. A rise of 18 in 2 hours is far too fast and can injure the brain.

options.text: She is awake and follows commands
options.rationale: The brain is the organ at risk, and improving alertness shows the swelling is easing.

options.text: She reports a new headache and nausea
options.rationale: A new neuro symptom during treatment needs follow up.

options.text: Urine output is 35 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. It says nothing about whether the brain swelling is easing.

questions.takeaway: With sodium, the brain tells you how treatment is going. A number that jumps fast is a problem even if it looks normal.
questions.strategy: The near normal lab looks like success. Check how fast it got there.

steps.action: Cut what does not show the goal
steps.detail: A new headache with nausea needs a call, and urine output is not the target.

steps.action: Do the math on the sodium
steps.detail: From 116 to 134 in 2 hours is too rapid.
Awake and following commands is the goal.

elimination.verdict: Awake and following commands.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 0.9 mEq/L and a prolonged QT interval asks to come off the cardiac monitor to shower. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Remove the monitor for a 10 minute shower
options.rationale: Tempting because it respects his wishes and is brief. A prolonged QT can turn into a lethal rhythm in seconds.

options.text: Remove the monitor and have a nursing assistant stay nearby
options.rationale: Someone nearby cannot see a rhythm change.

options.text: Offer a shower after tomorrow's magnesium level
options.rationale: Reasonable sounding, but it leaves today's hygiene need unmet when a bedside wash solves it safely.

options.text: Keep the monitor on and help him wash at the bedside
options.rationale: Keeps him monitored while the magnesium is low and still meets his hygiene need.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium with a prolonged QT is a dysrhythmia risk every minute. Meet the patient's need without giving up the monitor.
questions.strategy: Two options honor his request and two keep him monitored. Find the one that does both jobs.

steps.detail: Prolonged QT with low magnesium can become a fatal rhythm.

steps.action: Cut options that remove the monitor
steps.detail: Short time and a helper do not replace telemetry.

steps.action: Choose the option that still serves him
steps.detail: A bedside wash meets the need safely.

elimination.verdict: Keep the monitor on and help him wash at the bedside.

questions.stem: The day after major abdominal surgery, a patient has puffy hands and face, a blood pressure of 90/54 and urine output of 20 mL per hour. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: Low volume in the blood vessels
options.rationale: Low pressure and low urine output show the vessels are underfilled. Fluid has moved into the tissue, and organs are not being perfused.

options.text: Excess fluid in the tissues
options.rationale: Tempting because the swelling is what you see. Treating it as overload would empty the vessels further.

options.text: Risk for skin breakdown over swollen areas
options.rationale: A real risk, and a potential problem comes after an actual one.

options.text: Risk for falls when getting out of bed
options.rationale: A real risk with low pressure, and it is still a potential problem.

questions.takeaway: A patient can be swollen and still dry in the vessels. Blood pressure and urine output tell you about the plasma; edema does not.
questions.strategy: The edema and the low pressure point in opposite directions. Ask which finding describes the compartment that perfuses organs.

steps.detail: Puffiness is interstitial. Pressure and urine output reflect plasma.
Skin and fall risks have not happened yet.
Underfilled vessels threaten the kidneys now.

elimination.verdict: Low vascular volume comes first.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old taking prednisone long term has a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and weak legs. Which actions does the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place her on a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Low potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias.

options.text: Give oral potassium with meals
options.rationale: Food reduces the nausea oral potassium causes.

options.text: Start fall precautions
options.rationale: Weak legs make a fall likely.

options.text: Limit potatoes, oranges and spinach
options.rationale: These are potassium rich foods. She needs more of them, not fewer.

options.text: Watch breathing depth and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Severe low potassium weakens the breathing muscles.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium: watch the heart, replace potassium safely, protect from falls and keep an eye on breathing.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction of the imbalance first. Then test each action: does it fit a patient who needs more potassium and has weak muscles?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2.9 is low, and corticosteroids waste potassium.
Monitor, fall precautions and breathing checks.
Limiting potassium foods belongs to high potassium.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and E.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with chronic hypocalcemia from kidney disease needs to be moved up in bed. Which instruction does the nurse give the assistive personnel?

options.text: Have her pull up using the overhead trapeze
options.rationale: Tempting because it builds independence. Her bones are fragile, and pulling her weight on them risks a fracture.

options.text: Use a lift sheet with two people and support her limbs
options.rationale: Chronic low calcium thins the bones. A lift sheet moves her without pulling on arms or legs.

options.text: Lift her under the arms with one person on each side
options.rationale: Pulling under the arms loads fragile shoulders and ribs.

options.text: Reposition her only once a shift to limit handling
options.rationale: Less handling sounds protective, but it trades fracture risk for skin breakdown. Gentle is the answer, not seldom.

questions.takeaway: Long standing low calcium means fragile bones. Move the patient gently, with the sheet carrying the load.
questions.strategy: Independence is usually the better answer. Here the chronic low calcium changes what is safe for her bones.

steps.action: Link the lab to the bones
steps.detail: Chronic low calcium pulls calcium from bone.

steps.action: Cut options that load her bones
steps.detail: The trapeze and pulling under the arms both do.
Not repositioning causes other harm.

elimination.verdict: Lift sheet, two people, limbs supported.

questions.stem: A patient on a continuous insulin infusion for 6 hours has new leg weakness and a U wave on the monitor. The last hourly glucose was 164 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick glucose now
options.rationale: Tempting with insulin running. The glucose was just checked and weakness with a U wave is not how low glucose presents.

options.text: Request a serum calcium level
options.rationale: Low calcium causes tingling, spasm and a long QT, not weakness with a U wave.

options.text: Slow the insulin infusion by half
options.rationale: Changing the rate is the provider's decision, and it does not tell you what the potassium is.

options.text: Request a serum potassium level
options.rationale: A fast insulin infusion moves potassium into cells. Weak legs and a U wave are the picture of low potassium.

questions.takeaway: Insulin carries potassium into cells along with glucose. Weakness and a U wave during an insulin infusion mean check the potassium.
questions.strategy: Insulin makes you think glucose. The stem already gives a safe glucose, so ask what else insulin moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use the glucose in the stem
steps.detail: 164 an hour ago rules out low glucose as the cause.
A U wave belongs to low potassium.
Insulin shifts potassium into cells.

elimination.verdict: Request a potassium level.

questions.scenario: A patient with a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L from diuretic use has received IV and oral potassium for 12 hours. On admission he had hypoactive bowel sounds, leg strength of 3 out of 5 and a U wave on the monitor.
questions.stem: For each reassessment finding, indicate whether it shows he is improving or requires follow up.

rows.text: Bowel sounds are active in all four quadrants
rows.rationale: The gut is waking up as potassium returns.

rows.text: Tall peaked T waves on the monitor
rows.rationale: This is the high potassium pattern. Replacement may have overshot.

rows.text: Leg strength is 5 out of 5
rows.rationale: Muscle strength has returned.

rows.text: New tingling in the hands with watery diarrhea
rows.rationale: Early signs of high potassium, the opposite imbalance.

rows.text: The U wave is no longer visible
rows.rationale: The low potassium ECG sign has resolved.

rows.text: Heart rate is 50, down from 82
rows.rationale: A slowing heart during potassium replacement suggests the level is now too high.

questions.takeaway: When you treat an imbalance, watch for the opposite one. Improvement is the admission signs resolving; trouble is the other imbalance appearing.
questions.strategy: Compare each row with the admission findings. If it reverses one of them, he is improving. If it is a new finding, ask whether it fits high potassium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bowel sounds, leg strength and the U wave have all reversed.
Peaked T waves, tingling with diarrhea and a slow heart rate.
The new findings are high potassium.

elimination.verdict: Improving: r1, r3, r5. Follow up: r2, r4, r6.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L takes oral potassium chloride before breakfast and is nauseated after each dose. He is not vomiting. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the next dose with his breakfast tray
options.rationale: Oral potassium irritates an empty stomach. Giving it with food reduces the nausea and keeps the replacement on track.

options.text: Hold the next dose and report the nausea
options.rationale: Tempting because a side effect is being reported. His potassium is still low, and a simple change in timing solves the problem without a missed dose.

options.text: Request a change to IV potassium
options.rationale: IV potassium carries more risk. He is absorbing the oral doses, so the less invasive route stays.

options.text: Have him take the dose at bedtime
options.rationale: An empty stomach at bedtime irritates just as much, and he would be lying down with it.

questions.takeaway: Oral potassium goes with food. Fix a tolerable side effect with the smallest change before you stop or escalate a replacement the patient still needs.
questions.strategy: Holding the dose sounds like the safe choice. Ask whether the patient still needs the drug and whether a smaller change removes the problem.

steps.action: Check whether he still needs it
steps.detail: 3.2 is low, so the replacement should continue.

steps.action: Find the cause of the nausea
steps.detail: The dose is going onto an empty stomach.
Food with the dose, before a held dose or an IV.

elimination.verdict: Give the dose with breakfast.

questions.stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder still has a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L after 2 days of replacement. His reflexes are hyperactive. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask to raise the IV potassium rate
options.rationale: Tempting because the level has not moved. More potassium will not hold while the cause is untreated, and faster rates are unsafe.

options.text: Recheck the potassium the next morning
options.rationale: Waiting does not explain why two days of replacement failed.

options.text: Request a serum magnesium level
options.rationale: Malnutrition and alcohol use drain magnesium, hyperactive reflexes fit low magnesium, and potassium often will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

options.text: Ask to change to oral potassium
options.rationale: A different route does not fix the reason the potassium is not holding.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium rides along with low potassium. When potassium will not come up, check and correct the magnesium.
questions.strategy: Two options push more potassium. Ask why the first two days did not work, and use the reflexes as the clue.

steps.detail: Three keep working on potassium alone.
Hyperactive reflexes are not a low potassium finding.
Malnutrition and alcohol use point to low magnesium.

elimination.verdict: Request a magnesium level.

questions.stem: A patient on a psychiatric unit drinks water constantly. This afternoon he has a headache and is newly confused. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the as-needed acetaminophen for headache
options.rationale: Treats a symptom and hides a neurologic change that needs explaining.

options.text: Request a serum sodium level
options.rationale: Constant water drinking dilutes sodium. Headache and new confusion mean brain cells may be swelling.

options.text: Measure lying and standing blood pressures
options.rationale: An assessment, and a tempting one. It looks for a fluid deficit, and his problem is too much water.

options.text: Offer a sports drink in place of water
options.rationale: Still adds fluid to a patient who is already water loaded.

questions.takeaway: Psychiatric polydipsia causes water intoxication and dilutional hyponatremia. A headache with new confusion is the brain's warning.
questions.strategy: Two options gather data. Pick the one that tests the problem his intake predicts.

steps.action: Name the risk from the cue
steps.detail: Too much water dilutes sodium.
Acetaminophen answers the headache and nothing else.
Orthostatic pressures look for low volume. Sodium looks for dilution.

elimination.verdict: Request a sodium level.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients with fluid or electrolyte problems. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Fluid overload, crackles in both bases, sitting upright after furosemide
options.rationale: Tempting because it is breathing. The crackles are expected for overload and treatment is already working on them.

options.text: Potassium 3.2 mEq/L on furosemide, pulse newly irregular
options.rationale: A new irregular pulse means the low potassium has reached the heart. It is the only finding that is new and not yet treated.

options.text: Calcium 7.8 mg/dL, tingling fingers, IV calcium now infusing
options.rationale: Tingling is the expected early sign and the treatment is running. No airway or spasm finding is reported.

options.text: Fluid deficit, heart rate 112, first fluid bolus now infusing
options.rationale: A fast heart rate is the expected response to low volume and the bolus is addressing it.

questions.takeaway: Rank by what is new and untreated. An expected finding under treatment waits behind a change in heart rhythm.
questions.strategy: All four sound unstable. Ask of each one: is this what the condition normally looks like, and is something already being done?

steps.detail: Crackles in overload, tingling in low calcium, a fast pulse in fluid deficit.
Furosemide, calcium and the bolus are all running.
A pulse that became irregular with a low potassium.

elimination.verdict: The patient with the newly irregular pulse. A rhythm change is circulation and it is new.

questions.stem: After IV furosemide for fluid overload, a patient's crackles have cleared and his weight is down 2.5 kg. He felt lightheaded when he sat up. His next dose is due in 6 hours. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Encourage extra oral fluids for the rest of the shift
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats a deficit. It guesses at the problem in a patient who was overloaded yesterday.

options.text: Document the clear lungs and weight loss as the expected response
options.rationale: Two findings fit a good result. The lightheadedness does not, and charting past it misses a possible overshoot.

options.text: Ask the provider to lower the furosemide dose
options.rationale: May be the outcome. The provider will ask for the pressures, and the nurse has time to get them before the dose is due.

options.text: Measure his blood pressure lying, sitting and standing
options.rationale: Lightheadedness after a 2.5 L loss suggests he may now be dry. Orthostatic pressures turn a vague report into a finding the nurse can act on and report.

questions.takeaway: A treatment can overshoot. When one finding does not fit a good result and nothing is urgent, measure it before you treat or call.
questions.strategy: Two findings say improved and one does not fit. He is in bed and the next dose is hours away, so there is time to assess.

steps.detail: Lightheaded on sitting up does not belong with a good result.
He is not about to walk and the dose is 6 hours away.

steps.action: Choose between treating, calling and measuring
steps.detail: Fluids and a dose change both assume a deficit. Orthostatic pressures confirm it.

elimination.verdict: Measure orthostatic blood pressure first, then report.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure had an intake of 1,400 mL and a recorded output of 2,300 mL yesterday. On the same scale before breakfast, he weighs 1.2 kg more. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: He is retaining fluid despite the recorded output
options.rationale: A 1.2 kg overnight gain is about 1.2 L of fluid. Weight measured the same way each day is more reliable than an intake and output record.

options.text: The furosemide is working because output exceeded intake
options.rationale: This is what the numbers on the record say. Records miss intake such as IV flushes and food fluids, and the scale contradicts them.

options.text: The scale reading is likely an error, so reweigh tomorrow
options.rationale: Reasonable if the method had changed. The stem says same scale, same time, so the reading stands.

options.text: The gain reflects food and stool and is expected
options.rationale: Solid weight does not change by more than a kilogram overnight. A sudden change is fluid.

questions.takeaway: Daily weight is the best single measure of fluid status. When weight and the intake and output record disagree, believe the weight.
questions.strategy: Two measures conflict. Decide which one is more reliable, then check whether the stem gives any reason to doubt it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Output higher than intake, yet weight is up.
Same scale, before breakfast. No reason to doubt it.
1.2 kg is about 1.2 L retained.

elimination.verdict: He is retaining fluid. The scale outranks the record.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney disease who missed dialysis reports leg weakness and tingling. The monitor shows tall peaked T waves. The potassium result is pending. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Hold his scheduled lisinopril and spironolactone doses
options.rationale: Correct, since both raise potassium. Holding them prevents more rise and does nothing for the heart right now.

options.text: Ask the laboratory to run the potassium result first
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is not back. The ECG has already shown the effect on the heart, so waiting for the number delays treatment.

options.text: Report the rhythm now and prepare IV calcium
options.rationale: Peaked T waves are the heart's response to high potassium. The cue is enough to act on, and calcium protects the heart while the level is lowered.

options.text: Give the prescribed patiromer earlier than scheduled
options.rationale: A binder removes potassium over hours. It is part of the plan and too slow for an ECG change.

questions.takeaway: An ECG change from potassium is treated as an emergency on the cue, without waiting for the lab value.
questions.strategy: Every option belongs in this patient's care. Ask which one protects the heart in the next few minutes.

steps.detail: Missed dialysis, weakness, tingling and peaked T waves point to high potassium.

steps.action: Decide whether more data is needed
steps.detail: The monitor already shows cardiac effect.
Holding drugs and binders work over hours. Calcium works in minutes.

elimination.verdict: Report the rhythm and prepare IV calcium. Circulation first, the cause after.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with fluid volume deficit has received 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride. Blood pressure rose from 88/50 to 112/68, urine output is 50 mL per hour, and she has a new cough. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue the current rate until the bag is finished
options.rationale: The pressure and urine output say the deficit is corrected, which is the reason to stop pushing fluid.

options.text: Slow the infusion and listen to her lungs
options.rationale: A new cough after 2 L in an older adult is an early sign of overload. The goal is met, so reduce the fluid and assess breathing.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the IV catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because the fluid is the cause. She has not been assessed yet, and removing the catheter gives up the access she may need for a diuretic.

options.text: Request a chest x-ray before changing the rate
options.rationale: Imaging may follow. The nurse can slow the fluid and auscultate now without waiting for a result.

questions.takeaway: When the goal of fluid replacement is met, the next risk is too much. In older adults a new cough is the quiet first sign.
questions.strategy: Two findings show the therapy worked. One small finding is new. Ask what that finding means in someone who just received 2 L.

steps.detail: Pressure up, urine above 30 mL per hour.
Fluid moving into the lungs in an older heart.
Slowing cuts the fluid and keeps the line. Then the lungs tell you what comes next.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion and listen to her lungs.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with presbycusis does not respond when the nurse gives discharge instructions from the doorway. His reading glasses are at home. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Sit facing him at eye level with the light on the nurse's face
options.rationale: Correct. He needs to see the speaker's face, and this fixes the distance and the lighting at once.

options.text: Hand him the printed discharge instructions to read
options.rationale: Tempting, because written information is a real strategy for hearing loss. Without his reading glasses he cannot use it.

options.text: Repeat the instructions from the doorway in a louder voice
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and raises the pitch he hears worst.

options.text: Give the instructions to his daughter by telephone
options.rationale: This goes around him. He is able to learn once the nurse communicates the right way.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss: get close, face the client, put the light on your face, speak slowly in a lower pitch.
questions.strategy: Written material is a good answer only when the client can see it. The missing glasses are the detail that decides.

steps.action: Cut the option that goes around him
steps.detail: The phone call to the daughter leaves him out.
Shouting distorts sound.
No reading glasses removes the printed sheet.

elimination.verdict: Sit facing him at eye level in good light.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old medical coder has burning eyes and blurred vision by midafternoon on workdays. Her eye exam last month was normal. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Raise the screen brightness and sit closer to it
options.rationale: More brightness and a shorter distance add to the strain.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: The pattern fits digital eyestrain, and the 20-20-20 rule rests the focusing muscles through the day.

options.text: Schedule another eye exam to check for new glasses
options.rationale: Tempting because blur suggests a refractive change, but her exam a month ago was normal.

options.text: Wear tinted glasses indoors during the afternoon
options.rationale: Tinted lenses do not rest the eyes from close focus.

questions.takeaway: Eyestrain that follows the workday and clears with rest is managed with the 20-20-20 rule.
questions.strategy: Use the timing. Symptoms that build over a day of screen work and a normal recent exam point to habit, not disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Workdays, midafternoon, screen job.
A repeat exam would find nothing new.

steps.action: Pick the measure that rests the eyes
steps.detail: Regular distance breaks.

elimination.verdict: The 20-20-20 rule.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old on bed rest for 8 days became confused about the date. The nurse added a large clock, family photos and scheduled visits. Which finding shows the plan is working?

options.text: He lies quietly and has stopped using the call light
options.rationale: Looks calm, but a quiet client who stops calling may be withdrawing further.

options.text: He watches television from breakfast until bedtime
options.rationale: More stimulation is not the same as meaningful stimulation, and it does not show orientation.

options.text: He names the day and the people in the photos
options.rationale: Orientation has returned and he is responding to stimuli that mean something to him.

options.text: He follows directions when the nurse repositions him
options.rationale: He could do that while still disoriented to time.

questions.takeaway: Sensory deprivation is treated with meaningful stimuli. You evaluate it by orientation and engagement.
questions.strategy: Match the outcome to the problem. The problem was confusion about the date, so look for the option that shows orientation.

steps.detail: Disorientation from too little meaningful input.

steps.action: Cut calm that is not engagement
steps.detail: Lying quietly and following directions do not show orientation.
A television left on is quantity, not quality.

elimination.verdict: Names the day and the people in the photos.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with new vision loss in both eyes has stopped going to her card group and has tripped twice this week on her back step. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Refer her to a low vision support group
options.rationale: Helpful for isolation, and it can follow once she is safe at home.

options.text: Explore how she feels about losing her sight
options.rationale: Therapeutic and important, but feelings rank below an injury that is already happening.

options.text: Arrange a ride so she can rejoin the card group
options.rationale: Addresses socialization, which is a real problem and not the most urgent one.

options.text: Mark the step edge and have a handrail secured
options.rationale: She has already tripped twice, so the fall hazard is an actual problem and safety comes first.

questions.takeaway: With sensory loss, risk for injury outranks socialization and coping. An actual hazard is fixed first.
questions.strategy: All four help her. Ask which problem has already caused harm this week.

steps.detail: Isolation, grief and falls.
Two trips on the same step.
Contrast on the edge and a secure rail.

elimination.verdict: Mark the step and secure a handrail.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with a hearing aid has answered several questions incorrectly this morning. Which task does the nurse assign to the assistive personnel?

options.text: Clean the hearing aid, check the battery and reinsert it
options.rationale: Correct. Routine care of an assistive device is a standard task with a predictable result.

options.text: Find out why the client is answering incorrectly
options.rationale: Working out the cause is assessment, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Teach the client how to tell when the battery is low
options.rationale: Teaching is the nurse's responsibility.

options.text: Decide whether a writing board would work better for this client
options.rationale: Choosing a communication method takes nursing judgment.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel care for the device. The nurse assesses, teaches and decides.
questions.strategy: Look at the verbs. Find out, teach and decide belong to the nurse. Clean and check can be delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find out, teach and decide are judgment.
Cleaning and checking a battery follows fixed steps.

elimination.verdict: Clean the aid, check the battery and reinsert it.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old with diabetic retinopathy lives alone and can no longer read the markings on her insulin syringe. She wants to keep managing her own insulin. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Arrange for a neighbor to draw up and give each dose
options.rationale: This is safe, and it takes away the independence she asked to keep.

options.text: Teach her to use an insulin pen with audible dose clicks
options.rationale: Correct. It replaces the lost visual cue with sound, so she stays safe and stays independent.

options.text: Have her daughter prefill a week of syringes on each visit
options.rationale: Tempting and sometimes used. She still depends on someone else and cannot adjust a dose herself.

options.text: Advise her to use a brighter overhead kitchen light
options.rationale: More light can add glare and does not make fine markings readable with retinal damage.

questions.takeaway: Adapt the task to the senses that still work. Keep the client as independent as safety allows.
questions.strategy: Two options are safe. The stem says she lives alone and wants to do it herself, and that picks the one that keeps her in charge.

steps.action: Cut the option that does not fix the problem
steps.detail: Bright light does not restore fine vision.
A neighbor or daughter makes her dependent.
She wants to manage her own insulin.

elimination.verdict: The insulin pen with audible clicks.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old says she cannot tell where her feet are when she walks to the bathroom at night. Which statement shows the home safety teaching was effective?

options.text: "I keep the hall dark so I fall back asleep faster."
options.rationale: In the dark she loses the one sense that can stand in for position sense.

options.text: "I wear thick cushioned socks so my steps are softer."
options.rationale: Sounds protective, but padding dulls what her feet can still feel and socks slip.

options.text: "I walk there quickly so I am up for less time."
options.rationale: Tempting as less time at risk. Hurrying with poor position sense makes a misstep more likely.

options.text: "I leave a hall light on and hold the handrail."
options.rationale: Position sense declines after 60, so she replaces it with vision and a secure rail.

questions.takeaway: When a sense declines, safety depends on replacing it with another cue, such as light and a handrail, not on being careful with the sense that is fading.
questions.strategy: Ask of each statement: does it give her another way to know where her feet are?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position sense in the feet, an expected change after 60.
A dark hall and padded socks.
Speed does not replace a sense.
Light and a handrail.

elimination.verdict: The hall light and handrail statement.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic pain on a step-down unit is restless and cannot focus. Staff enter hourly at night for separate vital signs, laboratory draws and repositioning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request a prescription for a medication to help him sleep
options.rationale: Tempting, because he is not resting. A drug adds another factor that alters perception and leaves the cause in place.

options.text: Request transfer to a private room at the end of the hall
options.rationale: Tempting, because it lowers noise. The interruptions come from the care schedule and would follow him.

options.text: Combine the night tasks and schedule protected rest periods
options.rationale: Correct. The stem names the cause, hourly separate entries, and clustering care removes it.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time at every entry
options.rationale: Reorientation helps confusion. Doing it at every entry adds more stimulation.

questions.takeaway: Sensory overload: combine activities, schedule rest, set quiet time. Fix the environment before adding a drug.
questions.strategy: Find the cause in the stem. It is the schedule, not the room and not the client.

steps.detail: Hourly separate entries at night.
Reorienting at every entry is more stimulation.

steps.action: Test the room and the drug
steps.detail: Neither one changes how often staff walk in.

elimination.verdict: Combine the tasks and protect rest periods.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with macular degeneration says she manages her medications fine at home. Which assessment best tells the nurse whether that is safe?

options.text: Have her read a pill bottle label and set up a dose
options.rationale: Functional ability is judged by watching the task itself, here reading a label and preparing a dose.

options.text: Measure her visual acuity with a Snellen chart
options.rationale: Gives a number for distance vision, which does not show whether she can read a label.

options.text: Ask her daughter how she has been managing her pills at home
options.rationale: Useful background, but it is secondhand and the client is able to show the nurse directly.

options.text: Review the eye clinic's most recent examination
options.rationale: Describes the disease, not how she functions with it.

questions.takeaway: Assess function by watching the client do the task. A chart result or a report from someone else does not replace that.
questions.strategy: Three options describe her vision. One tests the thing the nurse needs to know.

steps.detail: Can she take medications safely?
Acuity, records and family report.
Label and dose in front of the nurse.

elimination.verdict: Watch her read the label and set up a dose.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old carpenter has ringing in his ears after work, and testing shows mild high frequency hearing loss. He says the damage is already done. Which teaching is the priority?

options.text: Have his hearing tested again each year
options.rationale: Tempting and worthwhile, but testing only measures loss. It does not prevent it.

options.text: Wear ear protection every time the saws are running
options.rationale: Noise damage is permanent and keeps adding up, so protection at every exposure prevents further loss.

options.text: Ask about a hearing aid for the loss he has
options.rationale: Mild loss does not need a device yet, and an aid does not stop more damage.

options.text: Rest in a quiet room for an hour after every work shift
options.rationale: Eases the ringing without reducing the exposure that causes it.

questions.takeaway: Noise related hearing loss cannot be reversed. The nurse's priority is prevention of more loss with consistent protection.
questions.strategy: Screening and prevention both sound right. Ask which one changes what happens to his hearing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More exposure means more loss.
A yearly test only records it.
Protection at each exposure.

elimination.verdict: Ear protection at every exposure.

questions.stem: The nurse taught the wife of a 66-year-old with expressive aphasia how to communicate with him. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: She finishes his sentences when he pauses
options.rationale: This takes away his chance to speak and raises frustration.

options.text: She speaks louder and repeats each question twice
options.rationale: His hearing and understanding are intact. Volume does not help him produce words.

options.text: She asks whether he wants tea, then waits for his nod
options.rationale: Correct. A yes or no question with time to answer lets him communicate with what he still has.

options.text: She points to objects and asks him to name each one
options.rationale: Naming on demand is the hardest task for him and turns conversation into a test.

questions.takeaway: Expressive aphasia: listen patiently, ask yes or no questions, use a board, allow time.
questions.strategy: Ask which option lowers the amount of speech he has to produce and gives him time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the options that speak for him
steps.detail: Finishing his sentences.

steps.action: Cut the options that treat the wrong problem
steps.detail: Loud speech treats hearing loss.
Naming objects demands the skill he lost.

elimination.verdict: A yes or no question, then waiting.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old who wears contact lenses was taught lens care after an eye irritation. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I rinse them with tap water if I run out of solution."
options.rationale: Tap water is not sterile and carries organisms to the cornea.

options.text: "I top off the solution in the case each night."
options.rationale: Sounds thrifty and careful, but old solution loses its disinfecting effect.

options.text: "I keep them in if my eye is only a little red."
options.rationale: A red eye is the signal to remove the lenses, not to wait.

options.text: "I take them out before I sleep or swim."
options.rationale: Removing lenses for sleep and water keeps organisms from being trapped against the cornea.

questions.takeaway: Proper contact lens care is prevention. Lenses come out for sleep, water and any redness.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that reduces contact between the cornea and organisms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tap water rinse.
Topping off.
Redness means remove them.

elimination.verdict: Out before sleep or swimming.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old arrives on the unit at night, and the emergency department reports him as confused because he answers questions inappropriately. His daughter is at the bedside with his belongings. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Start a bed alarm and move him near the nurses' station
options.rationale: Tempting, because safety matters for a confused client. The cause is not known yet, and the answer may be in the bag of belongings.

options.text: Ask the daughter whether he uses hearing aids or glasses
options.rationale: Correct. Establishing the baseline comes first, and an uncorrected hearing deficit looks like confusion.

options.text: Request a prescription for a urinalysis and blood work
options.rationale: Reasonable if the confusion is real. A quick baseline check comes before testing.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time every hour
options.rationale: Reorientation does not help a client who cannot hear it.

questions.takeaway: In acute care, establish the baseline. Know whether the client already has a deficit before you label the behavior.
questions.strategy: Here the assessment is not done. The daughter and the belongings are the stem's way of telling you where to look.

steps.detail: Only that his answers do not match the questions.
Asking about hearing aids and glasses.
Alarm, laboratory work and reorientation all assume the confusion is real.

elimination.verdict: Ask the daughter about hearing aids and glasses.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old received his first hearing aid. Which statement shows he understood the teaching?

options.text: "At bedtime I will take it out, turn it off and open the battery door."
options.rationale: Correct. This saves the battery and lets moisture dry out.

options.text: "I will leave it in while I shower so I can hear the smoke alarm."
options.rationale: Water damages the aid. A flashing alert system covers alarm safety.

options.text: "I will put it in before I use hairspray so it stays in place."
options.rationale: Spray clogs the microphone. It goes in after hair products.

options.text: "If it whistles I will turn the volume up until it stops."
options.rationale: Whistling means poor fit or too much volume. Turning it up makes it worse.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aid care: keep it dry, off and open at night, in after hair products, reseat it if it whistles.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against two enemies of a hearing aid: moisture and blockage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The shower.
Hairspray on the aid.
More volume increases feedback.

elimination.verdict: Out, off and battery door open at bedtime.

questions.stem: An 87-year-old with cataracts becomes agitated at dusk and tries to climb out of bed. The room is dim and her glasses are on the windowsill. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and raise all side rails
options.rationale: Tempting, because she is trying to get up. An alarm reports the attempt and does nothing about why she is frightened, and four rails act as a restraint.

options.text: Request a prescription for a sitter overnight
options.rationale: A sitter may be needed later. A simpler step has not been tried.

options.text: Turn on soft lighting and put her glasses on
options.rationale: Correct. Aging pupils and cataracts need more light, and the stem shows both the light and the glasses are missing.

options.text: Request a prescription for a low dose sedative
options.rationale: A sedative adds fall risk and clouds perception further.

questions.takeaway: Older eyes adapt poorly to the dark. Correct the light and the device before using alarms, sitters or drugs.
questions.strategy: Use the least restrictive fix that matches the cause. The stem gives the cause in its second sentence.

steps.detail: Dim room, no glasses.
Light and glasses, then alarm, then sitter, then sedative.

steps.action: Start at the bottom of that list
steps.detail: It also treats the cause.

elimination.verdict: Soft lighting and her glasses.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with muffled hearing and ear fullness had impacted cerumen removed by irrigation. Which finding best shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: He denies pain in the ear
options.rationale: He had no pain before. This shows no harm, not benefit.

options.text: He reports no dizziness or nausea after the procedure
options.rationale: This means he tolerated the irrigation. It says nothing about his hearing.

options.text: The return fluid ran clear at the end
options.rationale: Clear return suggests the wax is out. It does not confirm that function returned.

options.text: He repeats words the nurse whispers from 2 feet away
options.rationale: Correct. The problem was conductive hearing loss, so restored hearing is the outcome that counts.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate by the problem you treated. Cerumen impaction is a correctable conductive loss, so check hearing.
questions.strategy: Separate three ideas: the procedure went safely, the wax came out, the hearing came back. The question asks about the third.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Muffled hearing.
No pain and no dizziness.
Clear return is about the wax. Whispered words are about the client.

elimination.verdict: He repeats whispered words.

questions.stem: An 89-year-old began an opioid and a sleeping pill 2 nights ago. She now misjudges the distance to her chair and reaches for objects that are not there. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request an eye examination for new glasses
options.rationale: Tempting because the problem looks visual, but vision does not change in two nights without a cause.

options.text: Review the two new medications with the provider
options.rationale: The change is new and began with drugs known to alter perception, so the cause is addressed first.

options.text: Place a clock and calendar and reorient her
options.rationale: Right for deprivation. Her cues began with new medications, not with too little stimulation.

options.text: Explain to the family that perception declines with age
options.rationale: A new change is not assumed to be aging.

questions.takeaway: Opioids and psychotropic drugs can impair perception. A new sensory change is traced to its cause before it is called aging.
questions.strategy: Use the timing. What started 2 nights ago?

steps.detail: Two nights, not years.
Opioid and sleeping pill started then.

steps.action: Cut the fixes for other causes
steps.detail: Glasses, reorientation, reassurance.

elimination.verdict: Review the new medications with the provider.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with both eyes patched after a chemical splash is admitted. His hearing is normal. Which actions does the nurse include in his care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Describe the room layout and let him touch the call bell
options.rationale: Touch and description replace sight. He must be able to find the call bell without help.

options.text: Keep his water, tissues and telephone in the same places
options.rationale: A consistent layout is what lets him move safely on his own.

options.text: Say who you are on entering and say when you are leaving
options.rationale: He cannot see who came in or whether anyone is still there.

options.text: Speak louder and more slowly than usual
options.rationale: His hearing is intact. Speak in a normal voice.

options.text: Move the furniture each shift to suit the staff workflow
options.rationale: Every change in layout erases the map he has learned.

questions.takeaway: Sudden vision loss: orient fully, keep things in the same place, announce yourself, speak normally.
questions.strategy: Judge each option alone. Ask whether it helps a person who can hear and cannot see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Touch, description, announcing and a fixed layout.

steps.action: Cut the option that treats the wrong sense
steps.detail: Loud, slow speech is for hearing loss.
Moving furniture.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.nursesNote: 0900: 82-year-old admitted 2 days ago with heart failure. Needs a brighter lamp to read the menu. Has trouble telling the blue cup from the green one. Misses high pitched voices in conversation. Says the left ear "went quiet" when she woke today. Started IV furosemide yesterday. Unsteady when standing this morning, steady yesterday.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up and should not be attributed to aging.

segments.text: Needs a brighter lamp to read the menu
segments.rationale: Aging pupils dilate less, so more light is needed. Expected.

segments.text: Has trouble telling the blue cup from the green one
segments.rationale: Blue and green discrimination declines with age. Expected.

segments.text: Misses high pitched voices in conversation
segments.rationale: High frequencies are lost first in presbycusis. Expected and gradual.

segments.text: Says the left ear "went quiet" when she woke today
segments.rationale: Sudden hearing loss in one ear is new, not aging. It needs prompt evaluation.

segments.text: Started IV furosemide yesterday
segments.rationale: A loop diuretic is ototoxic, and the timing fits the new hearing loss. The provider needs to know.

segments.text: Unsteady when standing this morning, steady yesterday
segments.rationale: A new balance change with an ear change raises fall risk and points to the inner ear.

questions.takeaway: Gradual and both sides is aging. Sudden, one sided or new since yesterday is reported, and you look for an ototoxic drug.
questions.strategy: For each finding ask whether it came on slowly over years or appeared since admission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More light, blue and green, high pitches.
The left ear and the new unsteadiness.
The diuretic started the day before.

elimination.verdict: Left ear went quiet, IV furosemide, new unsteadiness.

questions.scenario: A 61-year-old in the emergency department observation unit for 30 hours was restless and anxious with racing thoughts. The nurse lowered alarm volumes, combined care tasks and set quiet time. Six hours later the nurse reassesses.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the plan to reduce sensory overload was effective or not effective.

rows.text: Naps for 90 minutes without interruption in the afternoon
rows.rationale: Protected rest is the goal of clustered care and quiet time.

rows.text: Picks at his IV dressing and tubing
rows.rationale: Playing with tubes and dressings is a behavior of overload that is still present.

rows.text: Follows a 10 minute teaching session and asks relevant questions
rows.rationale: Attention is no longer scattered.

rows.text: Needs reorientation each time staff enter
rows.rationale: Constant reorientation shows his brain is still not sorting the input.

rows.text: States the alarms no longer startle him since the volume was lowered
rows.rationale: The stimulus was reduced and he reports the change himself.

questions.takeaway: Overload resolves as rest, focused attention and leaving equipment alone. Picking at tubes and repeated reorientation mean it continues.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with how he looked before: restless, anxious, scattered. Better or the same?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark rest and focus as improvement
steps.detail: The nap, the teaching session and his own report.
Picking at tubing and needing reorientation.

elimination.verdict: Effective, not effective, effective, not effective, effective.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse reviews four messages. Which client does the nurse call first?

options.text: Cataract surgery yesterday, eye itchy with slightly blurred vision
options.rationale: Itching and mild blurring are expected early; best vision takes weeks.

options.text: Meniere disease, vomiting during a spinning attack since morning
options.rationale: Dramatic and miserable, and expected for an attack. She needs safety and antiemetics, not emergency care.

options.text: Cataract surgery yesterday, worsening pain in that eye with nausea
options.rationale: Pain with nausea after eye surgery suggests rising pressure in the eye and must be reported at once.

options.text: Open-angle glaucoma, halos and narrowing side vision for months
options.rationale: Real damage, and gradual. It is chronic and needs follow-up, not a call first.

questions.takeaway: After eye surgery, pain with nausea is never expected. Acute and unexpected beats chronic and dramatic.
questions.strategy: Two clients had the same surgery. Compare their symptoms against what is expected the day after.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Months of halos is not new.
Vomiting with vertigo fits Meniere disease.
Itching is expected. Worsening pain with nausea is not.

elimination.verdict: The surgical client with worsening pain and nausea.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old with expressive aphasia grimaces and holds his abdomen. An as-needed analgesic is prescribed for his knee pain. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the as-needed analgesic and reassess within the hour
options.rationale: Defensible because he is clearly in pain. The site is new and unassessed, and the drug was ordered for his knee.

options.text: Ask his wife what she thinks he is feeling
options.rationale: She knows him well, but her guess replaces his own report when he can still answer.

options.text: Wait at the bedside until he finds the words
options.rationale: Patience is part of aphasia care. On its own it delays assessment of a new pain.

options.text: Ask yes or no questions about the pain with a board
options.rationale: The assessment is not done yet. Yes or no questions and a board let him tell the nurse where and what the pain is.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia changes how you assess, not whether you assess. Use yes or no questions and a board before treating a new complaint.
questions.strategy: Treating the grimace feels kind. Check whether the nurse knows what is being treated.

steps.detail: Abdomen now, analgesic ordered for the knee.
Location and type of pain are unknown.

steps.action: Pick the method that fits aphasia
steps.detail: Yes or no questions and pictures.

elimination.verdict: Assess the pain with yes or no questions and a picture board.

questions.stem: An older adult with long-standing cataracts and presbycusis ate from only the right half of his tray at lunch and walked into the left door frame. Yesterday he did neither. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Assess him now for other new changes
options.rationale: A one-sided change since yesterday is new and unexplained, so the nurse assesses before adapting the room.

options.text: Put his glasses on and brighten the room
options.rationale: The usual first step for his known deficits and tempting here. Cataracts blur the whole field gradually, not one side overnight.

options.text: Have the tray and call bell placed on his right
options.rationale: A sensible adaptation that accepts the change without finding out why it happened.

options.text: Document the change as progression of his cataracts
options.rationale: Cataract change is slow and painless over months.

questions.takeaway: A new or sudden sensory change is never assumed to be the old problem getting worse. Assess it.
questions.strategy: Compare the finding with what his known conditions do. Gradual and whole field does not match sudden and one-sided.

steps.detail: Different from yesterday.
Left side only.
Cataracts and aging do not act this way.

elimination.verdict: Assess him now for other new changes.

questions.stem: A client with hearing loss nodded and said yes throughout insulin pen teaching. The nurse sat facing him in good light and spoke slowly. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Give him the steps in writing to take home
options.rationale: Defensible because written information supports hearing loss. It reinforces the teaching without showing whether he understood.

options.text: Have him show the steps with the pen
options.rationale: Nodding is not understanding. A return demonstration is the only way to evaluate what he took in.

options.text: Repeat the teaching with his better ear toward the nurse
options.rationale: A good technique, but the delivery was already sound and the gap is evaluation.

options.text: Document that the teaching was done and understood
options.rationale: A nod is a social response and many people with hearing loss nod to avoid asking again.

questions.takeaway: With hearing loss, agreement is not evidence. Evaluate teaching by having the client show or explain it back.
questions.strategy: The nurse already communicated well. Ask which nursing process step is still missing.

steps.detail: Facing, lit and slow were all done.
Evaluation.
Supports learning, does not measure it.

elimination.verdict: Have him demonstrate the steps.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease follows a low-sodium diet and takes a diuretic. She reports fewer vertigo attacks this month, and says she twice dropped to the floor with no dizziness beforehand. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Reinforce the plan because the attacks have decreased
options.rationale: Fewer attacks is real progress. The two falls show a new and more dangerous problem.

options.text: Teach her to sit down when dizziness begins
options.rationale: Standard teaching for vertigo. These falls came with no warning, so there is nothing to act on.

options.text: Report the falls and add fall precautions
options.rationale: Sudden falls without warning are drop attacks. They mark a serious safety risk that the current plan does not cover.

options.text: Refer her for balance exercises with therapy
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation helps balance and tempts. It does not prevent a sudden drop with no warning.

questions.takeaway: Fewer vertigo attacks does not mean safer. Falls without warning in Meniere disease are drop attacks and change the safety plan.
questions.strategy: The good news comes first in the stem. Read to the end and ask what the falls had in common.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fewer vertigo attacks.
Two falls with no dizziness first.
Sitting when dizzy needs a warning she does not get.

elimination.verdict: Report and add fall precautions.

questions.stem: An alert 44-year-old with mild dehydration from a stomach virus vomits each time he drinks a full cup of oral rehydration solution. An as-needed antiemetic is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antiemetic, then offer small frequent sips
options.rationale: He is alert and can swallow, so the oral route still fits. Treating the vomiting and shrinking the volume lets him keep the fluid down.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV fluids
options.rationale: Tempting because he is not keeping fluids down. The dehydration is mild and the cause has a prescribed treatment that has not been tried.

options.text: Wait until the nausea passes, then offer another cup
options.rationale: The deficit grows while the nurse waits, and a full cup is what triggered the vomiting.

options.text: Switch from rehydration solution to plain water
options.rationale: Water replaces no electrolytes, and the volume is the trigger, not the type of fluid.

questions.takeaway: Dehydration care includes treating the cause. Use the prescribed antiemetic and small volumes before moving an alert patient to the IV route.
questions.strategy: IV fluids and the antiemetic both address the problem. Mild dehydration and an untried prescription tip it to the less invasive choice.

steps.detail: Alert and able to swallow. Only tolerance is missing.
An antiemetic and smaller volumes.
More invasive, and not yet needed for a mild deficit.

elimination.verdict: Give the antiemetic and offer small sips.

questions.stem: One hour after regular insulin with dextrose for a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L, a patient is sweaty, shaky and anxious. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a repeat serum potassium level
options.rationale: Tempting because rebound hypokalemia is a watch item. Low potassium causes weakness and a slow gut, not sweating and shaking.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV calcium
options.rationale: Calcium protects the heart from high potassium. It does nothing for these new findings.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose
options.rationale: Sweaty, shaky and anxious after insulin points to hypoglycemia. A bedside glucose takes seconds and directs the treatment.

options.text: Give the next scheduled dose of patiromer
options.rationale: A binder removes potassium over hours. It does nothing for what is happening to him now.

questions.takeaway: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can drop the glucose with it. Watch for hypoglycemia and rebound hypokalemia during treatment.
questions.strategy: Match the new findings to the drug that was just given. Two complications are possible; the symptoms tell you which one.

steps.detail: The change came one hour after insulin.
Low glucose is sweaty and shaky. Low potassium is weak and limp.

steps.action: Pick the fastest check that directs care
steps.detail: A fingerstick glucose.

elimination.verdict: Check the glucose first.

questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer has a calcium of 11.9 mg/dL. Which scheduled item does the nurse hold and clarify with the provider?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusion
options.rationale: Fits. Saline helps the kidneys flush calcium out.

options.text: Oral hydrochlorothiazide
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics make the kidneys keep calcium, so this one is stopped in hypercalcemia.

options.text: IV furosemide
options.rationale: Fits, and it is the tempting choice because it is also a diuretic. Loop diuretics help excrete calcium.

options.text: Subcutaneous calcitonin
options.rationale: Fits. It slows the release of calcium from bone.

questions.takeaway: In hypercalcemia, loop diuretics help and thiazides hurt. Stop every calcium source and anything that makes the kidneys hold calcium.
questions.strategy: Two options are diuretics. They do opposite things to calcium, so decide which one keeps it.

steps.detail: You want the item that does not belong.
Saline, furosemide and calcitonin all lower it.
Loop flushes calcium. Thiazide holds it.

elimination.verdict: Hold the hydrochlorothiazide.

questions.stem: A patient with a calcium of 12.6 mg/dL has received IV 0.9% sodium chloride and furosemide since yesterday. Which finding best indicates the calcium is coming down?

options.text: Urine output of 200 mL per hour
options.rationale: Tempting because the plan depends on flushing calcium out. It shows the drugs are producing urine, not that the calcium effect on the body has eased.

options.text: Heart rate has slowed from 96 to 54
options.rationale: A slowing heart is the severe, prolonged picture of high calcium. This is worsening.

options.text: Patient sleeps most of the day but wakes to voice
options.rationale: Lethargy is a high calcium finding. More sleep is not improvement.

options.text: Bowel sounds are active and the patient is alert
options.rationale: High calcium slows the gut and dulls the mind. Return of bowel sounds and alertness shows the excitability is recovering.

questions.takeaway: High calcium slows everything: heart, muscles, mind and gut. Improvement looks like those systems waking back up.
questions.strategy: Separate proof that the drug is acting from proof that the patient is better. The outcome is in the patient.

steps.detail: Slow gut, weakness, lethargy, slowing heart.

steps.action: Remove findings that match high calcium
steps.detail: A heart rate of 54 and more sleeping are the problem itself.

steps.action: Compare output with the body response
steps.detail: Urine shows the mechanism. Bowel sounds and alertness show the result.

elimination.verdict: Active bowel sounds and a more alert patient.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old who takes furosemide and a daily laxative is seen during morning rounds. Which finding requires follow-up?

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand tents when pinched
options.rationale: Aging skin tents on the hand even when hydrated. Turgor is checked at the sternum.

options.text: She cannot state the day but could yesterday
options.rationale: Acute confusion may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance in an older adult. Both of her drugs waste fluid and electrolytes.

options.text: She says she is not thirsty this morning
options.rationale: Tempting because poor intake matters. A weak thirst reflex is an expected aging change, so the nurse offers fluids on a schedule rather than reporting it.

options.text: She voided 350 mL of yellow urine overnight
options.rationale: An adequate amount with a normal color. Concern starts below 500 mL in a full day.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion is a change in condition. Check fluid status and labs before blaming age or dementia.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected with aging or new for this patient. Only the new one needs follow up.

steps.detail: Hand tenting and weak thirst.

steps.action: Check the urine against the threshold
steps.detail: 350 mL overnight is not low.
Oriented yesterday, not today.

elimination.verdict: The new disorientation.

questions.stem: The evening after a thyroidectomy, a patient who reported tingling lips now makes a high-pitched sound with each breath in. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Tap the cheek to check for facial twitching
options.rationale: More assessment, and tempting. The airway is already narrowing, so the time for bedside signs has passed.

options.text: Request a stat serum calcium level
options.rationale: Useful later. A lab draw does not open an airway.

options.text: Give the scheduled oral calcium dose early
options.rationale: Too slow, and swallowing is unsafe with stridor.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Stridor after thyroid surgery means laryngospasm from low calcium. She needs airway help and IV calcium now.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium after neck surgery can close the airway. Tingling is the warning; stridor is the emergency.
questions.strategy: Assess first is the reflex. Here the stem has already done the assessing, so act on the airway.

steps.detail: A high-pitched sound on breathing in is stridor.
Tingling plus stridor is enough to act.
Only the response team protects the airway now.

elimination.verdict: Call the rapid response team.

questions.stem: A patient with celiac disease and chronic diarrhea has a calcium of 8.1 mg/dL. Which findings does the nurse report as signs the low calcium is affecting nerves and muscles? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tingling around the lips
options.rationale: Nerves are firing too easily. This is the early sign.

options.text: One side of the face twitches when the cheek is tapped
options.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign.

options.text: Knee jerk reflexes are absent
options.rationale: Absent reflexes mean slowed nerves, as in high magnesium or high calcium.

options.text: Bowel sounds are hypoactive
options.rationale: Low calcium speeds the gut. A quiet gut fits high calcium or low potassium.

options.text: Painful calf cramps at night
options.rationale: Cramps come before tetany as muscles become overexcited.

questions.takeaway: Calcium is the brake on nerves and muscles. Low calcium means too much firing: tingling, twitching, cramps and spasm.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding: is this a nerve or muscle doing too much, or too little? Low calcium only explains too much.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium excites nerves and muscles.
Tingling, facial twitch and cramps.
Absent reflexes and a quiet gut point the other way.

elimination.verdict: A, B and E.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old with a sodium of 156 mEq/L from poor intake has received 0.45% sodium chloride for 8 hours. Which finding indicates the therapy is working as intended?

options.text: Sodium is 152 mEq/L and she is less agitated
options.rationale: A gradual fall with easing agitation is the goal. Sodium is lowered slowly.

options.text: Sodium is 139 mEq/L and she reports a new headache
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is normal. A drop this fast pulls water into brain cells, so the headache suggests cerebral edema.

options.text: Sodium is 156 mEq/L and urine output has increased
options.rationale: The sodium has not moved. More urine without a change in sodium is not the goal.

options.text: Sodium is 154 mEq/L and her twitching has become weakness
options.rationale: Twitching that progresses to weakness is the worsening pattern, even with a slightly lower number.

questions.takeaway: Replace free water and bring a high sodium down gradually. A fast fall to normal can swell the brain.
questions.strategy: Read the number and the patient together. A normal value reached too fast with a new neuro symptom is a complication.

steps.detail: A slow fall plus a calmer brain.

steps.action: Remove the options where the patient is worse or unchanged
steps.detail: Weakness after twitching and a sodium that has not moved.
Four points with less agitation is safe. Seventeen points with a headache is not.

elimination.verdict: Sodium 152 and less agitated.

questions.stem: After three days of nasogastric suction, a patient has leg weakness, hypoactive bowel sounds and flat T waves on the monitor. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Tempting, since suction removes fluid. The findings are weak muscles, a quiet gut and flat T waves, which is potassium, not volume.

options.text: IV calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Low calcium excites nerves and the gut: tingling, cramps and diarrhea. This patient is slowed down.

options.text: IV potassium chloride diluted on a pump
options.rationale: GI suction removes potassium. Weakness, a quiet gut and flat T waves are the low potassium picture, replaced slowly on a pump.

options.text: Oral potassium chloride with food
options.rationale: The right electrolyte by the wrong route. A patient on nasogastric suction cannot take or keep oral doses.

questions.takeaway: GI losses drain potassium. Low potassium weakens skeletal muscle, quiets the gut and flattens the T wave.
questions.strategy: Two imbalances share weakness and a slow gut. Use the cause and the ECG to separate them.

steps.detail: Three days of suction is a potassium loss.
Low calcium twitches and cramps.
Flat T waves and a GI loss fit low potassium, not high calcium.

elimination.verdict: Diluted IV potassium on a pump.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure who takes a magnesium antacid daily is drowsy with absent knee jerks and respirations of 9. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: IV furosemide with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A real treatment for high magnesium when the kidneys work. His do not.

options.text: A serum magnesium level in the morning
options.rationale: His breathing is already slowing. This cannot wait until morning.

options.text: Hemodialysis later today
options.rationale: Removes magnesium and he will likely need it. It takes hours to arrange, and his breathing needs protection now.

options.text: IV calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Calcium is the antidote. It opposes magnesium at the nerves and muscles while removal is arranged.

questions.takeaway: Magnesium toxicity runs from lost reflexes to slow breathing to the heart. Stop the source and give IV calcium first; removal comes after.
questions.strategy: Dialysis and calcium are both right for him. Ask which one works in minutes.

steps.action: Cut the option his kidneys rule out
steps.detail: Fluids and a loop diuretic need working kidneys.
Respirations of 9 cannot wait.
Calcium acts now. Dialysis removes magnesium later.

elimination.verdict: IV calcium gluconate first.

questions.stem: A patient with a sodium of 118 mEq/L is drowsy and confused. Hypertonic saline is prescribed and is being prepared by pharmacy. Which action does the nurse take while waiting?

options.text: Perform a complete neurologic assessment
options.rationale: Tempting because neuro checks are part of the care. The stem already gives the neuro change, so repeating it leaves the patient unprotected.

options.text: Pad the side rails and place suction at the bedside
options.rationale: Confusion and drowsiness at this level are the steps before a seizure. Seizure precautions protect the patient now.

options.text: Start a fluid restriction of 1 liter per day
options.rationale: Restriction treats mild dilutional cases and needs a prescription. It does not protect a brain that may seize in the next hour.

options.text: Request a repeat sodium level to confirm the result
options.rationale: The patient's brain is already showing the effect. Confirming the number delays protection.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium swells brain cells inside a rigid skull. With confusion at a very low level, put seizure precautions in place before the seizure.
questions.strategy: When the assessment is already in the stem and the treatment is on its way, the open slot is safety.

steps.detail: The number, the neuro change and the prescription.

steps.action: Remove what makes it worse or only repeats data
steps.detail: A repeat lab, a repeat exam, an order the nurse cannot start.

steps.action: Ask what could happen in the next ten minutes
steps.detail: A seizure. Prepare for it.

elimination.verdict: Seizure precautions now.

questions.scenario: A 64-year-old with kidney failure has a potassium of 6.3 mEq/L and tall peaked T waves. Urine output has been 10 mL per hour. He uses a salt substitute at meals.
questions.stem: For each prescription, indicate whether the nurse anticipates it or questions it for this patient.

rows.text: Continuous cardiac telemetry
rows.rationale: The heart is the organ at risk. Peaked T waves need continuous watching.

rows.text: IV calcium
rows.rationale: Stabilizes the heart muscle while other drugs lower the potassium.

rows.text: Regular insulin with dextrose
rows.rationale: Shifts potassium into cells. Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia.

rows.text: IV furosemide to increase potassium excretion
