rows.rationale: Diuretics remove potassium only when kidney function is adequate. He is making 10 mL per hour.

rows.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate
rows.rationale: A binder removes potassium through the gut, which does not depend on his kidneys.

rows.text: Continue the salt substitute on his meal trays
rows.rationale: Salt substitutes are a potassium source. All potassium sources stop.

questions.takeaway: High potassium: stop every source, protect the heart, shift potassium into cells, then remove it by a route that works for this patient.
questions.strategy: Two details in the scenario decide the questioned rows: almost no urine, plus a hidden potassium source on the tray.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Peaked T waves mean the heart. Telemetry and calcium fit.

steps.action: Check each removal route against his kidneys
steps.detail: A diuretic needs working kidneys. A binder does not.

steps.action: Hunt for potassium still going in
steps.detail: The salt substitute.

elimination.verdict: Anticipate telemetry, calcium, insulin with dextrose and the binder. Question furosemide and the salt substitute.

questions.stem: A patient with fluid overload needs a daily weight. Which instruction does the nurse give the assistive personnel?

options.text: Weigh him after breakfast, once he has voided
options.rationale: Voiding first is right. After breakfast adds the weight of the meal, and the time drifts from day to day.

options.text: Weigh him at the same time, on any free scale
options.rationale: Same time is right. Scales differ, so a change between scales is not a change in the patient.

options.text: Use the same scale before breakfast, in a similar gown
options.rationale: Same time, same scale, same clothing. Only then does a change mean fluid.

options.text: Weigh him at bedtime, after the day's fluids are counted
options.rationale: Evening weights include the day's food and drink and cannot be compared with morning ones.

questions.takeaway: A daily weight only means something if the time, the scale and the clothing stay the same.
questions.strategy: Every option is a weighing instruction and each gets something right. Pick the one that controls all three variables.

steps.detail: Time, scale and clothing.
After breakfast, any scale and bedtime each change one variable.
Only one option fixes all three.

elimination.verdict: Same scale, before breakfast, similar gown.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with dehydration had a hematocrit of 52% on admission. After 24 hours of IV fluid it is 43%. Her stools are brown and her lungs are clear. Which conclusion guides the nurse?

options.text: Expected as replaced fluid dilutes the blood
options.rationale: Dehydration concentrates the blood. As water returns, the same red cells sit in more plasma and the value falls to normal.

options.text: Possible hidden bleeding, so test her stool
options.rationale: Tempting, since a falling hematocrit can mean blood loss. Brown stools and the fluid she received explain it better.

options.text: Fluid overload, so stop the infusion
options.rationale: Tempting because overshoot is a real risk in older adults. Clear lungs and a value in the normal range argue against it, and she still needs the fluid.

options.text: A laboratory error, so repeat the sample
options.rationale: The change fits her treatment, so there is no reason to doubt it.

questions.takeaway: Dehydration makes hematocrit look high because the water is gone, not because cells were added. A fall toward normal during rehydration is the goal.
questions.strategy: A dropping hematocrit sounds like bleeding. Check what the stem gives you about bleeding and about her lungs before you choose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 52% was concentrated blood.
Brown stools give no sign of blood loss.
Clear lungs and a normal value do not fit.

elimination.verdict: Expected dilution as fluid is replaced.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest with bone cancer has a calcium of 12.9 mg/dL. The left calf is warm and larger than the right. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Measure both calves and recheck in four hours
options.rationale: More assessment is tempting. The difference is already found, and waiting four hours delays the report.

options.text: Apply the compression device to that leg
options.rationale: Compression on a leg with a suspected clot can dislodge it.

options.text: Help the patient walk to keep blood moving
options.rationale: Walking helps prevent clots. Once a clot is suspected, activity can break it loose.

options.text: Keep the leg still and notify the provider
options.rationale: High calcium raises clot risk in the legs and pelvis. A warm, larger calf is reported promptly while the leg is protected.

questions.takeaway: High calcium increases clotting. Compare calf size, temperature and color, then report a difference without squeezing or exercising the leg.
questions.strategy: Three options do something to the leg or wait. With a possible clot, the finding is already made, so protect the leg and report.

steps.detail: One calf warm and larger.

steps.action: Remove anything that moves or squeezes the leg
steps.detail: Walking and compression.
A possible clot is not rechecked in four hours.

elimination.verdict: Keep the leg still and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury and rising intracranial pressure has a new prescription for 0.45% sodium chloride at 100 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Start the infusion and perform hourly neuro checks
options.rationale: Monitoring does not undo the harm. Hypotonic fluid moves water into brain cells.

options.text: Hold the fluid and clarify it with the provider
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells. In a swelling brain inside a rigid skull, that raises the pressure further.

options.text: Start the infusion at half the prescribed rate
options.rationale: Changing the rate is outside nursing scope and still delivers the wrong fluid.

options.text: Start the infusion and raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Raising the head helps pressure, and it cannot offset fluid that swells brain cells.

questions.takeaway: Match the fluid to where the water needs to go. Hypotonic fluid swells cells, so question it when intracranial pressure is a concern.
questions.strategy: Three options start the fluid with a safeguard added. Decide first whether the fluid itself fits this patient.

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic.
Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells.
His brain cells have no room to swell.

elimination.verdict: Hold it and clarify the fluid.

questions.stem: A patient receiving IV fluids at 150 mL per hour develops new crackles and becomes short of breath lying flat. Place the nurse's actions in priority order.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to a high sitting position
options.rationale: First. Positioning eases breathing immediately and needs no prescription.

options.text: Slow the IV fluid to a keep open rate
options.rationale: Next, reduce the fluid going in while keeping the access.

options.text: Notify the provider of the crackles and breathing change
options.rationale: With the patient positioned and the fluid slowed, report the findings to get treatment.

options.text: Give IV furosemide as prescribed
options.rationale: The loop diuretic removes the extra fluid once it is prescribed.

options.text: Recheck lung sounds and measure urine output
options.rationale: Last, evaluate whether the diuretic worked.

questions.takeaway: Fluid overload with new crackles: sit the patient up, cut the fluid going in, report, give the diuretic, then check the response.
questions.strategy: Start with what the nurse can do alone in seconds, then what needs the provider, then the evaluation.

steps.detail: Upright positioning helps right away.
Slow the fluid but keep the line.
A diuretic needs a prescription and its effect needs checking.

elimination.verdict: Sit up, slow the IV, notify, furosemide, recheck.

questions.stem: A patient with Crohn disease has a calcium of 7.4 mg/dL and the hand spasms each time the blood pressure cuff inflates. Which intervention does the nurse add to the plan of care?

options.text: Walk the patient in the hall three times a day
options.rationale: Tempting because weight bearing protects bone. With nerves this excitable and fragile bones, the present need is calm and injury prevention.

options.text: Recheck for hand spasm with the cuff every hour
options.rationale: The sign is already positive. Repeating it provokes painful spasm and adds stimulation.

options.text: Keep the room quiet and limit visitors
options.rationale: Low calcium makes nerves fire too easily. Reducing stimulation lowers the chance of tetany while calcium is replaced.

options.text: Encourage 3 liters of fluid daily
options.rationale: Hydration to flush calcium is for a high level, the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium removes the brake on nerves. Keep the environment quiet, protect from falls and move the patient gently.
questions.strategy: The hand spasm tells you the nerves are already irritable. Choose the option that lowers stimulation instead of adding it.

steps.detail: Spasm with the cuff means excitable nerves.
Hourly cuff testing and hall walks.
Flushing with fluid is for high calcium.

elimination.verdict: Quiet room, limited visitors.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure had a magnesium of 3.4 mEq/L after using a magnesium laxative daily. Which statement shows the discharge teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will check antacid and laxative labels for magnesium."
options.rationale: Failing kidneys cannot clear magnesium, so the fix is to stop the sources. Antacids and laxatives are the common ones.

options.text: "I will drink extra water each day to flush the magnesium out."
options.rationale: Tempting because fluids and diuretics are used when kidneys work. His do not, so extra water will not clear it.

options.text: "I will use the magnesium laxative only once a week."
options.rationale: Still a magnesium source his kidneys cannot remove.

options.text: "I will stop taking my calcium supplement."
options.rationale: Calcium is not the cause. Calcium is the antidote for magnesium's effects.

questions.takeaway: High magnesium usually comes from kidney failure plus a magnesium product. Stopping every source is the first treatment.
questions.strategy: The kidney failure in the stem rules out any plan that depends on the kidneys to remove magnesium.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: A magnesium laxative with kidneys that cannot excrete it.

steps.action: Remove plans that keep a source
steps.detail: Weekly use is still use.

steps.action: Test the flushing plan against his kidneys
steps.detail: It only works with adequate kidney function.

elimination.verdict: He will check labels and avoid magnesium products.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure treated for fluid overload reviews his low sodium diet before discharge. Which statement requires further teaching?

options.text: "I season my food with lemon juice and dried herbs."
options.rationale: Correct. Flavor without sodium.

options.text: "I buy frozen vegetables without added sauce."
options.rationale: Correct. Plain frozen vegetables are low in sodium.

options.text: "I switched to deli turkey because it is lean."
options.rationale: Lean is not low sodium. Deli meats are processed and salty, and sodium pulls water back in.

options.text: "I check each label for sodium per serving."
options.rationale: Correct. Labels show the hidden sodium.

questions.takeaway: Sodium hides in processed, canned and deli foods. A food can be lean and healthy sounding and still load a heart failure patient with fluid.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong statement. Do not judge by how healthy the food sounds; judge by how it was processed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that shows a gap.
Herbs, plain frozen vegetables and label reading all limit sodium.
Deli meat is salty whatever its fat content.

elimination.verdict: Deli turkey needs more teaching.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Potassium 5.9 mEq/L, kidney disease, weak legs, normal rhythm on monitor
options.rationale: A high value that needs treatment soon. The normal rhythm shows the heart is not yet affected.

options.text: Calcium 11.4 mg/dL, constipated, IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusing
options.rationale: Slow gut is expected with high calcium, and the treatment is already running.

options.text: Sodium 158 mEq/L, agitated this morning, now quiet and hard to wake
options.rationale: Quiet looks like improvement. Moving from agitation to hard to wake is a falling level of consciousness, which is the brain getting worse.

options.text: Fluid overload, weight up 0.8 kg, ankle edema unchanged
options.rationale: Needs attention today. There is no breathing change, so this patient is stable for now.

questions.takeaway: In sodium imbalance, a patient who goes from restless to quiet and hard to rouse is deteriorating, not settling.
questions.strategy: Look for the patient whose condition changed since the last check, and ask whether the change is toward better or worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A slow gut in high calcium under treatment, and edema with no breathing change.
Normal rhythm, so not yet cardiac.

steps.action: Read the change in the sodium patient
steps.detail: Agitated to hard to wake is a step down.

elimination.verdict: The patient with sodium 158 who is now hard to wake.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L has received IV magnesium sulfate for 3 hours. Her reflexes went from 4+ to 1+ and she is newly drowsy. Respirations are 14. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Pause the infusion and notify the provider
options.rationale: Reflexes below normal with new drowsiness mean the magnesium has passed the goal. Stop adding it before breathing slows.

options.text: Continue the infusion since the reflexes have calmed
options.rationale: Calmer reflexes look like success. The target is 2+, and 1+ with drowsiness is past it.

options.text: Recheck the reflexes and respirations in one hour
options.rationale: Tempting because respirations are still 14. Another hour of infusion moves her toward absent reflexes and slow breathing.

options.text: Request a magnesium level before changing anything
options.rationale: The level will be needed. The bedside signs already show the direction, so the infusion stops first.

questions.takeaway: Reflexes are the bedside gauge for magnesium. Normal is the goal. Below normal with drowsiness is early toxicity even when breathing is still fine.
questions.strategy: The finding moved in the right direction and then went past the target. Ask where normal is.

steps.detail: Reflexes of 2+.
1+ and drowsy is below normal.
Respirations fall last. Waiting for them is waiting too long.

elimination.verdict: Pause the infusion and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A patient with bone metastases has new lethargy, constipation, thirst and a large urine output. Her morning glucose was 98 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the prescribed stool softener and reassess later
options.rationale: Treats one symptom. The cluster points to a single cause that the stool softener will not touch.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose now
options.rationale: Thirst and a large urine output suggest high glucose. The stem already gives a normal glucose, so this repeats known data.

options.text: Let her rest and limit stimulation
options.rationale: Rest fits a tired patient with cancer. New lethargy is a change that needs a cause, not quiet.

options.text: Report the findings and request a calcium level
options.rationale: Bone metastases release calcium. Lethargy, constipation, thirst and a large urine output together are the picture of high calcium.

questions.takeaway: Bone cancer plus slowing of the brain and bowel with thirst and heavy urine output means high calcium until shown otherwise.
questions.strategy: Do not treat the findings one at a time. Find the one cause that explains all four, then check what the stem has already ruled out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Brain slow, bowel slow, thirsty, urinating a lot.
Glucose was 98.
Bone metastases raise calcium.

elimination.verdict: Report the findings and request a calcium level.

questions.stem: A patient with fluid overload has crackles, breathes comfortably at 18 per minute, and is due for IV furosemide. This morning's potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the furosemide now and recheck potassium afterward
options.rationale: Tempting because crackles are a breathing finding. He is comfortable, and furosemide will push a low potassium lower.

options.text: Report the potassium before giving the furosemide
options.rationale: He is not in distress, so there is time. A loop diuretic on a potassium of 3.1 risks dysrhythmia, and the provider can add replacement.

options.text: Hold the furosemide until his breathing worsens
options.rationale: Waiting for distress is not a plan. The overload still needs treatment once potassium is addressed.

options.text: Give half the furosemide dose and report the potassium
options.rationale: Changing a dose is not a nursing decision, and even half a dose lowers a potassium that is already low.

questions.takeaway: When breathing is stable, check what the drug will do to the lab value before giving it. Furosemide wastes potassium.
questions.strategy: Breathing versus a lab value looks like an ABC question. Read how the patient is breathing before letting ABCs decide.

steps.detail: Comfortable at 18 per minute. No urgency.
Potassium will fall below 3.1.

steps.action: Pick the option that treats both
steps.detail: The provider can order potassium with the diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Report the potassium first. The dose is delayed by minutes, and the heart is protected.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with dehydration has received IV 0.9% sodium chloride for 10 hours. Which finding requires follow up first?

options.text: Heart rate is 108, down from 118
options.rationale: Still fast, and moving the right way. It shows the fluid is helping.

options.text: Skin on her forearm stays tented
options.rationale: Looks alarming. Forearm skin tents in most older adults, so it says little about her fluid status.

options.text: She asks for water several times
options.rationale: Thirst is expected with dehydration and is easy to address.

options.text: Urine output is 18 mL per hour
options.rationale: Below 30 mL per hour after 10 hours of fluid means the kidneys are still underperfused. This is the finding that shows replacement is not enough.

questions.takeaway: Urine output is the quiet measure of whether replaced fluid is reaching the organs. Under 30 mL per hour is not acceptable.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as improving, unreliable, expected or not responding. Only one is not responding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate is coming down.
Forearm turgor in an 84-year-old.
Thirst is expected. Low output after 10 hours of fluid is failure to respond.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 18 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis has received 2 liters of 0.9% sodium chloride. Blood pressure is now 118/72, and the provider changes the fluid to 0.45% sodium chloride. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hang the 0.45% sodium chloride as prescribed
options.rationale: Once the pressure is stable, hypotonic fluid is the expected next step in diabetic ketoacidosis. It moves water back into dry cells.

options.text: Hold the fluid and question the order
options.rationale: Tempting because hypotonic fluid is wrong for low blood pressure or a brain problem. Her pressure is now 118/72 and she has neither.

options.text: Keep the 0.9% sodium chloride running for now
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid refilled the vessels. Staying on it leaves the cells dry and adds volume she no longer needs.

options.text: Ask for 5% dextrose in 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypertonic fluid pulls more water out of cells that are already dehydrated.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid is questioned with low blood pressure, head injury or increased intracranial pressure. In diabetic ketoacidosis with a stable pressure it is the expected order.
questions.strategy: Do not question an order only because the fluid is hypotonic. Check the client for the contraindications first. Here the pressure is the detail that clears it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic and hydrates cells.
No brain problem, and the pressure is no longer low.
More isotonic fluid stays in the vessels. Hypertonic fluid dries the cells further.

elimination.verdict: Hang it as prescribed. The order fits this client now.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a bone infection will go home on IV vancomycin for 6 weeks. Her forearm veins are scarred. Which device does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A midline catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: Tempting because a midline suits antibiotics and poor veins. Its dwell time is up to 4 weeks, and this therapy is 6.

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter
options.rationale: Weeks to months of therapy with an irritating drug fits a PICC, and it spares repeated sticks in scarred veins.

options.text: A short peripheral catheter restarted as needed
options.rationale: Six weeks of restarts in scarred veins means repeated failed sticks and phlebitis.

options.text: A nontunneled catheter in the subclavian vein
options.rationale: Short term acute care device with the highest infection risk. It is a poor choice for home.

questions.takeaway: Ask how long, how irritating and how good the veins are. Past 4 weeks a midline no longer fits, so the PICC is the answer.
questions.strategy: Midline and PICC both go in at the upper arm and both carry antibiotics. The 6 weeks in the stem is what separates them.

steps.detail: A nontunneled line is for days in the hospital.
Scarred veins will not last 6 weeks.
A midline dwells up to 4 weeks. A PICC dwells weeks to months.

elimination.verdict: The PICC. Duration tips it.

questions.stem: The nurse started a unit of packed red blood cells 15 minutes ago on a stable 60-year-old. An AP is free to help. Which action is best?

options.text: Ask the AP to take the vital signs and report them
options.rationale: Tempting because vital signs on a stable patient are delegable. This set is a check for a transfusion reaction, which is assessment.

options.text: Increase the rate so the unit finishes within 4 hours
options.rationale: The rate is not raised until the 15 minute check shows no reaction.

options.text: Take the vital signs and assess the patient personally
options.rationale: The 15 minute reassessment looks for a reaction and needs the nurse's judgment, so the nurse does it.

options.text: Document the baseline vital signs and return in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Skips the 15 minute check, the point where most severe reactions appear.

questions.takeaway: The 15 minute transfusion check is an assessment for a reaction. The RN keeps it even when the patient looks stable.
questions.strategy: The word stable invites delegation. Ask what the vital signs are for. Here they are the nurse's evaluation of a blood product.

steps.action: Cut the option that skips the check
steps.detail: Reassessment at 15 minutes is required.
You assess before you speed up.

steps.action: Decide who takes the vital signs
steps.detail: Looking for a reaction is interpretation, which stays with the RN.

elimination.verdict: The nurse takes the vital signs and assesses.

questions.stem: The nurse scrubs a forearm site with chlorhexidine and lets it dry. With the tourniquet on, the vein can no longer be seen. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Feel for the vein through a fresh pair of clean gloves
options.rationale: Tempting because the gloves are new. Clean gloves are not sterile, so touching the site undoes the prep.

options.text: Feel for the vein, then scrub again and let it dry
options.rationale: Touching the prepped skin contaminates it. If the vein must be felt again, the 30 second scrub and the full dry time are repeated.

options.text: Insert the catheter where the vein was seen earlier
options.rationale: A blind stick risks a missed vein or a nerve, and attempts are limited.

options.text: Feel for the vein, then wipe once with alcohol
options.rationale: A quick wipe is not a 30 second scrub with friction and a full dry time.

questions.takeaway: After the skin prep, the site is not touched. If you must palpate again, you prep again: scrub with friction for 30 seconds and let it air dry.
questions.strategy: Three options try to save time. Ask whether the skin is still clean at the moment the catheter goes in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No touch after the prep.
Guessing at the vein is unsafe.
Only one restores the full prep afterward.

elimination.verdict: Palpate, then repeat the scrub and let it dry.

questions.stem: A confused 63-year-old with a serum sodium of 116 mEq/L has received 3% sodium chloride by pump for 6 hours. Which finding indicates the therapy is working as intended?

options.text: Sodium 136 mEq/L and the patient is now drowsy
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is normal. A rise of 20 in 6 hours is far too fast, and the drowsiness is a new neurologic change.

options.text: Sodium 120 mEq/L and the patient states the correct date
options.rationale: A gradual rise with clearer thinking is the goal of hypertonic saline.

options.text: Sodium 117 mEq/L with new crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: Almost no correction, plus a sign of circulatory overload from fluid pulled into the vessels.

options.text: Sodium 119 mEq/L with a new report of headache and nausea
options.rationale: The number is rising, but new neurologic symptoms need follow up before calling it a success.

questions.takeaway: With hypertonic saline, success is a slow rise in sodium with improving neurologic status and clear lungs.
questions.strategy: The normal sodium looks like the win. Check how fast it got there and what the patient looks like.

steps.detail: Crackles are a listed risk of hypertonic fluid.
Headache and nausea are not improvement.
A slow rise with better orientation beats a fast rise with drowsiness.

elimination.verdict: Sodium 120 and oriented to the date.

questions.stem: The nurse hung 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's to run over 8 hours by gravity with 15 drops per mL tubing. Ten minutes later it runs at 44 drops per minute. The client is comfortable. Which action is best?

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider
options.rationale: Tempting because the fluid is running too fast. Only 10 minutes have passed and the client has no symptoms, so the nurse corrects the rate and keeps monitoring.

options.text: Leave the rate and recount the drops in 1 hour
options.rationale: At 44 drops per minute the bag would empty hours early.

options.text: Adjust the clamp to 31 drops per minute
options.rationale: 1,000 mL over 8 hours is 125 mL per hour. 125 times 15, divided by 60, is 31 drops per minute.

options.text: Adjust the clamp to 21 drops per minute
options.rationale: This is the answer for 10 drops per mL tubing. The set in use delivers 15 drops per mL.

questions.takeaway: Drops per minute equals mL per hour times the drop factor, divided by 60. A gravity line drifts, so count it and correct it.
questions.strategy: Work the number before reading the options. Then ask whether a fast rate with no symptoms needs more than a correction.

steps.detail: 1,000 divided by 8 is 125 mL per hour.
125 times 15, divided by 60, is about 31.
No dyspnea and only 10 minutes at the wrong rate. Correct it and reassess.

elimination.verdict: Set the clamp to 31 drops per minute.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old admitted with dehydration and a blood pressure of 92/58 has received 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL per hour for 12 hours. Which findings indicate the therapy is effective and tolerated? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blood pressure 114/70
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and restores volume, so the pressure rises toward normal.

options.text: Urine output rose from 20 to 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: Better kidney perfusion shows the volume is being restored.

options.text: Heart rate rose from 92 to 118
options.rationale: A rising heart rate means the volume is still low or the heart is straining. Neither is the goal.

options.text: New fine crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: An early sign of fluid overload. Older adults have less cardiac and renal reserve.

options.text: Lungs clear with respirations of 16
options.rationale: Shows she is tolerating the volume. Clear lungs are the tolerated half of the question.

options.text: New restlessness with neck vein distention
options.rationale: Signs of circulatory overload, which calls for slowing the fluid and notifying the provider.

questions.takeaway: Fluid replacement in an older adult is judged two ways: is the volume back, and are the lungs still clear.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for effective and tolerated. Volume signs answer the first word. Lung and neck vein findings answer the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is the volume back? Pressure and urine output say yes.
Is she tolerating it? Clear lungs say yes.
A faster heart rate, crackles and neck vein distention all mean trouble.

elimination.verdict: Blood pressure up, urine output up, lungs clear. Three of six.

questions.stem: Halfway through an IV push given faster than prescribed, a 52-year-old becomes flushed and reports a pounding headache and chest tightness. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Take a full set of vital signs
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. The cues already identify the problem, and the drug is still going in.

options.text: Finish the dose slowly over the correct time
options.rationale: More drug worsens a reaction to rapid infusion.

options.text: Notify the provider of the reaction
options.rationale: Needed, after the cause is stopped.

options.text: Stop the injection
options.rationale: Flushing, headache and chest tightness during a rapid push are speed shock. Stopping the drug removes the cause.

questions.takeaway: Speed shock comes from a drug given too fast. Stop the drug first, then check vital signs and notify.
questions.strategy: When the stem already gives the assessment, the first step is the action that removes the cause.

steps.detail: A rapid push with flushing, headache and chest tightness.
It adds more of the cause.
Stop, then vital signs, then notify.

elimination.verdict: Stop the injection.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with left arm paralysis from a stroke needs 2 days of isotonic fluid. She has a visible vein on the back of the right hand. Which site does the nurse choose?

options.text: The left forearm, to keep her working arm free
options.rationale: A paralyzed limb is a contraindicated site.

options.text: The right antecubital fossa
options.rationale: Avoided for short peripheral catheters because bending the elbow kinks and dislodges them.

options.text: The right forearm
options.rationale: A forearm vein in the unaffected arm fits the site rules and spares the fragile hand veins of an older adult.

options.text: The back of the right hand
options.rationale: Tempting because the rule is most distal site first. In older adults the dorsal hand is avoided: thin skin and fragile veins infiltrate easily.

questions.takeaway: Distal first applies among appropriate sites. For an older adult the appropriate range starts at the forearm, not the hand.
questions.strategy: Two rules compete here: start distal, and avoid the dorsal hand in older adults. Her age decides which rule wins.

steps.detail: Contraindicated regardless of convenience.

steps.action: Cut the bend of the elbow
steps.detail: Not for short peripheral catheters.
At 82, skip the hand.

elimination.verdict: The right forearm.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with a hemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL, dizziness and a heart rate of 112 received 2 units of packed red blood cells. Which finding indicates the transfusion was effective?

options.text: Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL and heart rate 108
options.rationale: Two units should raise the hemoglobin about 2 g/dL. This is almost no change.

options.text: Hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL with new crackles
options.rationale: Tempting because the number is right. New crackles mean the volume overloaded her, which is a complication.

options.text: Heart rate 94 with chills and a new fever
options.rationale: The slower heart rate looks good, but chills and fever point to a transfusion reaction.

options.text: Hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL and heart rate 88
options.rationale: About 1 g/dL per unit, and the heart no longer has to race to deliver oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Expect roughly 1 g/dL per unit of red cells, with the symptoms of anemia easing and no new problem from the transfusion.
questions.strategy: Effective means the goal was met without harm. Check each option for the expected rise and for a new finding that spoils it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6.9 plus about 2 is near 9.
7.2 is too small a rise.
Crackles and fever are complications, whatever the hemoglobin.

elimination.verdict: 8.8 g/dL with a heart rate of 88. Goal met, nothing new.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught an orientee about infection prevention with IV lines. Which action by the orientee shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Wipes the needleless connector for 5 seconds before a flush
options.rationale: Too short. The scrub is at least 15 seconds.

options.text: Scrubs the needleless connector for 15 seconds before each access
options.rationale: Scrub the hub for at least 15 seconds every time the line is entered.

options.text: Fans the chlorhexidine dry before inserting the catheter
options.rationale: The antiseptic must air dry on its own. Fanning or blotting cuts its effect.

options.text: Changes an intact, dry transparent dressing every 2 days
options.rationale: Two days is the gauze interval. An intact transparent dressing stays 7 days, and extra changes expose the site.

questions.takeaway: Hub scrub at least 15 seconds every access. Antiseptic air dries. Transparent dressing every 7 days, gauze every 2.
questions.strategy: Each option holds one number or one technique detail. Check each against the slide value.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only 15 meets the minimum.
Air dry only.
Every 2 days belongs to gauze.

elimination.verdict: The 15 second scrub before each access.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has had a femoral nontunneled central line for 9 days. Which finding does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: The tubing label is a week old
options.rationale: Overdue for a change and needs correcting. It is a risk, not yet a problem in the patient.

options.text: The dressing is damp and lifted at one corner
options.rationale: Tempting because a damp dressing must be changed. It can be changed right after the patient is assessed.

options.text: New confusion with a temperature of 38.9 C
options.rationale: Fever and new confusion with a high risk line suggest a bloodstream infection. An actual systemic problem comes before the risks.

options.text: The insertion site is pink and slightly tender
options.rationale: A local finding that is watched and reported. The systemic signs are more urgent.

questions.takeaway: Femoral site plus many line days is the highest risk combination. Fever and new confusion with no other source point to CRBSI.
questions.strategy: All four need attention. Rank actual before potential and systemic before local.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Old tubing and a damp dressing raise risk.
A pink site is local. Fever and confusion are systemic.
A possible bloodstream infection cannot wait.

elimination.verdict: New confusion with fever. Think sepsis from the line.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old has 0.9% sodium chloride running through a left hand catheter. The pump has alarmed twice. The hand is cool, pale and puffy, and no blood return is obtained.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: The slide action for infiltration: stop immediately and remove.

options.text: Elevate the left arm
options.rationale: Elevation helps the leaked fluid reabsorb.

options.text: Slow the rate and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Fluid keeps entering the tissue at any rate.

options.text: Flush the catheter with saline to clear it
options.rationale: Pushes more fluid into tissue that is already full.

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: Cool, pale, swollen skin, a slowed infusion and no blood return.

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is warm and red with a streak or cord along the vein.

options.text: Venous thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis swells and pains the limb. It does not make the skin at the site cool and pale.

options.text: Catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: That is systemic: fever, chills, hypotension.

options.text: Size of the edema and the infiltration grade
options.rationale: Shows whether the swelling is resolving, and the grade is documented.

options.text: Sensation and capillary refill in the fingers
options.rationale: Swelling in thin older skin can press on nerves and vessels.

options.text: Length of the red streak along the vein
options.rationale: A phlebitis measure. No streak is present.

options.text: Blood culture results
options.rationale: Nothing here suggests bloodstream infection.

questions.takeaway: Cool, pale and puffy with no blood return is infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, then grade it and keep reassessing the hand.
questions.strategy: Decide the condition from skin temperature first. Then pick the actions and the monitoring that belong to that condition only.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool and pale is infiltration. Warm and red is phlebitis.

steps.action: Cut actions that keep fluid running
steps.detail: Slowing or flushing adds to the leak.
Edema, grade and circulation in the fingers follow from infiltration.

elimination.verdict: Stop and remove, elevate; infiltration; edema and grade, sensation and capillary refill.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with thin skin and small forearm veins is prescribed 1 unit of packed red blood cells. Which catheter does the nurse select?

options.text: An 18 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because 18 is the preferred blood gauge. In fragile veins the larger catheter raises the risk of vein trauma and hematoma.

options.text: A 16 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Large bore is for trauma and rapid resuscitation, and rapid infusion is poorly tolerated at 84.

options.text: A 24 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Kind to the vein but below the 18 to 20 gauge required for blood products.

options.text: A 20 gauge catheter
options.rationale: Meets the 18 to 20 gauge requirement for blood while following the older adult rule of the smallest effective gauge.

questions.takeaway: Blood needs an 18 to 20 gauge. Older adults get the smallest gauge that does the job. The overlap is a 20.
questions.strategy: Two rules apply at once. Find the size that satisfies both instead of choosing one rule and ignoring the other.

steps.detail: No trauma and no need for speed.
Outside the range for blood.
Fragile veins tip it to the smaller acceptable size.

elimination.verdict: The 20 gauge.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old receiving subcutaneous fluid in the abdomen for mild dehydration is now hard to rouse with a blood pressure of 78/44. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request an order for IV access and fluids
options.rationale: Subcutaneous fluid absorbs slowly and is not used in severe dehydration or shock. She needs a route that reaches the vessels directly.

options.text: Raise the subcutaneous rate to the maximum
options.rationale: The route tops out at about 1 mL per minute, far too slow for shock.

options.text: Add a second subcutaneous site in the thigh
options.rationale: Tempting because it doubles the volume. Two slow sites are still too slow, and absorption is poor when perfusion is low.

options.text: Give oral fluids and recheck in 20 minutes
options.rationale: She is hard to rouse, so oral fluid is an aspiration risk and a delay.

questions.takeaway: Hypodermoclysis is for mild to moderate dehydration. Once the patient is in shock, the route has to change.
questions.strategy: The assessment is done and she is unstable. Ask whether the current route can ever deliver enough, then change it.

steps.detail: Mild dehydration has become hypotension with a falling level of consciousness.
Subcutaneous fluid is slow by design.

steps.action: Cut what keeps the slow route
steps.detail: More rate and a second site stay subcutaneous. Oral fluid is unsafe.

elimination.verdict: Call for IV access. The route no longer fits the patient.

questions.stem: While a client sits up in bed, the cap falls off his subclavian central line. He gasps, grabs his chest and reports sudden shortness of breath. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Clamp the catheter
options.rationale: Air is entering through the open line. Closing it stops more air before anything else is done.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed higher
options.rationale: Tempting for any dyspnea. For air embolism he goes on the left side with the head down to trap air in the right atrium.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 100%
options.rationale: Needed, and it follows clamping and positioning. Oxygen does not stop air from entering.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Needed, and it comes after the source of air is closed.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: clamp, left side with head down, 100% oxygen, call rapid response. Stop the air first.
questions.strategy: Every option except one belongs in the response. Ask which action stops the cause, because the cause is still active.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Open central line plus sudden dyspnea and chest pain.
Upright lets air travel toward the lungs.
Clamp, position, oxygen, call.

elimination.verdict: Clamp the catheter. Then left side, head down, oxygen and help.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with a hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL is prescribed 1 unit of packed red blood cells. The type and crossmatch is complete. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Confirm written informed consent is on file
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before the blood leaves the blood bank.

options.text: Record baseline vital signs
options.rationale: Taken before the unit is picked up so the 4 hour clock is not used on preparation, and so later changes can be judged.

options.text: Obtain the unit from the blood bank
options.rationale: The clock starts at issue, so everything else is ready first.

options.text: Verify the unit with a second nurse at the bedside
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses independently match the label to the identification band, then both sign.

options.text: Start the transfusion and reassess at 15 minutes
options.rationale: The infusion begins only after verification, with the first reassessment at 15 minutes.

questions.takeaway: Consent and baseline vital signs come before the blood is picked up. The 4 hour limit starts when the unit is issued.
questions.strategy: Students fetch the blood first because it feels like the start. Anything that can be done without the unit in hand is done before the clock starts.

steps.action: Find what must exist before retrieval
steps.detail: Consent on file.

steps.action: Do the assessment before the unit arrives
steps.detail: Baseline vital signs.
Pick up, verify with a second nurse, start, reassess at 15 minutes.

elimination.verdict: Consent, baseline vital signs, obtain unit, two nurse check, start and reassess.

questions.stem: A patient going home with a PICC in the right arm has completed teaching. Which statement shows the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I can swim as long as I wear the waterproof cover."
options.rationale: Tempting because the cover is correct for showers. The arm is never submerged, so swimming and baths are out.

options.text: "Flushing should take a firm push if the line is sluggish."
options.rationale: Resistance means stop and call. Forcing a flush is unsafe.

options.text: "If I get a fever or chills, I will call right away."
options.rationale: Fever over 38 C or chills are warning signs of a line infection that need care immediately.

options.text: "My blood pressure can be taken on either arm."
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuffs or needle sticks on the PICC arm.

questions.takeaway: PICC at home: keep it dry, shower with a cover, never submerge, no cuff on that arm, stop if a flush resists, report fever or chills at once.
questions.strategy: The swimming option is half right. The cover is real, and it is for showering only.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Resistance means do not use the line.
The PICC arm is off limits for a cuff.
A cover does not make submerging safe.

elimination.verdict: Calling right away for fever or chills.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old trauma patient has a tibial intraosseous line placed 20 hours ago during resuscitation. Two forearm peripheral IVs now run well. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the intraosseous line as backup until discharge from the unit
options.rationale: Tempting because extra access feels safer in a trauma patient. The device is limited to 24 hours and working IV access now exists.

options.text: Ask the provider about removing the intraosseous line now
options.rationale: Intraosseous access is a bridge when IV access fails. With IVs working and the 24 hour limit close, it should come out.

options.text: Move the maintenance fluid to the intraosseous line to rest the veins
options.rationale: Adds use of an emergency device that is due for removal.

options.text: Change the intraosseous dressing and reassess next shift
options.rationale: That would pass the 24 hour limit.

questions.takeaway: Intraosseous access is emergency access, limited to 24 hours. Once IV access is established, plan its removal.
questions.strategy: Count the hours in the stem. Twenty hours in with two good IVs means the reason for the device is gone.

steps.detail: 24 hours.

steps.action: Notice three options keep the device
steps.detail: Backup, more use and a later recheck all extend the dwell.

steps.action: Pick the one that removes it
steps.detail: The need has ended.

elimination.verdict: Ask about removing it now.

questions.stem: During a morning peritoneal dialysis exchange, a 55-year-old's outflow is cloudy. She has no fever and says she feels fine. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue exchanges and check her temperature each shift
options.rationale: Tempting because she looks well. Cloudy outflow is often the first sign, before fever or pain.

options.text: Warm the next bag of dialysate a little longer
options.rationale: Warming is for comfort and has nothing to do with cloudiness.

options.text: Record it and compare with the next exchange
options.rationale: Waiting for a second cloudy bag delays treatment of a peritoneal infection.

options.text: Report the cloudy outflow to the provider now
options.rationale: Cloudy effluent means peritonitis until proven otherwise, and it is reported when first seen.

questions.takeaway: With peritoneal dialysis, look at the outflow every exchange. Cloudy means peritonitis until proven otherwise, even in a patient who feels well.
questions.strategy: Do not let a normal temperature cancel an abnormal finding. Ask whether cloudy outflow is ever expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Outflow should be clear.
No fever and feeling fine do not rule out early infection.
Monitoring and comparing later both delay the report.

elimination.verdict: Report it now. Cloudy outflow is the early sign.

questions.stem: Ten minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient reports itching and has hives on the chest. Vital signs match the baseline. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the vein open
options.rationale: Hives are a listed reaction sign. Every reaction starts the same way: stop the blood so no more enters, then keep the vein open with saline through new tubing.

options.text: Slow the rate and give prescribed diphenhydramine
options.rationale: Tempting because the reaction looks mild and vitals are stable. Blood keeps entering while a reaction is under way.

options.text: Take a full set of vital signs
options.rationale: Vitals are needed and come after the blood is stopped. The stem already gives stable vitals.

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank
options.rationale: Required, and it follows stopping the transfusion.

questions.takeaway: Any sign of a transfusion reaction, mild or severe, gets the same first action: stop the blood.
questions.strategy: All four are real steps in a reaction. Put them in order and pick the one that stops the exposure.

steps.detail: Itching and hives during blood is a reaction.
Vitals are given and stable.
Stop, saline with new tubing, vitals, notify.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion.

questions.stem: After removing a peripheral IV catheter from the forearm, the nurse sees the tip is jagged and shorter than expected. The patient has no symptoms. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Take vital signs and watch for chest pain
options.rationale: Assessment is tempting because the patient feels fine. The fragment can still travel, so it is contained first.

options.text: Notify the provider and save the catheter
options.rationale: Both are required and follow securing the limb. They do not keep the fragment in the arm.

options.text: Apply a tourniquet high on that arm
options.rationale: A missing tip means a piece is in the vein. A tourniquet high on the limb keeps it from reaching the heart and lungs.

options.text: Apply pressure to the site and elevate the arm
options.rationale: Routine after removal. It does nothing for a fragment already in the vein.

questions.takeaway: A catheter that comes out short is a catheter embolism. Trap the fragment in the limb first, then notify and keep the piece.
questions.strategy: No symptoms does not mean no problem. Infer what the jagged tip means, then choose the action that prevents the harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A piece broke off inside the vein.
Travel to the heart or lungs.
Only the tourniquet stops travel.

elimination.verdict: Apply a tourniquet high on the arm.

questions.stem: A patient who had a right mastectomy with lymph node removal has a dialysis fistula in the left forearm. She needs IV antibiotics. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Use the left hand, below the fistula
options.rationale: The right arm is excluded, which makes the left look like the answer. The whole fistula arm is off limits.

options.text: Use the right forearm, since the surgery was years ago
options.rationale: Time does not restore the lymph drainage. That arm stays protected.

options.text: Use a vein on the top of the foot
options.rationale: Tempting because both arms are out. Legs are on the avoid list for adults, so the foot fails the same check the arms do.

options.text: Ask the provider about another access option
options.rationale: Every site offered is on the avoid list, and a restricted limb is not used without a provider's order. The provider decides on other access.

questions.takeaway: Never use the mastectomy side, the fistula arm or an adult's leg. When every site is excluded, the answer is to escalate, not to pick the least bad site.
questions.strategy: Check each site against the avoid list before comparing them. If every site fails, the answer is the option that is not a site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mastectomy with node removal.
Fistula, including the hand below it.
Legs are on the avoid list for adults.

elimination.verdict: Ask the provider about another access option.

questions.stem: The RN is busy with a patient who has new chest tightness. Which task does the RN assign to the LPN?

options.text: Start the second unit of packed red blood cells
options.rationale: It sounds routine because the first unit went well. Starting any unit of blood stays with the RN.

options.text: Hang the next liter of saline on a stable patient
options.rationale: A routine fluid on an established line in a stable patient is within the LPN role.

options.text: Choose the IV site for a patient after mastectomy
options.rationale: Initial access assessment and site selection are RN judgment.

options.text: Flush the PICC that met resistance this morning
options.rationale: LPNs flush established lines, which makes this tempting. Resistance is a problem that needs RN assessment, and a line is not flushed against it.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the routine task on the stable patient. Blood, site selection and any line with a problem stay with the RN.
questions.strategy: For each task ask two things: is it routine, and is the patient or the line stable? One detail in each wrong option answers no.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Any unit is an RN start.
Site selection is assessment.
Resistance makes it unstable.

elimination.verdict: The next liter of saline on a stable patient.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old with heart failure has 0.9% sodium chloride running at 100 mL per hour. She is newly short of breath with crackles in both bases. The forearm site is soft and painless. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Slow the infusion and sit her upright
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid is overloading her circulation. Slowing it to the lowest rate and raising the head of the bed act on the cause at once and keep the access she will need.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: Tempting because stopping is the first action for a bad site. Her site is fine. The problem is volume, and the line is needed for a diuretic.

options.text: Call the provider to request a diuretic
options.rationale: Needed, and it follows the actions the nurse can take right away.

options.text: Take full vital signs and total the intake and output
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. Dyspnea and crackles on IV fluid already identify the problem, and fluid keeps running while you count.

questions.takeaway: Circulatory overload: slow the IV, sit the client upright, give oxygen, take vital signs, notify. Stop and remove is the response to a failing site, not to too much volume.
questions.strategy: Decide whether the problem is the site or the volume. The stem tells you the site is soft and painless, so the catheter stays and the rate changes.

steps.detail: New dyspnea and crackles in a weak heart on isotonic fluid.
Soft and painless, so there is no reason to remove the catheter.
Slow and sit upright, then vital signs, then call for a diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion and sit her upright.

questions.stem: A carpenter arrives with a nail fragment protruding from his right eye. He is in pain and asks the nurse to pull it out. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Shield the eye without touching the object
options.rationale: A protruding object is never removed by the nurse. Protecting it from movement prevents more damage until the eye care provider arrives.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline to clear debris
options.rationale: Right for a surface foreign body and tempting here. Irrigation can move a penetrating object.

options.text: Apply a pressure patch to control the bleeding
options.rationale: Pressure on a penetrated eye can push out its contents.

options.text: Remove it gently and cover the eye with gauze
options.rationale: Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.

questions.takeaway: A penetrating eye injury is left alone and protected. Only the eye care provider removes the object.
questions.strategy: Three options put force or fluid on the eye. One protects it.

steps.detail: Protruding means penetrating, not surface.
Removal, irrigation and pressure.
A shield with no contact.

elimination.verdict: Shield the eye and leave the object in place.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma has used latanoprost nightly for 6 months. Which statement indicates the treatment goal is being met?

options.text: "My eyes feel comfortable and never ache."
options.rationale: Tempting, but open-angle glaucoma is silent, so comfort tells you nothing about the optic nerve.

options.text: "My side vision is starting to come back."
options.rationale: Lost vision does not return. This statement shows a wrong expectation.

options.text: "My field test is unchanged from last time."
options.rationale: The goal is to prevent further damage. A stable visual field is exactly that.

options.text: "My pressure is normal, so I use drops as needed."
options.rationale: Treatment is lifelong and daily. Stopping lets the pressure climb again.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma treatment succeeds when nothing more is lost. It does not restore vision and it does not depend on how the eye feels.
questions.strategy: Comfort sounds like success. In a painless disease, the only evidence is a measurement that has not worsened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevent further damage, not restore vision.
Vision returning and drops as needed.

steps.action: Compare comfort with a stable test
steps.detail: This disease never hurt, so comfort proves nothing.

elimination.verdict: The unchanged field test.

questions.stem: A very nearsighted client awaiting scleral buckling for a retinal detachment wants to walk to the lounge to read. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Walk with him to the lounge and offer an arm for guidance
options.rationale: Tempting because it prevents a fall, but walking and reading both move the eye and head and can extend the detachment.

options.text: Keep him resting with head still and the eye patched
options.rationale: Before surgery, head movement and activity are restricted and a patch reduces eye movement.

options.text: Bring a large print book to his bedside chair
options.rationale: Keeps him in the room, but reading moves the eye back and forth.

options.text: Raise the lighting so he can read in bed
options.rationale: Good for low vision in general. Here the problem is eye movement, not light.

questions.takeaway: Before retinal detachment repair, the priority is to stop the detachment from spreading: limit activity and head movement and patch the eye.
questions.strategy: Three options help him read safely. Ask whether he should be reading or walking at all.

steps.detail: More retina can detach before surgery.

steps.action: Notice three options keep him reading
steps.detail: Reading means eye movement.
Safe walking is still activity he should not have.

elimination.verdict: Rest, head still, eye patched.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old's daughter sorts his morning and evening pills into a blue box and a green box. He took the evening pills this morning. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the daughter give every dose herself
options.rationale: Solves the error by removing his independence when a simpler fix exists.

options.text: Add a bright fluorescent light over the pill boxes
options.rationale: More light helps aging eyes, but fluorescent glare makes it worse and blue still looks like green.

options.text: Switch the boxes to violet and blue
options.rationale: Blues, greens and violets are the colors aging eyes separate least well.

options.text: Label the boxes in large high contrast print
options.rationale: Aging eyes lose blue and green discrimination, so the cue must be print and contrast, not color.

questions.takeaway: Never teach an older adult medications by color, especially blue, green or violet. Use large print, contrast and shape.
questions.strategy: More light is a real need in older eyes, so that option pulls. The error here came from two colors he cannot tell apart.

steps.action: Find the cause of the error
steps.detail: Blue and green look alike to him.

steps.action: Cut the option that repeats the cause
steps.detail: Violet and blue.
Labels keep him independent; the daughter taking over does not.

elimination.verdict: Large high contrast labels.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four clients waiting. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with open-angle glaucoma whose pressure today is 26 mmHg
options.rationale: Elevated and needs attention, but this is a chronic, slow problem that will not change in the next hour.

options.text: A contact lens wearer with a painful red eye and a hazy cornea
options.rationale: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so a possible corneal infection is an emergency.

options.text: A client with cataracts who reports worse glare when driving
options.rationale: Gradual and expected. Safety teaching can wait.

options.text: A client 1 month after LASIK who sees halos at night
options.rationale: A known complication that is not an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden and painful with a hazy cornea outranks any slowly progressive eye problem, even one with an abnormal number.
questions.strategy: The pressure of 26 is the only number on the page, which makes it look like the priority. Acute beats chronic.

steps.detail: Three are gradual or expected.
26 is open-angle range and chronic.
Painful red eye with a hazy cornea.

elimination.verdict: The contact lens wearer.

questions.stem: Two days after cataract surgery a client calls the clinic. Which report indicates recovery is not progressing as expected?

options.text: "The eye feels a little scratchy."
options.rationale: Mild scratchiness is expected early.

options.text: "I still can't see sharply out of that eye."
options.rationale: Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, so blurry vision on day 2 is expected.

options.text: "I could see better yesterday than I can today."
options.rationale: Vision should improve steadily. A drop from one day to the next is a vision loss to report now.

options.text: "I bent to pick up a shoe before I remembered."
options.rationale: Bending raises eye pressure and needs reteaching, but one slip with no symptoms is not a failing recovery.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, vision that is imperfect is expected. Vision that is getting worse is not.
questions.strategy: Two options mention poor vision. One is slow improvement and the other is a decline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scratchiness.
Not sharp yet versus worse than yesterday.
A teaching need without any symptom.

elimination.verdict: Vision worse today than yesterday.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old who is legally blind and lives alone receives her lunch tray. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Describe where each item sits and let her touch it
options.rationale: Describing in detail and allowing touch lets her eat on her own, as she does at home.

options.text: Stay and feed her to prevent spills and burns
options.rationale: Tempting as the safest choice, but she manages meals alone at home and feeding her removes independence she has.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to cut and feed the meal
options.rationale: Delegation is allowed, but it is still more help than she needs.

options.text: Cut the food and butter the bread for her
options.rationale: Kindly meant and less than feeding her, but she does these things herself at home once she knows where they are.

questions.takeaway: For vision loss: speak normally, describe in detail, allow touch. Give the least help that keeps the patient safe.
questions.strategy: Feeding her looks like the safety answer. The detail that she lives alone tells you she already feeds herself.

steps.detail: She lives alone, so she eats without help.
Both do the task for her.
Preparing her food is still doing it for her.

elimination.verdict: Describe the tray and let her touch it.

questions.stem: A machinist felt something strike his eye while grinding steel. No object is visible, and an MRI of the orbits is prescribed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline before the scan
options.rationale: Right for a surface foreign body, but a high speed metal fragment may have penetrated, and irrigation is not for that.

options.text: Send him and tell the technologist about the grinding
options.rationale: Tempting because the information is passed on. He should not reach the scanner at all.

options.text: Check his acuity and proceed if it is normal
options.rationale: Normal acuity does not rule out a small metal fragment inside the eye.

options.text: Hold the scan and report the metal exposure
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected. X-ray or CT is used instead.

questions.takeaway: Suspected metal in the eye means no MRI. The magnet can move the fragment and cause more injury.
questions.strategy: Three options end with him in the scanner. The stem already told you why that is unsafe.

steps.detail: Grinding steel means metal.

steps.action: Cut what sends him to the scanner
steps.detail: Irrigating first, telling the technologist and checking acuity all end in MRI.
Hold and report so X-ray or CT is ordered.

elimination.verdict: Hold the scan and report the metal.

questions.stem: A client had a laser peripheral iridotomy for angle-closure glaucoma this morning. Which finding best indicates the procedure was effective?

options.text: Eye pressure 16 mmHg with the pain gone
options.rationale: The iridotomy reopens drainage, so pressure falls into the normal range and the pain goes with it.

options.text: No nausea since the antiemetic was given
options.rationale: Tempting, but the drug explains this. It says nothing about the pressure.

options.text: Client resting quietly in a darkened room
options.rationale: Quiet may be relief or may be sedation. It does not measure anything.

options.text: Eye redness slightly less than on arrival
options.rationale: A good sign that lags behind and is too soft to judge the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Judge a treatment by the thing it was meant to change. For angle closure that is the pressure, measured.
questions.strategy: Several findings look like improvement. Ask which one could only come from the iridotomy working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blocked drainage and high pressure.
The antiemetic and the dark room.
16 is inside both normal ranges.

elimination.verdict: Pressure 16 mmHg with pain relieved.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma starts timolol eye drops. Which statements show the teaching was understood? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will press the inner corner of my eye after each drop."
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion keeps the drug in the eye and limits absorption into the body.

options.text: "I can stop the drops once my pressure reading is normal."
options.rationale: The pressure is normal because of the drops. Treatment is lifelong.

options.text: "I will use them every day even when my eyes feel fine."
options.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms to guide dosing, so strict adherence is what protects the nerve.

options.text: "New glasses will sharpen what the glaucoma took away."
options.rationale: Vision lost to glaucoma is nerve damage and is not corrected by lenses.

options.text: "If I skip a few days I will feel it and restart."
options.rationale: Rising pressure in open-angle glaucoma is silent, so there is nothing to feel.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma drops are lifelong and daily. Punctal occlusion limits systemic effects, and lost vision does not return.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. Any statement that treats glaucoma as something he can feel or reverse is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressing the inner corner after each drop.
Daily use without symptoms.
Stopping, feeling it and regaining vision all assume the disease is reversible or noticeable.

elimination.verdict: A and C.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 88-year-old who has had poor intake for 3 days. Which finding most needs follow up?

options.text: Eyes that look sunken and dull in the orbits
options.rationale: Expected with age related loss of orbital fat, so not a reliable hydration sign in an older adult.

options.text: Sclera with a dull yellow tint
options.rationale: Common in older adults. Eye appearance is not used to judge jaundice at this age.

options.text: Dry furrowed tongue with scant dark urine
options.rationale: These are reliable signs of fluid deficit and fit 3 days of poor intake.

options.text: Eyes that feel gritty and dry
options.rationale: Reduced tear production is an expected aging change.

questions.takeaway: Do not use the sclera or eye appearance to judge hydration or jaundice in older adults. Look at the mouth and the urine.
questions.strategy: The eye findings look alarming. In an 88-year-old they are the least trustworthy data.

steps.detail: Three options rest on eye appearance.
Eye appearance misleads in older adults.

steps.action: Take the finding outside the eye
steps.detail: Tongue and urine.

elimination.verdict: Dry furrowed tongue with scant dark urine.

questions.stem: A client with a corneal infection from contact lens wear completes discharge teaching. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll use the drops until the pain is gone."
options.rationale: The full antibiotic course is finished even after symptoms stop.

options.text: "I'll wear glasses until I'm told it has healed."
options.rationale: No contact lenses until the cornea is fully healed, and healing is confirmed by the provider.

options.text: "I'll put my lenses back in once the redness clears."
options.rationale: Tempting because it waits for improvement, but a clear looking eye is not a healed cornea.

options.text: "I'll save the leftover drops for next time."
options.rationale: Leftover drops mean the course was not finished.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infection teaching: finish the antibiotics and keep contacts out until the cornea is fully healed, not just until it looks better.
questions.strategy: Two options delay the contacts. One uses the client's own judgment and one uses the provider's exam.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stopping when pain ends and saving leftovers.
Redness clearing versus confirmed healing.
Symptoms fade before the cornea is whole.

elimination.verdict: Glasses until told it has healed.

questions.stem: A client going home with a corneal ulcer is prescribed antibiotic drops every hour for the first 24 hours. He asks to skip the night doses so he can sleep. Which response is best?

options.text: "Use two drops at bedtime and two when you wake."
options.rationale: Doubling a dose does not replace the steady level that hourly dosing gives.

options.text: "I will ask whether an ointment can cover the night."
options.rationale: Tempting because it respects his need for sleep. The first 24 hours call for hourly dosing as prescribed.

options.text: "Restart the hourly schedule in the morning."
options.rationale: Leaves the infection untreated for hours when vision is at risk.

options.text: "Set an alarm, because the hourly drops continue overnight."
options.rationale: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so the drops are its only defense and the first day is the critical one.

questions.takeaway: A corneal infection is an emergency. Antibiotic drops are often hourly for the first 24 hours, day and night.
questions.strategy: Sleep is a comfort need. Weigh it against what a gap in dosing can cost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Corneal infection can take vision quickly.

steps.action: Cut the options that leave a gap
steps.detail: Double doses and restarting in the morning.
An ointment request delays a schedule that matters tonight.

elimination.verdict: The hourly drops continue overnight.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with cataracts has stopped driving at night and can no longer read her pill labels. She asks if she should wait until they are worse. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: "Surgery is timed by how it limits daily life."
options.rationale: Surgery is the only treatment and is done when ADLs are affected. Night driving and reading labels are ADLs.

options.text: "Stronger glasses and brighter light may be enough for now."
options.rationale: Reasonable early on and tempting as the conservative choice. Her daily function is already limited, so it is past that point.

options.text: "Surgery is done once the pupil turns bluish white."
options.rationale: A mature cataract is not the trigger. Function is.

options.text: "Eye drops can slow the clouding while you wait."
options.rationale: No drop treats a cataract. That belongs to glaucoma.

questions.takeaway: Cataract surgery is timed by function, not by how the lens looks. When ADLs are affected, it is time.
questions.strategy: The conservative option would be right for a client who is still functioning. Two details in the stem say she is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No night driving, cannot read labels.
Drops and waiting for a white pupil.
Fine before ADLs are affected, not after.

elimination.verdict: Surgery is considered now because ADLs are affected.

questions.scenario: A telephone triage nurse takes six calls from adult clients about their eyes.
questions.stem: For each report, indicate whether the nurse arranges an immediate evaluation or provides routine teaching.

rows.text: A 47-year-old now holds the menu at arm's length to read it
rows.rationale: Presbyopia is expected from the 40s on.

rows.text: A 57-year-old has had a painless gray shadow over one eye since waking
rows.rationale: Sudden and painless with a curtain suggests retinal detachment. Painless does not mean minor.

rows.text: An 80-year-old cannot see for a minute after walking into a dark room
rows.rationale: Poor dark adaptation is an aging change. Teach night lights and pausing in doorways.

rows.text: A client 5 days after scleral buckling woke with sudden sharp pain in that eye
rows.rationale: Sudden pain after retinal surgery is reported immediately.

rows.text: A client 3 weeks after LASIK has dry eyes and halos at night
rows.rationale: Known complications of LASIK that are not emergencies.

rows.text: A 62-year-old has sudden severe pain in a red eye with blurred vision
rows.rationale: Sudden pain, redness and vision loss fit angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency.

questions.takeaway: Sudden is never aging. Gradual changes get teaching; sudden changes get seen, with or without pain.
questions.strategy: Ask one question of each row: did this come on suddenly? Do not let the absence of pain lower the urgency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three are gradual or expected after a procedure.
A sudden shadow is still an emergency.
Sudden pain is on the report list.

elimination.verdict: Routine, immediate, routine, immediate, routine, immediate.

questions.stem: A client is going home after scleral buckling for a retinal detachment. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll keep my head the way the surgeon showed me, even at night."
options.rationale: Correct. Positioning follows the surgeon's instructions exactly.

options.text: "My son will carry the groceries this week."
options.rationale: Correct. Lifting raises eye pressure.

options.text: "If the eye hurts and I feel sick, I'll take my nausea pill."
options.rationale: Pain with nausea is reported immediately. Treating it at home hides a rise in eye pressure.

options.text: "I'll listen to audiobooks instead of reading."
options.rationale: Correct. No reading or close work in the first week.

questions.takeaway: After retinal surgery, report at once: sudden pain, pain with nausea, sudden vision change. Do not self treat them.
questions.strategy: The nausea statement sounds sensible because vomiting would raise eye pressure. The combination of pain and nausea is the warning itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You want the wrong statement.

steps.action: Clear the three that follow the rules
steps.detail: Position, no lifting, no reading.
It manages a reportable sign at home.

elimination.verdict: Taking a nausea pill for pain with nausea.

questions.stem: At 0800 a client's pupils were 3 mm, equal and brisk. At 1200 the right is 3 mm and the left is 6 mm and sluggish. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the pupils in 30 minutes for a trend
options.rationale: Tempting, but the nurse already has a baseline and a change. Waiting adds delay, not information.

options.text: Notify the provider of the change now
options.rationale: A new unequal, sluggish pupil is a change from a documented baseline and is reported right away.

options.text: Document the sizes and continue routine checks
options.rationale: Recording size in mm is right. Stopping there treats a new finding as stable.

options.text: Ask if his pupils have always been unequal
options.rationale: Some people do have a small lifelong difference. The 0800 exam already shows these were equal.

questions.takeaway: Record pupil size in mm every time so that a change is obvious. A new unequal or sluggish pupil is reported now.
questions.strategy: Two options gather more data. The 0800 baseline in the stem already answers both of them.

steps.detail: Equal at 0800, unequal at 1200.
History and recheck are answered by the baseline.
A new change needs action.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: A landscaper has tearing and light sensitivity after debris blew into his eye. The fluorescein exam shows a speck on the surface with no penetration. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Lift the speck off with a dry cotton swab
options.rationale: A dry swab can scratch the cornea.

options.text: Shield the eye and wait for the eye surgeon
options.rationale: The right move for a penetrating object and tempting as the cautious choice. The exam showed the speck is on the surface.
