options.text: Start IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster
options.rationale: These are the steps before surgery for a penetrating injury.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: A surface foreign body is treated with a fluorescein exam and then saline irrigation.

questions.takeaway: Surface foreign body: fluorescein exam, then saline irrigation. Penetrating object: leave it, protect it, get the eye care provider.
questions.strategy: Leaving it alone is the rule for a penetrating injury. One phrase in the stem tells you this is not one.

steps.detail: On the surface, no penetration.
Shielding and IV antibiotics belong to a different injury.
Saline does not scratch.

elimination.verdict: Irrigate with sterile saline.

questions.nursesNote: Health fair screening. 64-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes. Mother used daily eye drops for "pressure". Says he has clipped door frames with his shoulder lately. Sees halos around streetlights. Denies eye pain. Reads the 20/20 line with each eye. Uses reading glasses for small print. Tonometry 27 mmHg in both eyes.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support referring this client for glaucoma evaluation.

segments.text: 64-year-old Black man with type 2 diabetes
segments.rationale: African American over 40 is a risk group, and diabetes raises risk.

segments.text: Mother used daily eye drops for "pressure"
segments.rationale: A family history of glaucoma.

segments.text: Says he has clipped door frames with his shoulder lately
segments.rationale: Peripheral vision is lost first, and he may not notice it as a vision problem.

segments.text: Sees halos around streetlights
segments.rationale: Halos around lights are listed with open-angle glaucoma.

segments.text: Denies eye pain
segments.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma is painless, so this neither supports nor rules it out.

segments.text: Reads the 20/20 line with each eye
segments.rationale: Central acuity stays normal until late. A normal result here is falsely reassuring, not a reason to refer.

segments.text: Uses reading glasses for small print
segments.rationale: Presbyopia, expected at his age.

segments.text: Tonometry 27 mmHg in both eyes
segments.rationale: Above normal and inside the 22 to 32 open-angle range.

questions.takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma hides behind a normal Snellen result and no pain. Risk group, family history, side vision loss and pressure are what find it.
questions.strategy: The 20/20 acuity and absent pain make him sound healthy. Neither one tests the part of vision glaucoma takes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age and race, diabetes, family history.
Bumping door frames, halos, pressure of 27.

steps.action: Leave the normal and the expected
steps.detail: No pain, 20/20, reading glasses.

elimination.verdict: Risk profile, family history, door frames, halos and tonometry.

questions.stem: A nurse revisits an older adult with low vision after teaching home safety. Which observation indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: New fluorescent tubes brighten the hallway
options.rationale: More light was the intent, but fluorescent light adds glare. Warm incandescent light is recommended.

options.text: Bright yellow tape marks the edge of each stair
options.rationale: Sharp contrast on stair edges is the recommended change and shows the teaching was applied.

options.text: Throw rugs are taped down at the corners
options.rationale: Tempting because it shows effort, but throw rugs are removed, not secured.

options.text: Furniture was rearranged this week to open the room
options.rationale: Objects stay in consistent places. A new layout is a new hazard.

questions.takeaway: Home adaptations for low vision: warm light without glare, clear pathways with no throw rugs, sharp contrast, and everything kept in the same place.
questions.strategy: Every option shows the client tried. Match each one against what was actually taught.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluorescent means glare.
Taped is not removed.
Rearranging breaks consistency.

elimination.verdict: Yellow tape on the stair edges.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma and COPD started timolol drops 2 weeks ago. Intraocular pressure fell from 28 to 17 mm Hg. He mentions new wheezing on the stairs. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document that the treatment goal is being met
options.rationale: Tempting because the pressure is now normal. The new wheeze is an unexpected finding that the pressure reading does not cancel.

options.text: Reteach punctal occlusion and recheck him next month
options.rationale: Tempting because punctal occlusion does cut systemic absorption. It is teaching for an actual breathing problem that the prescriber needs to hear about today.

options.text: Report the wheezing to the prescriber before the next dose
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new wheezing in a client with COPD on a beta blocker drop. The drug is reaching his lungs, and breathing outranks a good pressure reading.

options.text: Advise using his rescue inhaler before each eye drop
options.rationale: Treats the symptom and keeps giving the cause. Changing how he uses another drug is not the nurse's call.

questions.takeaway: A beta blocker eye drop can act on the lungs and heart. A good eye pressure does not make the plan effective if the drop causes wheezing.
questions.strategy: Two results are in the stem. One is expected and good. Ask which one is new and belongs to breathing.

steps.detail: Pressure 17 is the goal. Wheezing is new.

steps.action: Link the wheeze to the drug
steps.detail: Timolol is a beta blocker and he has COPD.
Reteaching is slower than reporting an actual airway effect.

elimination.verdict: Report the wheezing before the next dose.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse has four clients waiting. Each problem began or was noticed this morning. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Very nearsighted client with a painless shadow at one edge of vision
options.rationale: The quiet one is the urgent one. A new painless shadow in a nearsighted client suggests the retina is detaching, and it spreads while he waits.

options.text: Client 1 day after cataract surgery with a scratchy eye and vision not yet sharp
options.rationale: Sounds like a surgical problem and is expected on day 1. Mild scratchiness and vision that is not yet sharp are normal, with no pain or sudden loss.

options.text: Client with a corneal abrasion who has tearing and marked light sensitivity
options.rationale: The most uncomfortable client. Tearing and photophobia are expected with an abrasion that is already diagnosed.

options.text: Client with open-angle glaucoma whose side vision has narrowed since the last visit
options.rationale: Tempting because vision is being lost. This is slow, chronic loss that a short wait will not change.

questions.takeaway: Painless does not mean minor. A new shadow or curtain is acute and can progress, so it outranks expected discomfort and chronic loss.
questions.strategy: Three clients have findings that fit what they already have. Find the one whose finding is new and unexplained.

steps.detail: Day 1 cataract scratchiness and blur, abrasion tearing and photophobia.
Open-angle glaucoma loss is gradual.
New shadow in a nearsighted eye.

elimination.verdict: The nearsighted client with the new shadow.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old on a dim medical unit received a first dose of an anticholinergic 2 hours ago. She now reports brow pain, halos around the night light and nausea. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed as-needed antiemetic and reassess
options.rationale: Tempting because nausea is the complaint she wants fixed. Here nausea is a sign of rising eye pressure, so treating it alone delays the real problem.

options.text: Check visual acuity in each eye with a chart
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. The stem already gives the cue cluster, and a chart reading in a dim room will not change what must happen next.

options.text: Offer a cool cloth and darken the room further
options.rationale: A comfort measure for headache. Dim light dilates the pupil more and can worsen a blocked drainage angle.

options.text: Notify the provider now and hold the next dose
options.rationale: The deciding detail is a pupil dilating drug plus dim light followed by eye pain, halos and nausea. That cluster means a suddenly blocked drain, which is an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Eye pain with halos and nausea after a dilating drug or dim light is angle closure until proven otherwise. Recognize it and escalate.
questions.strategy: First decide what the three symptoms add up to and what happened 2 hours ago. Then pick the action that matches that problem, not the loudest symptom.

steps.detail: Brow pain, halos, nausea, dim room, anticholinergic.
Sudden rise in eye pressure.
Antiemetic and cool cloth do not lower pressure.
Enough is known to call.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now and hold the next dose.

questions.stem: Three days after cataract surgery, a client says vision is sharper each day and the eye itches a little. He adds that a few new floaters and one flash appeared last night. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document steady improvement and confirm the next visit
options.rationale: Tempting because acuity is improving and itching is expected. New floaters and a flash are not part of normal recovery.

options.text: Arrange for him to be examined today
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new floaters with a flash of light. They warn of a retinal tear even while central vision is getting better.

options.text: Reinforce no bending, lifting or straining
options.rationale: Correct teaching after cataract surgery and worth repeating. It does not address a finding that needs an eye examination.

options.text: Ask him to call if a curtain appears
options.rationale: Tempting because a curtain is the classic sign. Waiting for it means waiting for the detachment to progress.

questions.takeaway: Improving sharpness can hide a new problem. New floaters or flashes after eye surgery need a same day examination.
questions.strategy: The stem gives good news first and the important detail last. Judge the recovery by the worst new finding, not the average.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharper vision and mild itching.
Floaters and a flash.
A curtain is a late sign.

elimination.verdict: Arrange an examination today.

questions.stem: A client who is legally blind was shown the route to the bathroom once on admission. At 0200 she wants to walk there alone and refuses the bedpan. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and ask her to call each time
options.rationale: Tempting as a fall precaution. It restricts a client who can walk and does nothing to build safe independence.

options.text: Place a commode at the bedside for the night
options.rationale: Tempting because it shortens the distance. It changes her environment without orienting her to it and avoids the route she must learn.

options.text: Walk with her offering an elbow and describe the route again
options.rationale: The deciding detail is one orientation only. She is able to walk, so the least restrictive safe action is to guide and reorient until she can do it alone.

options.text: Clear the path and let her go while watching from the door
options.rationale: Respects her wish and tempts for that reason. One walk through is not enough for her to know the route in the dark.

questions.takeaway: For vision loss, give the least help that keeps the client safe: orient, describe, guide by the elbow, then step back as she learns the room.
questions.strategy: Safety and independence both matter here. Look for the option that serves both instead of trading one for the other.

steps.detail: Fall safety and least restrictive care.
Alarm and commode limit her.
She has had only one orientation.

elimination.verdict: Guide her by the elbow and describe the route again.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old on day 6 of contact isolation now believes it is 1990. Vital signs and glucose are normal. Her hearing aids are in a drawer and the blinds are closed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request a prescription for a sitter at the bedside
options.rationale: A sitter adds supervision but does not treat the cause the stem already shows.

options.text: Complete a full cognitive screening tool
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives the cause, and a screen done without her hearing aids would only measure what she cannot hear.

options.text: Insert her hearing aids and open the blinds
options.rationale: Physical causes are already checked and the cues point to sensory deprivation. Restoring meaningful input is the least restrictive fix.

options.text: Ask the provider about a dementia evaluation
options.rationale: New confusion after days of isolation is not labeled dementia before a reversible cause is corrected.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in isolation with normal vital signs and hearing aids in a drawer is sensory deprivation until proven otherwise. Give the input back first.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you the assessment. When the cause is already visible, the next step is to fix it.

steps.detail: Normal vital signs and glucose, aids in a drawer, blinds closed, six days alone.

steps.action: Notice the assess option is late
steps.detail: A cognitive screen without hearing aids gives a false result.
Hearing aids and daylight cost nothing and treat the cause.

elimination.verdict: Insert the hearing aids and open the blinds.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes has used antibiotic ear drops for external otitis for 7 days. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Deeper, worsening ear pain with new drainage
options.rationale: Worsening pain and drainage in a client with diabetes suggests necrotizing otitis spreading into bone, which can be fatal.

options.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed
options.rationale: This is the expected sign of external otitis and does not show spread.

options.text: A plugged feeling with muffled hearing on that side
options.rationale: Canal swelling causes temporary hearing loss. It is expected while the canal heals.

options.text: A request to resume wearing earbuds
options.rationale: This needs teaching to keep earbuds out for 7 to 10 days. It is not a sign of a complication.

questions.takeaway: External otitis should improve on drops. Worsening pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised client means possible necrotizing otitis.
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected for swimmer's ear. Look for the one moving in the wrong direction in a high risk client.

steps.detail: Tragus pain and a plugged ear belong to the diagnosis.
Diabetes is why the stem mentions it.
Worse after 7 days of treatment is the red flag.

elimination.verdict: Deeper, worsening pain with new drainage.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a tympanoplasty. Which statement indicates a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I will keep my mouth open if I have to sneeze."
options.rationale: Correct. It keeps pressure off the repair.

options.text: "My husband will carry the laundry baskets."
options.rationale: Correct. Lifting is straining.

options.text: "I will dab my nose and not blow it."
options.rationale: Correct. Nose blowing pushes pressure into the middle ear.

options.text: "I fly out to see my daughter this weekend."
options.rationale: Air travel changes middle ear pressure and can disrupt the graft, so it is avoided until the surgeon clears it.

questions.takeaway: After ear surgery, avoid anything that changes middle ear pressure: straining, nose blowing and air travel.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the wrong statement. Ask which plan puts pressure on the repair.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs more teaching means find the error.
Open mouth sneeze, no lifting, no nose blowing.
A flight.

elimination.verdict: The flight this weekend.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old roofer newly diagnosed with Meniere disease has had three vertigo attacks this month. He plans to return to work tomorrow. Which plan is most important?

options.text: Start a low sodium diet and limit caffeine
options.rationale: Tempting because it is the core long term teaching. It reduces attacks over time but does not protect him on a roof tomorrow.

options.text: Arrange work off ladders until attacks are controlled
options.rationale: An attack on a roof or ladder could kill him, and attacks are not yet controlled, so the safety risk is addressed first.

options.text: Begin vestibular rehabilitation exercises with a therapist
options.rationale: Balance exercises help over weeks and do not prevent an attack.

options.text: Discuss surgical options with the provider
options.rationale: Surgery is a last resort after lifestyle and drug therapy fail.

questions.takeaway: In Meniere disease, safety comes before education. No ladders or driving while attacks are uncontrolled.
questions.strategy: All four are real parts of Meniere care. His job and his plan for tomorrow decide which one cannot wait.

steps.action: Find the detail that tips it
steps.detail: He is a roofer and goes back tomorrow.
Diet lowers attack frequency slowly.
Surgery is not first line.

elimination.verdict: Keep him off ladders and roofs.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old resident has seemed to ignore staff for a week. He reports itching and fullness in the right ear and turns his left ear toward speakers. Which problem does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: One sided fullness, itching and hearing loss over a short time fit a blocked canal, the most common and most correctable cause in older adults.

options.text: Worsening presbycusis
options.rationale: Tempting because of his age. Presbycusis is gradual and affects both ears, and it does not cause itching or fullness.

options.text: Early dementia
options.rationale: Unheard words can look like inattention. The ear symptoms point to hearing, not cognition.

options.text: Sensory overload
options.rationale: Overload causes restlessness and scattered attention from too much stimulation, which the stem does not describe.

questions.takeaway: Before blaming age or cognition, look in the ear. One sided fullness and itching in an older adult suggests impacted cerumen.
questions.strategy: Age makes presbycusis the reflex answer. One sided and itchy does not fit it.

steps.detail: One ear, a week, fullness, itching.
Gradual and bilateral does not match.
Wax explains every cue.

elimination.verdict: Cerumen impaction.

questions.stem: A parent reports that a 4-year-old pushed a dried bean into the ear an hour ago. A standing order allows ear irrigation for foreign bodies. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate gently with body temperature water
options.rationale: Tempting because the technique is correct and an order exists. Water makes a bean swell and wedge tighter.

options.text: Instill mineral oil and wait before removal
options.rationale: Oil is used to suffocate a live insect. It does not help with a bean.

options.text: Soften it with ear drops, then irrigate
options.rationale: That is the plan for cerumen. Drops and water both add fluid to a bean.

options.text: Leave it and arrange removal by the provider
options.rationale: Vegetable matter expands with water, so irrigation is withheld and the provider removes it.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate vegetable matter. It swells with water and locks itself in the canal.
questions.strategy: An order and perfect technique do not make an action safe. Ask what the object is made of.

steps.detail: A dried bean is vegetable matter.
Good technique cannot fix the wrong procedure.

steps.action: Send it to the right person
steps.detail: Manual removal by the provider.

elimination.verdict: No irrigation. The provider removes it.

questions.stem: An adult is discharged with oral antibiotics for acute otitis media. Which statement indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will stop the pills once my fever has been gone for two days."
options.rationale: Stopping early leaves infection behind and risks chronic otitis and hearing damage.

options.text: "I will take every dose even after the ear stops hurting."
options.rationale: The full course is completed even when pain and fever resolve.

options.text: "I will rinse the ear with warm water if it starts to drain."
options.rationale: Drainage suggests perforation, and irrigating then spreads infection into the middle ear.

options.text: "I will keep up my gym routine to help the fluid drain."
options.rationale: Rest is part of treatment, and straining does not drain the middle ear.

questions.takeaway: Otitis media: full antibiotic course, analgesics, mild heat, rest. Never put water in an ear that is draining.
questions.strategy: Symptom relief is not the end point. Look for the statement that separates feeling better from being finished.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fever gone is not cure.
A draining ear may be perforated.
The slide teaching is rest.

elimination.verdict: Takes every dose even after the pain stops.

questions.stem: The nurse receives four call lights at once. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Client with otitis media whose severe pain stopped suddenly an hour ago
options.rationale: Tempting because it is unexpected and means the eardrum likely perforated. It must be reported, but the pressure is released and he is not in immediate danger.

options.text: Client one day after tympanoplasty asking for a pain medication
options.rationale: Postoperative pain is expected and can wait a few minutes.

options.text: Client with Meniere disease standing at the sink who says the room began spinning
options.rationale: She is upright during an attack and can drop without warning. An actual, immediate fall risk comes first.

options.text: Client on gentamicin asking when the trough level will be drawn
options.rationale: A question about a scheduled lab is stable and can wait.

questions.takeaway: Ear disorders are balance disorders. A client on her feet as vertigo starts is the one about to be injured.
questions.strategy: Two clients have unexpected changes. Ask which one can be hurt in the next minute.

steps.detail: Expected pain and a lab question.
Perforation has already happened. The fall has not.
Get her seated or into bed now.

elimination.verdict: The standing client with Meniere disease.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old at a blood pressure check mentions he woke yesterday unable to hear from his left ear. His wife says his hearing has been fading for years. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Schedule a routine audiology screening
options.rationale: Tempting because audiometry is the most reliable hearing test. A routine appointment treats a sudden change as if it were gradual.

options.text: Report the change to the provider today
options.rationale: Sudden one sided loss is never assumed to be aging and needs same day evaluation.

options.text: Teach him about hearing aid styles
options.rationale: Devices are for established loss after the cause is known.

options.text: Reassure the couple that presbycusis progresses with age
options.rationale: Presbycusis is gradual and bilateral. This explanation dismisses a new finding.

questions.takeaway: New or sudden changes are not assumed to be age related. Sudden loss in one ear is reported the same day.
questions.strategy: The wife's comment pulls you toward aging. The words woke yesterday and left ear pull you back.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Years of fading is old. Overnight in one ear is new.

steps.action: Check the timing of each option
steps.detail: Routine screening is too slow.
It explains away the cue.

elimination.verdict: Report it to the provider today.

questions.stem: A competitive swimmer was treated for external otitis and returns for follow-up. Which statement shows the prevention teaching was effective?

options.text: "I went back to the pool once the pain eased on day 3."
options.rationale: Water is avoided for 7 to 10 days, not until the pain eases.

options.text: "I wear my earbuds at practice to keep the water out."
options.rationale: Sounds protective, but earbuds are one of the causes and are avoided during healing.

options.text: "I use the leftover drops after every swim."
options.rationale: Leftover antibiotic drops are not a prevention plan.

options.text: "I stopped cleaning my ears with cotton swabs."
options.rationale: Swabs injure the canal skin, which is a listed cause of external otitis.

questions.takeaway: External otitis is prevented by protecting the canal skin: no swabs or hairpins, and no water or earbuds for 7 to 10 days during treatment.
questions.strategy: Ask which statement removes a cause of the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trauma from swabs, earphones, water.
Pain easing is not healing.
Earbuds irritate the canal.

elimination.verdict: No more cotton swabs.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old who takes aspirin for arthritis tells the clinic nurse that both ears started ringing this week. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask how much aspirin she takes each day
options.rationale: The stem does not give the dose. Tinnitus can signal too much aspirin, so the nurse gathers that cue before anything else.

options.text: Suggest a sound machine to mask the ringing at night
options.rationale: Tempting because masking is real tinnitus care. It covers a symptom whose cause has not been looked for.

options.text: Tell her to stop all aspirin until the ringing clears
options.rationale: Changing a drug regimen is the provider's decision and the amount taken is still unknown.

options.text: Schedule a hearing test for next month
options.rationale: Testing may follow, but a month's delay ignores a possible drug cause.

questions.takeaway: When a new symptom appears, check the medication list before anything else. Aspirin and NSAIDs are ototoxic.
questions.strategy: Here the assessment has not been done. No dose is given, so you ask before you act.

steps.detail: How much aspirin is unknown.
Masking hides a warning sign.
Stopping a drug is not the nurse's call.

elimination.verdict: Ask how much aspirin she takes each day.

questions.stem: A veteran with chronic tinnitus and a normal workup says the ringing is worst in his silent bedroom and keeps him awake. Which intervention does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Wear foam earplugs to bed
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds protective. Blocking outside sound makes the internal ringing more noticeable.

options.text: Ask the provider for a nightly sleeping pill
options.rationale: Sedation does not address the tinnitus and is not the first approach.

options.text: Run a fan or sound machine at the bedside
options.rationale: Background noise masks the ringing, which is worst in silence.

options.text: Avoid all background noise during the day
options.rationale: Silence is his trigger. Ear protection is for loud noise, not ordinary sound.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus is managed, not cured: masking with background sound, retraining therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you when it is worst. Pick the option that changes that condition.

steps.detail: A silent room.
Earplugs and avoiding sound.
A fan or sound machine.

elimination.verdict: A fan or sound machine at the bedside.

questions.stem: One week after a stapedectomy, a client says hearing in the operated ear is no better. He has no pain, fever or drainage. How does the nurse evaluate this?

options.text: The prosthesis has likely moved and needs urgent review
options.rationale: Tempting because he expected to hear by now. With no pain, drainage or new symptoms, nothing suggests a complication.

options.text: This is expected, and hearing is reassessed at 4 to 6 weeks
options.rationale: Hearing improves about 4 to 6 weeks after surgery, so no change at 1 week is on track.

options.text: An infection is developing and antibiotics are needed
options.rationale: He has no fever, pain or drainage.

options.text: The canal needs irrigation to clear the packing
options.rationale: Nothing is flushed into a healing ear. Keeping it dry prevents infection.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, hearing returns in about 4 to 6 weeks. Report facial weakness, fever or drainage, not slow hearing.
questions.strategy: Compare the finding with the expected timeline before calling it a problem.

steps.detail: 4 to 6 weeks.
None in the stem.
No irrigation.

elimination.verdict: Expected. Reassess at 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel shouts each instruction to a newly admitted 92-year-old, who winces. The assistive personnel says residents that age cannot hear. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Coach the assistive personnel to lower the pitch instead
options.rationale: The right technique for hearing loss and tempting. It still assumes a loss no one has assessed.

options.text: Request a referral for audiometry
options.rationale: A test is not needed before a simple bedside check.

options.text: Post a hearing impairment sign above the bed
options.rationale: Labels him with a deficit that has not been found.

options.text: Assess how well the resident hears normal speech
options.rationale: Hearing loss is not assumed in an older adult. The wince suggests he hears well, and the nurse confirms it.

questions.takeaway: Do not assume every older adult has hearing loss. Assess each person, then match the communication plan to what you find.
questions.strategy: Three options act as if the hearing loss is real. Check what the stem actually shows.

steps.detail: He winces at the volume.
Age alone was the reason for shouting.
Normal speech first.

elimination.verdict: Assess his hearing with normal speech.

questions.stem: A camper arrives at urgent care frantic, reporting buzzing and movement in the ear. A live insect is visible in the canal. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Instill oil into the canal as prescribed
options.rationale: Oil suffocates the insect so it stops moving and can be removed safely.

options.text: Irrigate the canal with body temperature water
options.rationale: Tempting because irrigation removes many objects. A live insect is never irrigated.

options.text: Shine a light at the ear to draw it out
options.rationale: This is unreliable and leaves the insect moving against the eardrum.

options.text: Ask about past ear surgery and infections
options.rationale: Useful history before irrigation. The insect is already seen, and it is killed first.

questions.takeaway: Live insect in the ear: oil first to kill it, then removal. Never irrigate a live insect.
questions.strategy: The canal has already been inspected. The question is which fluid goes in.

steps.detail: A live insect is visible.
Water makes a live insect struggle.
Oil, then removal.

elimination.verdict: Instill oil.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease has followed a low sodium diet and taken a diuretic for 2 months. Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Hearing in the affected ear has returned to normal
options.rationale: Meniere disease is progressive, and treatment is not expected to restore hearing.

options.text: She has had no falls since she stopped driving
options.rationale: Tempting because safety matters. This shows her precautions work, not that the diet and diuretic are controlling the disease.

options.text: She had two vertigo attacks this month, down from eight
options.rationale: Diet and diuretics reduce endolymph volume, so fewer attacks is the outcome they target.

options.text: Her blood pressure is lower than at diagnosis
options.rationale: The diuretic lowers blood pressure, but that is not the goal of this plan.

questions.takeaway: Meniere treatment aims at fewer and milder vertigo attacks. It does not bring back lost hearing.
questions.strategy: Match the outcome to what the treatment acts on: fluid in the inner ear.

steps.detail: Less endolymph, fewer attacks.
No falls reflects not driving.
Hearing does not return to normal.

elimination.verdict: Two attacks this month, down from eight.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with presbycusis has impacted cerumen removed from both ears. Afterward he hears the nurse better but still misses words in conversation. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the irrigation to remove remaining wax
options.rationale: Tempting because hearing is still reduced. The stem says the wax is out, and more irrigation cannot fix a nerve problem.

options.text: Document that the procedure did not work
options.rationale: It did work. The correctable part of his loss improved.

options.text: Request a referral for audiometry
options.rationale: The conductive part is fixed. The remaining sensorineural loss needs formal testing and a device.

options.text: Teach him to use softening drops every day
options.rationale: Routine drops address wax, which is no longer the cause of what remains.

questions.takeaway: Mixed loss: clearing the canal fixes the conductive part only. What remains is sensorineural and needs audiology.
questions.strategy: Partial improvement tells you there were two problems. Treat the one that is left.

steps.detail: Better, not normal.
Presbycusis is sensorineural.
Audiometry is the most reliable measure.

elimination.verdict: Refer for audiometry and hearing aid evaluation.

questions.stem: A client who is deaf and communicates by sign language and lip reading needs discharge teaching about a new medication. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange a qualified interpreter through interpreter services
options.rationale: Effective communication is a legal and ethical duty, and interpreter services provide it.

options.text: Sit facing the client in good light
options.rationale: He reads lips, so he must see the nurse's face clearly.

options.text: Provide the instructions in writing
options.rationale: Written information supports what is taught and can be reread at home.

options.text: Ask the client's teenage son to sign the instructions
options.rationale: Convenient, but a family member may leave out or change medical information.

options.text: Raise the voice so he can catch more words
options.rationale: Shouting distorts lip movement and does not help a client who is deaf.

options.text: Have the client explain the plan back through the interpreter
options.rationale: A nod is not understanding. Explaining it back confirms the teaching worked.

questions.takeaway: For a client who is deaf: interpreter services, face to face in good light, written material, and confirm understanding. Not family, not volume.
questions.strategy: The son is in the room and willing, which makes him tempting. Ask who is accountable for accuracy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Louder does not help lip reading.
Accuracy and privacy are at risk.

steps.action: Keep what lets him see, read and confirm
steps.detail: Interpreter, light, writing, explaining back.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, F.

questions.scenario: A 34-year-old has had a cold for 4 days. He woke with throbbing right ear pain, muffled hearing and a temperature of 38.4 C. Moving the pinna does not change the pain. The provider notes a red, bulging eardrum.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Give the prescribed oral antibiotic and analgesic
options.rationale: Antibiotics treat the infection and analgesics treat the pressure pain.

options.text: Irrigate the right ear canal with warm water
options.rationale: Irrigation is never done when otitis media is suspected because it can spread infection.

options.text: Apply mild heat and encourage rest
options.rationale: Mild heat and rest are the comfort measures for otitis media.

options.text: Teach him to avoid earbuds and water for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: This is the plan for external otitis, where the canal skin is inflamed.

options.text: External otitis
options.rationale: External otitis hurts when the pinna or tragus is moved. His pain does not change.

options.text: Acute otitis media
options.rationale: A cold, deep throbbing pain, fever, muffled hearing and a bulging eardrum fit a middle ear infection.

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: Wax causes fullness and hearing loss without fever or a bulging eardrum.

options.text: Meniere disease
options.rationale: There is no vertigo, and Meniere disease does not cause fever.

options.text: Ear pain level and any new drainage
options.rationale: Sudden pain relief with drainage means the eardrum has perforated and must be reported.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Falling fever shows the antibiotic is working.

options.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed
options.rationale: This tracks external otitis, not a middle ear infection.

options.text: Daily sodium intake
options.rationale: Sodium matters in Meniere disease, not in otitis media.

questions.takeaway: Otitis media is deep pressure pain behind a bulging eardrum after a cold. Treat with antibiotics, analgesics, heat and rest, and watch for sudden pain relief with drainage.
questions.strategy: The pinna finding sorts the two infections. Once you choose middle ear, the external ear actions and checks drop out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No pain with movement rules out external otitis.

steps.action: Match actions to the middle ear
steps.detail: Oral drugs, heat and rest. No irrigation.
Temperature, pain and drainage.

elimination.verdict: Acute otitis media; antibiotic with analgesic, heat and rest; pain with drainage, temperature.

questions.scenario: A client is one day past a right stapedectomy. The nurse reviews the morning findings.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with safety measures or must be reported to the surgeon.

rows.text: Feels dizzy when he first stands up
rows.rationale: Vertigo is common after stapedectomy. The nurse assists with walking.

rows.text: Right side of the mouth droops when he smiles
rows.rationale: The facial nerve runs close to the surgical site, so new facial weakness is reported at once.

rows.text: Hearing in the right ear is muffled
rows.rationale: Hearing improves in about 4 to 6 weeks.

rows.text: Temperature 38.6 C with yellow drainage on the dressing
rows.rationale: Fever with purulent drainage suggests infection, a postoperative priority.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, dizziness and muffled hearing are expected. Facial weakness and signs of infection are not.
questions.strategy: Ask of each row: is this the surgery healing, or the surgery being harmed?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vertigo and delayed hearing.
Facial droop means possible cranial nerve VII injury.
Fever with yellow drainage.

elimination.verdict: Expected, report, expected, report.

questions.stem: A client with Meniere disease is in bed with the side rails up, call light in reach and lights dimmed. She is still spinning and has vomited twice. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic and antivertigo drugs
options.rationale: The deciding detail is that every safety measure is already in place. The actual problem left is the vertigo and vomiting, so treat it.

options.text: Stay at the bedside and reassess her fall risk
options.rationale: Tempting because safety usually comes first. Safety is already secured, and reassessing adds nothing while she keeps vomiting.

options.text: Encourage sips of oral fluids to replace what she has lost
options.rationale: Fluid loss matters after vomiting. She cannot keep fluids down until the nausea is controlled.

options.text: Review the low sodium diet while she rests
options.rationale: Useful prevention teaching for later. A client in an acute attack cannot learn.

questions.takeaway: In an acute vertigo attack, make her safe, then treat the symptoms. Once safety is done, do not keep repeating it.
questions.strategy: Check what the stem says is already done. The next step is whatever problem is still untreated.

steps.detail: Rails, call light, dim lights, in bed.
Spinning and vomiting.
Fluids and teaching wait for symptom control.

elimination.verdict: Give the prescribed medications.

questions.stem: A client on day 8 of IV gentamicin says his ears started ringing today and he feels off balance when he turns. The next dose is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose and report the symptoms on rounds
options.rationale: Tempting because the infection still needs treating. Another dose adds to damage that can become permanent.

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the prescriber
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new ringing plus imbalance on an ototoxic drug. Those are the early warning, and the nurse acts before the next dose goes in.

options.text: Do a whisper test before deciding about the dose
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. He has already reported the cues, and a normal whisper test would not make the dose safe.

options.text: Give the dose slowly and teach him to rise carefully
options.rationale: Addresses the fall risk and keeps giving the cause. Slowing the infusion is not a fix the nurse can assume.

questions.takeaway: New tinnitus, hearing change or dizziness on an ototoxic drug means stop and report before the next dose.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already in the stem. Ask whether more data would change what you do with the dose in your hand.

steps.action: Link the cues to the drug
steps.detail: Gentamicin is ototoxic.
The dose is due now.
Harm continues with each dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and notify the prescriber.

questions.stem: The nurse has four clients with ear problems. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Client the morning after stapedectomy who is dizzy when turning the head
options.rationale: Dizziness looks worrying and is expected early after ear surgery. Safety measures cover it.

options.text: Client with external otitis who has pain when the pinna is pulled
options.rationale: Painful and expected. Pain with movement of the pinna is how external otitis presents.

options.text: Client with otitis media who has new tender swelling behind the ear
options.rationale: The quiet finding is the unexpected one. Swelling and tenderness over the mastoid mean infection is spreading from the middle ear.

options.text: Client with Meniere disease who is spinning and vomiting in bed
options.rationale: The most dramatic client. Vertigo and vomiting are the expected attack, and she is already in bed.

questions.takeaway: Dizziness after ear surgery, pain with external otitis and vertigo with Meniere disease are expected. Redness, swelling or pain behind the ear is reported.
questions.strategy: Match each finding to its condition. Three fit. The one that does not fit its diagnosis is first.

steps.detail: Postoperative dizziness, pinna pain, Meniere vertigo.
Otitis media should not cause swelling behind the ear.
Vomiting in bed is unpleasant and expected.

elimination.verdict: The client with otitis media and mastoid swelling.

questions.stem: An older adult has ear fullness and visible cerumen. A standing order allows irrigation. He mentions the same ear drained fluid after an infection last month. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Irrigate with body temperature water aimed at the canal wall
options.rationale: Correct technique and the usual answer for cerumen. Recent drainage suggests the eardrum may not be intact, and water could enter the middle ear.

options.text: Instill softening drops now and irrigate tomorrow
options.rationale: Tempting because softening first is standard. Drops and irrigation both go through a possible perforation.

options.text: Irrigate gently and stop if he reports dizziness
options.rationale: Stopping for dizziness is right during a safe irrigation. It does not make this one safe to start.

options.text: Hold the irrigation until the eardrum is examined
options.rationale: The deciding detail is drainage after an infection last month. A possible perforation means nothing goes into the canal until the eardrum is seen.

questions.takeaway: A standing order covers the usual client. Recent ear drainage or a possible perforation means no irrigation and no drops until the eardrum is checked.
questions.strategy: Three options put fluid in the ear. Ask what one detail in the history makes any fluid unsafe.

steps.detail: Three options instill fluid.
Drainage after infection last month.
Possible perforation rules out all three.

elimination.verdict: Hold the irrigation until the eardrum is examined.

questions.stem: A client on day 2 of antibiotics for otitis media says the severe ear pain stopped suddenly overnight. He found drainage on the pillow and wants to stop the medicine. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: The pain relief shows the antibiotic is working well
options.rationale: Tempting because relief looks like success. Sudden relief with drainage means the eardrum ruptured, not that the infection cleared.

options.text: Keep the ear dry, finish the antibiotic and be examined
options.rationale: The deciding detail is sudden relief plus drainage. Pressure released through a perforation, so the infection still needs treatment and the eardrum needs a look.

options.text: Rinse the ear canal gently to clear the drainage
options.rationale: Tempting to clean the ear. Nothing is flushed into an ear with a likely perforation.

options.text: Stop the antibiotic if you stay pain free for a full day
options.rationale: Fits his wish and the lack of pain. Stopping early leaves the infection partly treated.

questions.takeaway: Ear pain that stops suddenly with drainage is a perforation. It looks like improvement and still needs the full antibiotic course, a dry ear and an examination.
questions.strategy: Ask how the pain went away. Gradual relief is the drug working. Sudden relief with drainage is something else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden relief, drainage, day 2.
The eardrum perforated.

steps.action: Cut options that add fluid or stop treatment
steps.detail: Irrigation and stopping early are both unsafe.

elimination.verdict: Keep the ear dry, finish the antibiotic and be examined.

questions.stem: Two days after knee arthroscopy, a client phones the clinic. The knee is more swollen than yesterday and the pain has gone from mild to severe. He has not taken today's analgesic. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Take the analgesic and call back in an hour
options.rationale: Tempting because he has not taken it yet. Pain and swelling that are increasing are reported first; an analgesic would only quiet the warning.

options.text: Ice the knee and raise it above the heart
options.rationale: Right for expected swelling that is settling. His is getting worse on day 2.

options.text: Call the surgeon about these changes now
options.rationale: Severe pain or increasing swelling after arthroscopy is reported to the surgeon right away. It can mean infection or a clot.

options.text: Rest today and mention it at the follow-up visit
options.rationale: Delays the report of a change that needs to be seen now.

questions.takeaway: After arthroscopy, pain or swelling that increases is reported to the surgeon at once. Comfort measures are for symptoms that are improving.
questions.strategy: Ask which direction the symptoms are moving. Worse on day 2 is unexpected, and unexpected findings are reported before they are treated.

steps.detail: More swollen than yesterday, mild to severe.
The missed analgesic explains some pain. It does not explain more swelling.
Ice, elevation and rest fit expected symptoms.

elimination.verdict: Call the surgeon now. Worsening after arthroscopy is not managed at home.

questions.stem: A patient has four hours until a bone scan after the isotope injection. Which statement indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "My family should stay out of the bathroom I use tonight."
options.rationale: No special handling of urine or stool is needed after a bone scan.

options.text: "I will drink extra fluids once the scan is done."
options.rationale: Fluids help the kidneys clear the isotope, which is the one piece of aftercare.

options.text: "I can have my contrast CT while I wait."
options.rationale: Other tests using contrast or isotopes cannot be done during the uptake period.

options.text: "I can shift around during the scan to stay comfortable."
options.rationale: The scan takes 30 to 60 minutes and the patient must lie still.

questions.takeaway: Bone scan: isotope 4 to 6 hours ahead, no other contrast tests in that window, lie still, then push fluids. No excreta precautions.
questions.strategy: The bathroom statement sounds careful, which is why it is tempting. The text says no precautions are needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check each statement against the procedure
steps.detail: Excreta precautions, a second contrast test and moving are all wrong.
Fluids speed urinary excretion of the isotope.

elimination.verdict: B. Extra fluids after the scan.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old soccer player twisted his knee, and it now buckles on stairs. He walks with mild pain, and the knee x-ray is normal. Which test does the nurse anticipate next?

options.text: A bone scan of the knee
options.rationale: Tempting because a normal x-ray followed by another test sounds like a hidden fracture. He bears weight with mild pain, and a twisting injury with buckling points to soft tissue.

options.text: A CT scan of the knee
options.rationale: CT gives more bone detail for a complex fracture. No fracture was seen and the cues are not bony.

options.text: A repeat x-ray in one week
options.rationale: A second plain film shows bone again. It cannot show a ligament or cartilage.

options.text: An MRI of the knee
options.rationale: A knee that gives way after a twist with a normal x-ray suggests a torn ligament or cartilage, and MRI is the soft tissue test.

questions.takeaway: Ask what needs to be seen. Bone starts with x-ray. A joint that gives way with a normal x-ray is a soft tissue question, which goes to MRI.
questions.strategy: A normal x-ray tells you to move on. The cues decide where: cannot bear weight after a fall points to a bone scan, while twisting and buckling point to MRI.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A twist, buckling, and he can still walk on it.
CT and a repeat x-ray look at bone, which already looked normal.
A bone scan hunts a hidden fracture. He bears weight, so soft tissue is the question.

elimination.verdict: MRI of the knee. Soft tissue injury is the likely problem.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with diabetes cannot feel light touch on either foot and has weak ankles. Thigh strength is full. Which intervention leads the mobility plan?

options.text: Quad sets and straight leg lifts twice a day
options.rationale: Her thigh strength is already full, so this treats a problem she does not have.

options.text: Longer hallway walks to build endurance
options.rationale: Tempting because activity is the goal. Walking farther on feet she cannot feel raises the fall risk before it is addressed.

options.text: Passive range of motion to both ankles
options.rationale: She can move her own joints, and this does nothing for lost sensation.

options.text: Supportive shoes and a walker evaluation
options.rationale: Distal weakness with sensory loss is a nerve pattern. She cannot sense the floor, so safety and a wider base of support come first.

questions.takeaway: Weakness and numbness in the feet point to nerve trouble, and in the legs that means fall risk. Safety leads the plan.
questions.strategy: Sort the cues: distal and sensory means nerve, proximal means muscle. Then pick the option that protects her before the one that conditions her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Numb feet and weak ankles with strong thighs.
Quad sets and passive motion miss the problem.
Endurance is a later goal. Protection from falls is first.

elimination.verdict: Shoes and a walker evaluation. Make walking safe, then make it longer.

questions.stem: In a cold emergency room, a patient with a sprained right ankle has a right foot that feels cool. The pedal pulse is palpable and capillary refill is 2 seconds. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Notify the provider of impaired circulation
options.rationale: Tempting because a cool extremity is a red flag, but pulse and refill are normal and the comparison is not done yet.

options.text: Feel the temperature of the left foot
options.rationale: Neurovascular findings are judged against the other side. Two equally cool feet in a cold room is not a circulation problem.

options.text: Wrap the foot in a warmed blanket
options.rationale: Warming before comparing can hide a real difference between the feet.

options.text: Lower the leg below heart level
options.rationale: Dependent positioning increases swelling in a fresh sprain.

questions.takeaway: Start with the injured side, then compare with the other. One finding alone is not a red flag until the comparison is done.
questions.strategy: Here the assess first reflex is right. The stem gives half an assessment: one foot.

steps.detail: Pulse and refill are normal. The other foot has not been checked.
The provider will ask how the left foot feels.
Compare sides.

elimination.verdict: B. Compare sides before deciding it is abnormal.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old with kyphosis walks with a widened gait and says she feels unsteady getting up from her low sofa. Which interventions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sit in a firm chair with armrests
options.rationale: A higher seat with arms lets her push up while her balance catches up.

options.text: Practice walking with the feet closer together
options.rationale: The widened gait is how she compensates for a shifted center of gravity. Narrowing it takes away her base of support.

options.text: Ask about a referral to assess the need for a cane or walker
options.rationale: A device widens the base of support, and therapy judges which one fits.

options.text: Wear supportive shoes that fit well
options.rationale: Stable footwear improves contact with the floor.

options.text: Replace daily walks with seated exercises
options.rationale: Sounds safer, but weight-bearing activity is what maintains bone and leg strength. Walking is made safe, not removed.

questions.takeaway: Kyphosis and a widened gait shift the center of gravity. Support balance with chairs with arms, a device if needed and good shoes, and keep her walking.
questions.strategy: Judge each option alone: does it steady her while keeping her active? Options that take away her base of support or her walking fail.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Armrests, a device evaluation and shoes.
A wide stance is her compensation, so narrowing it is unsafe.
Giving up weight bearing speeds bone and muscle loss.

elimination.verdict: Armrests, device referral, supportive shoes. Three of five.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest after hip surgery wears sequential compression devices and does ankle pumps hourly. Which finding on day 4 indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Both calves are equal in size, soft and nontender
options.rationale: No swelling, warmth or tenderness means no sign of thrombus, which is what the plan targets.

options.text: The patient sleeps through the night with the sleeves on
options.rationale: Shows the device is tolerated, which does not measure clot prevention.

options.text: Pedal pulses are strong in both feet
options.rationale: Arterial pulses do not show whether venous stasis was prevented.

options.text: The patient reports less incisional pain
options.rationale: A good outcome for analgesia, unrelated to this plan.

questions.takeaway: Judge an intervention by the complication it targets. Compression and leg exercises target venous stasis and thrombus.
questions.strategy: Strong pulses look like a circulation win. They are arterial. The plan is about veins.

steps.detail: Prevent venous stasis and thrombus.
Sleep, arterial pulses and incision pain.
Equal, soft, nontender.

elimination.verdict: A. Calves without signs of thrombus.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old has left groin pain and cannot bear weight after a fall. The hip x-ray is negative and a bone scan is scheduled. She asks to walk to the bathroom. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Walk her with a gait belt and a walker
options.rationale: Tempting because the x-ray is negative and the equipment looks safe. A walker still puts weight through a hip that may be broken.

options.text: Pivot her to a commode placed beside the bed
options.rationale: A pivot is still weight bearing on the painful leg.

options.text: Keep her off the leg and offer a bedpan
options.rationale: Pain with inability to bear weight after a fall is a hidden fracture until the bone scan says otherwise.

options.text: Give the analgesic, then reassess her ability to stand
options.rationale: Pain relief does not make the bone safe to load.

questions.takeaway: A normal test does not beat a clearly abnormal patient. Protect the limb while the next test finds the answer.
questions.strategy: Ask why a bone scan was ordered after a negative x-ray. The provider still suspects a fracture, so the nurse acts as if there is one.

steps.detail: Groin pain, cannot bear weight, another test pending.
Three options put weight on the leg in some form.
No weight bearing and toileting in bed.

elimination.verdict: Off the leg, bedpan. An occult fracture is assumed until ruled out.

questions.stem: The nurse checks a client the day after a needle biopsy of the tibia. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Site pain of 3 of 10 when walking
options.rationale: Mild pain the day after a bone biopsy is expected.

options.text: A dry stain no larger than yesterday's outline
options.rationale: Old drainage that has not spread means the bleeding stopped.

options.text: A small bruise around the puncture site
options.rationale: Tempting because it is visible and new. A small bruise is expected after a needle through tissue.

options.text: Skin around the site that is warm and tender
options.rationale: Warmth, tenderness or redness at a biopsy site suggests infection and is reported.

questions.takeaway: After a bone or muscle biopsy, watch for active bleeding and for tenderness, redness or warmth that suggests infection.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as expected or unexpected for day 1. Bruising and mild pain are expected. Warmth is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stain is dry and unchanged.
Small and local, an expected result of the needle.
Warm and tender is an infection cue.

elimination.verdict: Warm, tender skin. Report possible infection.

questions.stem: A client about to leave for a CT of the spine with contrast mentions breaking out in hives after a dye test years ago. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold transport and call the provider
options.rationale: A prior reaction to iodine contrast must reach the team before any contrast is given. They decide whether to premedicate, change the test or proceed.

options.text: Add the reaction to the chart, then send her
options.rationale: Charting is needed, but the chart alone does not stop the contrast.

options.text: Send her and alert radiology staff to watch closely
options.rationale: Tempting because radiology manages reactions. Watching for a reaction is not the same as preventing one.

options.text: Ask about shellfish allergy before sending her
options.rationale: Shellfish allergy is no longer treated as a contrast risk. The prior contrast reaction is the cue.

questions.takeaway: Before a CT with contrast, ask about any earlier contrast reaction. A positive answer pauses the test until the team decides.
questions.strategy: Three options send her to the scanner. Ask whether the new information should change the plan before she goes.

steps.detail: Hives after dye is a prior contrast reaction.
Three options let the contrast go ahead.
The provider and radiology decide what happens next.

elimination.verdict: Hold transport and call. The decision belongs to the team before contrast is given.

questions.stem: A woman treated for a muscle disease could not climb stairs or comb her hair last month. Which finding best indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: Creatine kinase unchanged, grip strength stronger
options.rationale: Tempting because strength improved. Her deficit was near the trunk, not in the hands, and the enzyme shows muscle is still leaking.

options.text: Less morning joint stiffness, stairs still difficult
options.rationale: Stiffness was not her problem, and the lost function has not returned.

options.text: Aldolase falling, climbs one flight unaided
options.rationale: A falling muscle enzyme means less muscle damage, and the function she lost has come back.

options.text: AST falling, still cannot rise from a chair alone
options.rationale: AST also comes from the liver, and her hip weakness is unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Damaged muscle leaks enzymes: CK-MM, LDH, AST, aldolase. Improvement shows as falling levels plus return of the lost function.
questions.strategy: Go back to what she could not do: stairs and hair, both proximal. The best evidence is a better lab and that same function returning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weak hips and shoulders.
Grip and joint stiffness were never the problem.
Only one pairs a falling enzyme with returned function.

elimination.verdict: Aldolase down and one flight climbed. Lab and function agree.

questions.scenario: A 76-year-old has been on bed rest for 8 days with a plan of turning every 2 hours, range of motion, incentive spirometry, fluids and compression devices.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the plan is effective or not effective.

rows.text: Breath sounds clear to both bases
rows.rationale: Lung expansion is maintained, so no atelectasis.

rows.text: Left ankle cannot be brought up to neutral
rows.rationale: A plantar flexion contracture is forming despite range of motion.

rows.text: Sacral skin intact and blanches
rows.rationale: Turning is relieving pressure.

rows.text: No bowel movement for 5 days
rows.rationale: Reduced motility has become constipation.

rows.text: Urine pale yellow and clear
rows.rationale: Good flow with no sign of stasis or infection.

rows.text: Feels lightheaded each time the head of the bed is raised
rows.rationale: Orthostatic intolerance is developing. She needs gradual position changes and leg exercises before she is stood.

questions.takeaway: Immobility touches every system, so evaluate the plan one system at a time: lungs, joints, skin, bowel, urine, circulation.
questions.strategy: For each row ask which complication the finding belongs to and whether it happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pair each finding with a system
steps.detail: Lungs, joint, skin, bowel, urine, circulation.
Contracture, constipation and lightheadedness did.

elimination.verdict: Effective, not, effective, not, effective, not.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest keeps two pillows under the knees all day because it eases his back. Which intervention does the nurse include in the plan?

options.text: Add a third pillow under the calves
options.rationale: More flexion and more pressure behind the knees.

options.text: Schedule periods with the legs extended and range of motion
options.rationale: Knees and hips held flexed all day shorten, so the joints need time in extension and movement.

options.text: Remove the pillows and keep him flat
options.rationale: Ignores his comfort when a schedule solves both.

options.text: Raise the knee section of the bed instead
options.rationale: The same constant flexion by another method.

questions.takeaway: A joint held in one position shortens. Prevent contractures with position changes, alignment and range of motion.
questions.strategy: Two options keep the knees bent and one takes away all comfort. The plan that alternates is the workable one.

steps.action: Remove the options that keep constant flexion
steps.detail: Extra pillow and knee gatch.
Alternating respects comfort and protects the joints.

elimination.verdict: B. Alternate extension with range of motion.

questions.stem: On day 2 after abdominal surgery, a client has diminished breath sounds at both bases, rates incisional pain 8 of 10 and refuses the incentive spirometer. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Explain how the spirometer prevents pneumonia
options.rationale: He is not refusing from lack of knowledge. He is refusing because it hurts.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic
options.rationale: Pain at 8 of 10 is the barrier. Once it is controlled he can sit up, splint and breathe deeply.

options.text: Coach him through ten spirometer breaths now
options.rationale: He cannot take a deep breath through this pain, so coaching fails.

options.text: Sit him upright and splint the incision
options.rationale: Tempting because both help lung expansion. They come second: at this pain level he still will not breathe deeply.

questions.takeaway: Pain blocks deep breathing and movement. Control it first so lung expansion can happen.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already done: pain is 8 and he refuses. Ask what is stopping him and remove that first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain of 8 of 10, not lack of understanding.
Neither changes the pain.
Analgesic first, then upright with splinting.

elimination.verdict: Analgesic first. Then position, splint and use the spirometer.

questions.stem: On day 9 of bed rest a 47-year-old says, "Every day is the same. I can't do anything for myself." Which intervention does the nurse include?

options.text: Have him plan the day and share in his care
options.rationale: He named loss of independence. Giving him choices and tasks he can do answers what he said.

options.text: Remind him the bed rest is temporary and he is healing
options.rationale: Brushes past the feeling he just described.

options.text: Ask the provider about an antidepressant
options.rationale: Tempting because immobility can lead to depression. One statement of frustration calls for nursing measures and continued assessment first.

options.text: Keep the television on and arrange more visitors
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats boredom. His second sentence is about control, which this leaves untouched.

questions.takeaway: Immobility has psychosocial effects: boredom, isolation, loss of independence, depression. Give back control wherever the client can take it.
questions.strategy: Listen to both sentences. The first is boredom. The second is loss of independence, and the best option answers that one.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: "I can't do anything for myself."
It dismisses what he said.
Only one option hands him decisions and tasks.

elimination.verdict: Let him plan the day and share his care. Independence is the problem he named.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients who are on bed rest. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: One with a heel that is red and blanches
options.rationale: Early pressure and needs offloading soon, but the skin is intact.

options.text: One whose casted foot is cool with new tingling
options.rationale: A true red flag and the strongest runner up. A limb is at risk, while another patient's breathing is failing.

options.text: One with sudden shortness of breath and chest pain
options.rationale: After bed rest this suggests a clot that has moved to the lung. Breathing comes before limb.

options.text: One with no bowel movement for 3 days
options.rationale: Uncomfortable and not urgent.

questions.takeaway: Two urgent patients: rank by ABCs. Sudden dyspnea in an immobile patient outranks a threatened limb, which is seen next.
questions.strategy: Do not stop at the first red flag you recognize. Read all four, then rank airway and breathing above circulation to a limb.

steps.detail: Blanching heel and constipation.
Breathing before limb circulation.

elimination.verdict: C. Sudden shortness of breath.

questions.stem: After a hallway walk, a patient's heart rate rose from 76 to 98 and returned to 78 within 3 minutes. He reports mild tiredness and no dyspnea or dizziness. Which decision about tomorrow's walk is most appropriate?

options.text: Cancel the walk and reassess in two days
options.rationale: Nothing shows intolerance, and rest costs strength.

options.text: Have him walk only to the doorway
options.rationale: Reduces activity after a good response.

options.text: Repeat the same distance each day for a week
options.rationale: Tempting as the cautious choice, but a quick recovery with no symptoms supports progressing.

options.text: Increase the distance a little and reassess
options.rationale: A modest rise with fast recovery means he tolerated it, so activity advances gradually.

questions.takeaway: Tolerance is judged by the response and the recovery. A quick return to baseline without symptoms supports progressive activity.
questions.strategy: The recovery time is the detail that tips it. Three minutes back to baseline is a pass.

steps.detail: Mild rise, mild tiredness, no warning symptoms.
Baseline in 3 minutes.
Small increase with reassessment.

elimination.verdict: D. Progress gradually.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: day 10 of bed rest after pelvic fracture. Turned to left side with pillows. Urinary catheter tubing lies under the right thigh. Heels rest on the mattress. Respirations 18 and unlabored. Right foot warm with palpable pulse. Reports comfort at 2 of 10. Left ear folded under the head.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up after this repositioning.

segments.text: Urinary catheter tubing lies under the right thigh
segments.rationale: Tubing under the body presses on skin and can block drainage.

segments.text: Heels rest on the mattress
segments.rationale: Heels are a pressure point and should be floated.

segments.text: Respirations 18 and unlabored
segments.rationale: She is breathing comfortably in the new position.

segments.text: Right foot warm with palpable pulse
segments.rationale: Normal circulation.

segments.text: Reports comfort at 2 of 10
segments.rationale: Acceptable comfort.

segments.text: Left ear folded under the head
segments.rationale: A folded ear on the down side is a pressure area.

questions.takeaway: After every reposition, recheck alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and breathing.
questions.strategy: Walk the reassessment list. Three findings are pressure or tubing problems the turn created.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both fine.
Tubing, heels and ear need correcting.

questions.stem: During a mobility assessment, a patient sits at the bedside for 4 minutes but tips sideways when asked to reach across to shake the nurse's hand. Which conclusion guides the transfer plan?

options.text: He needs total assist equipment for transfers
options.rationale: He cannot reach across midline, so seated balance fails and he is Level 1 despite sitting upright.

options.text: He can try straightening each knee next
options.rationale: Tempting because he sat for 4 minutes, but every part of the first test must be passed before moving on.

options.text: He can stand with a walker and one staff helper
options.rationale: Standing is two levels beyond what he has shown.

options.text: He can transfer with standing equipment
options.rationale: Standing equipment is for a client who straightens both knees but cannot stand. He has not passed the first test.

questions.takeaway: Sit and shake has three parts: sit unassisted over 2 minutes, reach across midline, shake the hand. Miss one and the patient is Level 1.
questions.strategy: Sitting time alone looks like a pass. The tipping on the reach is the cue that decides it.

steps.detail: Sitting time only.
Reaching across midline.
Fail any part, stay at that level.

elimination.verdict: A. Level 1, total assist.

questions.stem: A client is being admitted for same-day knee arthroscopy. Which finding does the nurse report to the surgeon before the procedure?

options.text: He asks how long to use ice afterward
options.rationale: A teaching need the nurse can meet.

options.text: The knee is warmer and redder than the other knee
options.rationale: Warmth and redness on one side suggest infection, and an infected joint rules out arthroscopy.

options.text: The knee is swollen and painful when bent to 90 degrees
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds abnormal. Swelling and pain are why he is having the procedure, and the joint still moves.

options.text: The knee has clicked and given way since the injury
options.rationale: The complaint that led to the arthroscopy.

questions.takeaway: Arthroscopy needs a joint that can move and is not infected. Signs of infection are reported before the procedure.
questions.strategy: Separate the findings that explain why he needs the scope from the one finding that would cancel it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Swelling, pain, clicking and giving way belong to the injury.
One knee warmer and redder than the other is new information.
Infection is a contraindication.

elimination.verdict: Warm, red knee. Report possible infection before the scope.

questions.stem: Four hours after a forearm cast, a client's fingers are pink and warm with brisk capillary refill. He now reports tingling and cannot feel light touch on the fingertips. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Elevate the arm, apply ice and recheck in 45 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because elevation and ice are right for swelling. New loss of sensation is a change in the nerve check and should not wait 45 minutes.

options.text: Document intact circulation and continue hourly checks
options.rationale: Tempting because color, warmth and refill are normal. Circulation is only half of the check, and sensation has changed.

options.text: Give the as-needed analgesic and reassess comfort
options.rationale: Treats discomfort. It can mask a finding that is getting worse.

options.text: Notify the provider of the change in sensation now
options.rationale: The deciding detail is new tingling and lost light touch. Nerve findings change before color and pulses do, so a normal looking hand does not clear him.

questions.takeaway: A neurovascular check has two halves. Normal color, warmth and refill do not cancel a new change in sensation or movement.
questions.strategy: The stem leads with reassuring findings. Check every part of the circ check before deciding the limb is fine.

steps.detail: Color, temperature, refill, sensation, movement, pain.
Sensation.
Elevation helps swelling. A new deficit is reported.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: After 5 days of bed rest a client dangles at the bedside. Blood pressure falls from 126/78 to 108/66 and he feels slightly lightheaded. He is alert and eager to walk. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep him sitting, have him pump his ankles, then recheck
options.rationale: The deciding details are that he is alert, sitting and only slightly lightheaded. Gradual progression continues at the step he has not yet tolerated.

options.text: Return him to supine and defer walking until tomorrow
options.rationale: Tempting as the safest choice. More bed rest worsens the orthostatic problem, and his symptoms do not require lying flat.

options.text: Stand him with a gait belt and two staff members
options.rationale: Tempting because help is present and he is eager. Dizziness while sitting means he is not ready for the next step.

options.text: Offer fluids and try standing after he drinks
options.rationale: Fluids help prevent orthostatic drops. Drinking does not replace rechecking his pressure and symptoms first.

questions.takeaway: Sit, dangle, then stand. If a step is not tolerated, stay at that step and recheck. Do not push on and do not give up the day.
questions.strategy: Safety says stop. Mobility says keep going. Look for the option that holds him where he is until the numbers say move.

steps.detail: Orthostatic drop after bed rest.
Dizzy while sitting means no standing yet.
Bed rest is the cause.

elimination.verdict: Keep him sitting, pump the ankles and recheck.

questions.stem: An unconscious client has had passive range of motion to the hips, knees and arms for 2 weeks. Those joints move fully. Both feet rest pointed down and cannot be brought to neutral. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Continue the current plan because joint motion is maintained
options.rationale: Tempting because most joints look good. The ankles show the plan left a joint out.

options.text: Increase passive range of motion to build leg strength
options.rationale: Tempting to do more of what works. Passive movement keeps joints flexible and does not build strength, and it misses the ankle.

options.text: Add ankle range of motion and neutral alignment supports
options.rationale: The deciding detail is feet fixed in plantar flexion. Foot drop is developing, so the ankle needs range of motion, neutral positioning and a supportive device.

options.text: Request physical therapy for isometric leg exercises
options.rationale: Therapy input is reasonable. Isometric exercise needs a client who can contract muscles on request.

questions.takeaway: Judge a mobility plan by every joint. Feet that rest pointed down are an early plantar flexion contracture and need neutral alignment, range of motion and support.
questions.strategy: Most of the stem is good news. The evaluation turns on the one joint that was not listed in the plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hips, knees and arms treated. Ankles not.
Foot drop.

steps.action: Check each fix against the client
steps.detail: He is unconscious, so only passive care and positioning apply.

elimination.verdict: Add ankle range of motion and neutral supports.

questions.stem: A nurse and an assistive personnel are planning morning care. Which activity does the nurse keep rather than delegate?

options.text: Walking a client who walked steadily in the hall twice yesterday
