options.rationale: Routine and stable. The client's response is already known, so it can be delegated.

options.text: Passive range of motion for a stable unconscious client
options.rationale: Tempting to keep because the client cannot report pain. It is a routine task in an established plan with a predictable outcome.

options.text: Turning a client whose reddened sacrum was assessed earlier
options.rationale: Tempting because skin is a concern. The nurse has already assessed, and turning on schedule is a task.

options.text: First dangle and stand after a week of bed rest
options.rationale: The deciding detail is first time up. The response is unknown, so the nurse assesses tolerance and blood pressure before anyone else takes over.

questions.takeaway: Delegate routine tasks with predictable outcomes. The first time out of bed after bed rest is an assessment, and assessment stays with the nurse.
questions.strategy: For each option ask one thing: is the client's response already known? Tasks delegate. Unknown responses do not.

steps.detail: Three repeat a known routine.
No one has seen this client upright yet.
Unconscious and reddened skin sound risky, but both are stable and assessed.

elimination.verdict: The first dangle and stand after bed rest.

questions.stem: On day 6 of bed rest a client's left calf is painless, warm and 2 cm larger than the right. Compression sleeves are off for a bath and a hallway walk is due. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Leave the sleeves off, cancel the walk, notify the provider
options.rationale: The deciding detail is one calf warmer and larger than the other. Prevention steps stop once a clot is suspected, because squeezing or walking could dislodge it.

options.text: Reapply the sleeves and walk him to improve blood flow
options.rationale: Tempting because both are the right way to prevent clots. This is now a possible actual clot, not a risk.

options.text: Elevate the leg, apply warmth and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Sounds like comfort care for swelling. It delays reporting, and no treatment is started without the provider.

options.text: Measure both calves again at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Tempting because he has no pain. A painless clot is still a clot, and the difference is already measured.

questions.takeaway: Compression and walking prevent clots. A warm, swollen calf on bed rest is treated as an actual clot: stop, keep him resting and report.
questions.strategy: Decide first whether this is a risk or an actual problem. Prevention rules apply only to the risk.

steps.detail: One warm, larger calf after bed rest.
Actual problem beats prevention routine.
No pain does not rule it out.

elimination.verdict: Leave the sleeves off, cancel the walk and notify the provider.

questions.stem: An assistive worker reports that a patient admitted after a fall this morning "seems sleepier than before lunch." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Call the provider with the assistive worker's report
options.rationale: Tempting because a change after a fall is urgent. The nurse has no findings of her own yet, so there is nothing specific to report.

options.text: Go to the bedside to check alertness and command following
options.rationale: A reported change is a cue that the nurse must assess herself right away and compare with baseline.

options.text: Ask the assistive worker to recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Waiting delays the assessment. Judging level of consciousness is not the assistive worker's role.

options.text: Review the chart for sedating medications given today
options.rationale: A reasonable cause to consider after the patient has been seen.

questions.takeaway: A secondhand report of a change is a cue. The nurse assesses the patient herself before she calls.
questions.strategy: Calling and assessing both sound urgent. The stem gives a report from someone else and no nursing assessment, so assessment is still due.

steps.action: Ask what the nurse knows firsthand
steps.detail: Nothing yet. "Sleepier" is another person's impression.
A 30 minute recheck and a chart review both leave the patient unseen.
A call needs findings and a baseline comparison.

elimination.verdict: Go to the bedside and assess level of consciousness now.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old admitted with cellulitis had equal hand grips at 0730. Which finding at 1130 is most concerning?

options.text: Fine tremor in both hands, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Abnormal, yet it matches the admission baseline.

options.text: Needs both arms to push up from the chair
options.rationale: Tempting because it is weakness. It is the same on both sides and common with age, so it does not point to the brain.

options.text: Takes longer to answer, with correct answers
options.rationale: Slower processing with accurate answers is an expected change with aging.

options.text: Right grip weaker than the left
options.rationale: A new one sided difference from this morning's baseline points to a new neurologic problem.

questions.takeaway: Compare right with left and now with baseline. New asymmetry is the finding you act on.
questions.strategy: Two options describe weakness. Ask which one is new and which one is on one side only.

steps.detail: The tremor is documented as unchanged.
Pushing up with both arms and slower answers affect both sides equally.
Grips were equal at 0730 and are not equal now.

elimination.verdict: The weaker right grip. New asymmetry needs immediate follow up.

questions.stem: During an admission assessment, a 79-year-old gives answers unrelated to the questions. His hearing aids are in a bag at the bedside. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert the hearing aids and then repeat the questions
options.rationale: A patient who cannot hear the question is not confused. Set him up first, then judge his thinking.

options.text: Document disorientation as his admission baseline
options.rationale: A baseline recorded without his hearing aids may be false, and every later check would be compared with it.

options.text: Ask his daughter whether this is his usual thinking
options.rationale: Useful for a baseline and tempting. It comes after the nurse removes the barrier she can see.

options.text: Report new confusion to the provider right away
options.rationale: Reporting is right for true confusion. The hearing aids in the bag mean the finding is not yet reliable.

questions.takeaway: Set the patient up before you test cognition: hearing aids in, glasses on, interpreter if needed.
questions.strategy: Before you label the answers as confusion, look for a stem detail that explains them another way.

steps.detail: The hearing aids are in a bag, so he may not hear the questions.
Documenting or reporting confusion assumes the finding is real.
The daughter can describe his baseline later. The nurse can fix the hearing now.

elimination.verdict: Hearing aids in, then ask again.

questions.stem: A patient develops a new left facial droop and slurred speech. The stroke team is on the way. The patient asks for water to take the morning blood pressure pill. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the pill with a small sip while sitting upright
options.rationale: Tempting because blood pressure matters in stroke and upright positioning helps. Swallowing has not been screened, so any sip risks aspiration.

options.text: Crush the pill in applesauce
options.rationale: Still an oral intake in a patient whose swallow is unknown.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO until a swallow screen is done
options.rationale: New droop and slurred speech signal aspiration risk, so nothing goes by mouth, including medications.

options.text: Offer ice chips to check swallowing
options.rationale: Testing with ice chips is an unscreened swallow trial.

questions.takeaway: New facial droop or slurred speech means NPO, including medications, until swallowing is screened. Airway comes before the medication schedule.
questions.strategy: Three options put something in the mouth. The cue is the new droop, which makes every one of them unsafe.

steps.detail: New droop and slurred speech point to cranial nerve weakness.
A sip, applesauce and ice chips are all oral intake.
The pill can wait or go by another route once ordered.

elimination.verdict: Keep the patient NPO until the swallow screen.

questions.stem: A patient's left pupil has been irregular since cataract surgery. On admission yesterday both pupils reacted briskly. Which finding this evening requires follow up?

options.text: Left pupil remains irregular in shape
options.rationale: Abnormal shape, yet it is this patient's documented baseline.

options.text: Right pupil now reacts sluggishly to light
options.rationale: A change from brisk to sluggish is new. Change from baseline is what matters most.

options.text: Both pupils measure 4 mm
options.rationale: Within the normal range of 2 to 6 mm and equal.

options.text: Pupils constrict when focusing on a near object
options.rationale: Normal accommodation.

questions.takeaway: A pupil finding matters when it differs from the patient's own baseline. Sluggish after brisk is an early warning.
questions.strategy: The irregular pupil looks like the abnormal one. The stem tells you it was already there, so look for what changed.

steps.detail: 4 mm and accommodation are normal.
The irregular shape dates from the surgery.
Brisk on admission, sluggish this evening.

elimination.verdict: The newly sluggish right pupil.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury pulled his hand away from nail bed pressure at 0400. At 0600, right nail bed pressure makes both arms flex to the chest, wrists curled. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document withdrawal from pain and continue hourly checks
options.rationale: Withdrawal pulls only the touched hand away. Both arms flexing to the chest is a different and worse response.

options.text: Request a sedative for the new agitated arm movements
options.rationale: Posturing is a reflex, not agitation. Sedation would hide the neuro status.

options.text: Report to the provider that he now localizes pain
options.rationale: Tempting because it also reports a change. Localizing means reaching toward the pain, which would be an improvement. This is not that.

options.text: Report the new abnormal flexion posturing to the provider now
options.rationale: Both arms flexing to the core with curled wrists is decorticate posturing, a decline from withdrawal that is reported now.

questions.takeaway: Withdrawal pulls the touched limb away. Both arms flexing to the core is posturing. New posturing is reported now.
questions.strategy: Two options report to the provider. Name the response correctly before you choose between them.

steps.detail: Both arms flex to the chest no matter which hand is pressed. That is abnormal flexion.
He withdrew before, so this is a step down the motor scale.
Localizing would be better than withdrawal. Abnormal flexion is worse.

elimination.verdict: Report new abnormal flexion posturing.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a patient follows commands correctly but struggles to find words and becomes frustrated. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan?

options.text: Offer a picture board and extra time to answer
options.rationale: Understanding is intact and word production is the problem, so give another way to express and do not rush.

options.text: Speak loudly and repeat each instruction twice, slowly
options.rationale: Hearing and understanding are intact, so volume and repetition add nothing.

options.text: Ask the family to answer the questions for the patient
options.rationale: Takes away the patient's voice and adds to the frustration.

options.text: Demonstrate each instruction with gestures
options.rationale: Helps a patient who cannot understand words, which is not this patient's problem.

questions.takeaway: Match the aid to the deficit. A patient who understands but cannot find words needs time and another way to express.
questions.strategy: Gestures and a picture board both sound like communication aids. One helps the patient understand and the other helps the patient express.

steps.detail: Follows commands, so understanding works. Word finding does not.
Loud speech, repetition and gestures.

steps.action: Keep the patient in the conversation
steps.detail: Family answering removes the patient.

elimination.verdict: Picture board plus extra time.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for an MRI of the brain to evaluate new weakness. Which statement by the patient indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I will wash my hair and skip hair gel that morning."
options.rationale: This is preparation for an EEG.

options.text: "I will lie on my side with my knees pulled up."
options.rationale: This is the position for a lumbar puncture.

options.text: "I will tell the staff about my aneurysm clip."
options.rationale: MRI uses a strong magnet, so implanted metal must be reported before the scan.

options.text: "I can shift around in the scanner if my back gets sore."
options.rationale: The patient must lie still for clear images.

questions.takeaway: MRI gives detailed soft tissue images with a magnet. The safety check is metal. The patient must lie still.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement is correct teaching for a different test or the opposite of MRI teaching. Match the statement to this test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A magnet, so metal is the hazard.
Clean hair is EEG. Side lying with knees up is lumbar puncture.
Movement blurs the images.

elimination.verdict: Reporting the aneurysm clip shows understanding.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a fall does not open his eyes when the nurse says his name in a normal voice. Which action is next?

options.text: Press firmly on a nail bed with a pen
options.rationale: A painful stimulus is used only after voice and touch have failed.

options.text: Call his name loudly, then shake his shoulder
options.rationale: Stimulation goes from least to most noxious: normal voice, loud voice, gentle shake, then pain.

options.text: Record eye opening as none on the GCS
options.rationale: He has not been given the stronger stimuli yet, so the best response is still unknown.

options.text: Squeeze the trapezius muscle for up to 10 seconds
options.rationale: A correct way to apply pain, and tempting. It skips the two gentler steps.

questions.takeaway: Raise the stimulus in order: normal voice, loud voice, gentle shake, then pain. Score the best response.
questions.strategy: Two options use pain. Ask what the nurse has not tried yet.

steps.detail: Nail bed pressure and the trapezius squeeze are both painful stimuli.
None is recorded only after every level of stimulus fails.
Only a normal voice has been tried.

elimination.verdict: Loud voice, then a gentle shake.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia is disoriented to time and place at baseline. Which finding at noon requires immediate follow up?

options.text: States the year is 1985
options.rationale: Disorientation to time is this patient's baseline.

options.text: Asks when her late husband will visit
options.rationale: Fits her baseline memory and orientation problems.

options.text: Opens her eyes only after repeated shaking
options.rationale: She now needs strong stimulation to wake, which is a drop in level of consciousness.

options.text: Pushes the lunch tray away and refuses to eat anything
options.rationale: Worth following. It is not a neurologic change.

questions.takeaway: Orientation and level of consciousness are separate. A patient who is always disoriented can still have a new drop in alertness.
questions.strategy: Two options are disorientation, which she already has. Look for the option that is about how awake she is.

steps.detail: The wrong year and the question about her husband are baseline.
Refusing lunch is not an acute neurologic sign.
Hard to arouse is new.

elimination.verdict: Difficulty arousing her. That is a change in level of consciousness.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches an 80-year-old with decreased sensation in both feet about safety at home. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will dip my toes in the bath first to test it."
options.rationale: The feet cannot judge temperature, so this risks a burn.

options.text: "I will use a heating pad on my feet when they feel cold."
options.rationale: Heat on skin that cannot feel it causes burns.

options.text: "I will go barefoot indoors so I can feel the floor."
options.rationale: Unprotected feet can be injured without the patient knowing.

options.text: "I will check the bath water with a thermometer."
options.rationale: Uses a tool in place of the lost sensation.

questions.takeaway: When sensation is reduced, safety has to come from something other than the patient's own feeling.
questions.strategy: Three statements rely on the feet to sense heat or injury. One replaces the missing sensation with a measurement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The feet do not feel temperature or pain well.
Toes, heating pad and bare feet all depend on feeling.
A thermometer does not depend on sensation.

elimination.verdict: Checking bath water with a thermometer.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old recovering from a hip fracture was oriented at breakfast. At 1530 she is suddenly confused and picking at the blanket. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Measure the oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Hypoxia is the cause that harms fastest and is the quickest to check. It sits at the top of the ABCs.

options.text: Take an oral temperature
options.rationale: Infection is a common cause and is checked next, after oxygenation.

options.text: Review the medications given today
options.rationale: A real cause of sudden confusion. A chart review takes the nurse away from the patient and comes after the bedside checks.

options.text: Request a serum electrolyte panel
options.rationale: Electrolytes can cause confusion, but the result takes time and needs a prescription.

questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion in an older adult is never aging. Check oxygen saturation first, then glucose, temperature and medications.
questions.strategy: All four look for a cause of confusion. Rank them by how fast the cause harms and how fast you can check it.

steps.action: Accept that all four are valid
steps.detail: Hypoxia, infection, drugs and electrolytes all cause sudden confusion.
Oxygenation is the breathing check and takes seconds.
Temperature next, then the chart, then the lab.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen saturation first.

questions.stem: A patient with a frontal lobe injury keeps getting up alone, so a bed alarm was started. Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: The patient says, "I will call before I get up."
options.rationale: Tempting as a teaching outcome. Frontal injury impairs judgment and impulse control, so a promise does not predict behavior.

options.text: The patient repeats the fall precautions correctly
options.rationale: Recall is intact. Acting on it is what the injury prevents.

options.text: Staff reach him before he stands at each alarm
options.rationale: The goal is no unassisted rising. This shows the alarm is doing the job the patient cannot.

options.text: The patient stays in bed when all four side rails are raised
options.rationale: Four rails act as a restraint and raise the risk of injury.

questions.takeaway: With frontal lobe injury, measure safety by what happens, since the patient's own judgment cannot be relied on.
questions.strategy: A correct statement by the patient usually proves teaching worked. In this patient the deficit is the gap between knowing and doing.

steps.detail: Judgment and impulse control.

steps.action: Cut outcomes that rely on it
steps.detail: Promising and repeating instructions.
Four side rails are a restraint.

elimination.verdict: Staff arriving before he stands shows the alarm is working.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease says, "For weeks nothing has interested me. I see no point in therapy." Which intervention should the nurse include first?

options.text: Explain that therapy keeps him moving and encourage attendance
options.rationale: Tempting because therapy matters. It answers the refusal and skips the mood change behind it.

options.text: Screen for depression using a standard tool
options.rationale: Weeks of lost interest in a chronic neurologic condition is a cue to screen for depression.

options.text: Arrange a chaplain visit to discuss meaning
options.rationale: Reasonable support once the nurse knows what the problem is.

options.text: Tell him that many patients feel this way at first
options.rationale: Dismisses what he said and closes the conversation.

questions.takeaway: Psychosocial status is part of the neurologic assessment. Lost interest for weeks calls for depression screening before solutions.
questions.strategy: Encouragement and a chaplain are both kind actions. The stem gives a cue that has not been assessed yet.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: "For weeks" and "nothing interests me."
"Many patients feel this way" denies his feelings.
Screening comes before encouragement or referral.

elimination.verdict: Screen for depression first.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old, normally oriented x4, was admitted with new confusion from a urinary infection. Which finding on day 3 best indicates the neurologic problem has resolved?

options.text: Repeat urine culture shows no bacterial growth
options.rationale: Shows the infection is treated. It does not show that her thinking is back to baseline.

options.text: Sleeps through the night without calling out for her family
options.rationale: Quiet sleep can also mean a lower level of alertness.

options.text: Tells the nurse her full name and her date of birth correctly
options.rationale: Orientation to person only. Her baseline is oriented x4.

options.text: States the date, the hospital and why she is here
options.rationale: Oriented to time, place and situation again, which matches her baseline.

questions.takeaway: Neurologic recovery is measured against the patient's own baseline, not against the lab result.
questions.strategy: A clean urine culture and full orientation are both good news. The question asks about the neurologic problem. Her baseline was oriented x4.

steps.detail: Return to oriented x4.
The culture tracks the infection, not her thinking.
Name alone is one of four.

elimination.verdict: Full orientation to time, place and situation.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four patients on a neurology unit with one assistive worker. Which task is appropriate to assign to the assistive worker?

options.text: Walking a patient who has a chronic unsteady gait
options.rationale: A stable, chronic problem and a routine task with a predictable outcome.

options.text: Taking vital signs on a patient who just became confused
options.rationale: Tempting because vital signs are routine. A sudden change makes the patient unstable, so the nurse goes herself.

options.text: Checking whether a patient with a new facial droop can swallow water
options.rationale: A swallow screen is an assessment with aspiration risk.

options.text: Asking orientation questions of a patient admitted an hour ago
options.rationale: Establishing the baseline is a nursing assessment.

questions.takeaway: Delegate routine tasks for stable patients. New changes, baselines and swallow screens stay with the nurse.
questions.strategy: Vital signs are usually delegated. The words "just became confused" make that patient unstable.

steps.detail: Only the chronic gait problem is stable.
Swallow screening and orientation are assessments.
Routine task, unstable patient.

elimination.verdict: Walking the patient whose unsteady gait is chronic.

questions.stem: A patient admitted 2 days ago with a stroke has stable left arm weakness. At the start of the shift, which assessment plan is most appropriate?

options.text: A comprehensive neurologic examination as on admission
options.rationale: Tempting as the thorough choice. It suits a new admission. This patient already has a documented baseline.

options.text: Vital signs only, unless the patient reports a change
options.rationale: Misses changes the patient may not notice or report.

options.text: A focused neurologic check compared with the last findings
options.rationale: A known condition is monitored with a targeted exam. Comparison is how change is caught.

options.text: A Glasgow Coma Scale score alone
options.rationale: Does not capture arm strength, speech or pupils.

questions.takeaway: Comprehensive exams set the baseline. Focused exams, compared with that baseline, monitor a known problem.
questions.strategy: Two options are real neurologic assessments. "Admitted 2 days ago" and "stable" tell you the baseline exists.

steps.detail: Vital signs alone or one score alone miss too much.
Day 2 with stable findings.
Targeted and compared with the prior shift.

elimination.verdict: A focused check compared with the last findings.

questions.scenario:
A 76-year-old, alert and oriented after hip surgery, received IV hydromorphone 30 minutes ago. He now opens his eyes only when shaken.
Respirations are 8 per minute and SpO2 is 88%.
Pupils are small and equal. He moves all four limbs equally and his face is symmetric.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Stimulate him, open the airway and apply oxygen
options.rationale: Breathing comes first. He is under breathing and his oxygen level is low.

options.text: Give naloxone as prescribed
options.rationale: Reverses the opioid that is depressing his breathing and alertness.

options.text: Give the next scheduled opioid dose
options.rationale: More opioid deepens the sedation.

options.text: Let him sleep and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Hard to arouse with respirations of 8 is not sleep.

options.text: Acute stroke
options.rationale: Equal movement and a symmetric face show no one sided deficit.

options.text: Opioid induced sedation with slowed breathing
options.rationale: A recent opioid dose, a global drop in alertness, small equal pupils and slow respirations fit a medication cause.

options.text: Expected sleepiness after surgery
options.rationale: Expected sleepiness does not come with respirations of 8 and an SpO2 of 88%.

options.text: Abnormal posturing from brain injury
options.rationale: He moves all limbs normally.

options.text: Respiratory rate and SpO2
options.rationale: Shows whether breathing recovers and whether sedation returns as naloxone wears off.

options.text: Level of consciousness
options.rationale: Return to his alert, oriented baseline is the outcome.

options.text: Facial symmetry
options.rationale: Already symmetric and not affected by this problem.

options.text: Sensation in the feet
options.rationale: Not related to opioid sedation.

questions.takeaway: A global change with equal limbs points to a systemic cause such as a medication. A one sided change points to the brain.
questions.strategy: Every line of the excerpt is a clue. The timing names the drug, the respirations name the danger, and the equal limbs rule out stroke.

steps.detail: Equal limbs and a symmetric face mean global.
Hydromorphone 30 minutes ago.
Airway and oxygen, reversal, then respirations and alertness.

elimination.verdict: Opioid sedation; airway with oxygen and naloxone; respirations with SpO2 and level of consciousness.

questions.stem: While passing a doorway, the nurse hears a patient who spoke clearly 30 minutes ago calling out in garbled words. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Check airway, breathing and vital signs
options.rationale: Fourth. With the change confirmed, check the ABCs and vital signs so the report is complete.

options.text: Enter the room and treat the speech as a new change
options.rationale: First. Recognize that this is different from 30 minutes ago and stop what you were doing.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response
options.rationale: Fifth. Escalate with findings, baseline and vital signs in hand.

options.text: Assess alertness, speech, face and limb strength
options.rationale: Second. A focused neurologic check shows what has changed.

options.text: Compare the findings with the last documented assessment
options.rationale: Third. Findings only mean something against this patient's baseline.

questions.takeaway: New neurologic change: recognize, assess, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, then notify.
questions.strategy: The step students drop is the comparison. It sits between the bedside check and the vital signs, before the call.

steps.detail: Clear speech 30 minutes ago, garbled now.
The focused check comes before the baseline comparison.

steps.action: Finish with ABCs and the call
steps.detail: Vital signs complete the picture you report.

elimination.verdict: Recognize, assess, compare, ABCs and vital signs, notify.

questions.scenario:
A patient with a head injury was treated for brain swelling.
0800: opens eyes to pain, says single words, pushes the nurse's hand away with either hand.
0800: pupils 3 mm, equal, brisk.
questions.stem: The nurse reassesses at 1200. For each finding, indicate whether it has improved, declined or is unchanged from 0800.

rows.text: Now opens eyes when his name is spoken
rows.rationale: Eye opening rose from pain to voice.

rows.text: Now speaks in confused sentences
rows.rationale: Verbal response rose from single words to confused conversation.

rows.text: Pupils 3 mm, equal, brisk
rows.rationale: Same as 0800.

rows.text: Right arm now extends rigidly to pain
rows.rationale: Extension is a lower motor response than pushing the stimulus away and needs immediate report.

rows.text: Left hand still pushes the nurse's hand away
rows.rationale: Localizing on the left is the same as 0800.

questions.takeaway: Trend each part of the assessment separately. One declining part needs action even when the others improve.
questions.strategy: Two better findings can hide one worse finding. Compare each row with its own 0800 line.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each row to its baseline line
steps.detail: Eyes, verbal and motor come from the first line. Pupils come from the second.
Pushing the hand away is localizing. Rigid extension is lower.
New extension on the right is reported at once.

elimination.verdict: Improved, improved, unchanged, declined, unchanged.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a head injury was alert at 1900. At 2100 the nurse must call his name twice to wake him. Pupils and vital signs are unchanged. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Repeat the neuro check in 15 minutes to confirm a trend
options.rationale: Tempting because only one thing changed. The change is already confirmed against the 1900 baseline, so waiting only delays treatment.

options.text: Notify the provider now of the change from baseline
options.rationale: A drop in LOC is the earliest sign of decline after a head injury. It is reported before the pupils or vital signs change.

options.text: Continue hourly checks because the other findings are stable
options.rationale: Pupils and vital signs change late. Stable late signs do not cancel an early one.

options.text: Review the record for sedating drugs given this morning
options.rationale: A reasonable cause to look for, and it can be done after the call. After a head injury the change is treated as the brain first.

questions.takeaway: Level of consciousness changes first. Pupils and vital signs change late. A quiet drop in alertness after a head injury is reported now, not trended.
questions.strategy: The stem gives one early sign and two normal late signs. Decide which of them carries more weight.

steps.detail: Alert at 1900 and hard to wake at 2100 is a completed comparison.
LOC falls first. Normal pupils and vital signs are not reassurance.
The chart review can follow the call.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: A patient with a severe headache, projectile vomiting and increasing drowsiness is scheduled for a lumbar puncture in 20 minutes. No brain imaging has been done. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Hold the preparation and call the provider
options.rationale: Headache, projectile vomiting and falling LOC suggest high intracranial pressure. A lumbar puncture without imaging risks herniation.

options.text: Have the patient empty the bladder before the procedure
options.rationale: Correct preparation for a lumbar puncture that should go ahead. This one should not, yet.

options.text: Position the patient side lying with knees drawn to chest
options.rationale: The right position for the procedure, and sharp flexion also raises intracranial pressure.

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic so the patient can lie still
options.rationale: Tempting because it treats the vomiting. It treats a cue as a nuisance and moves the procedure forward.

questions.takeaway: Before preparing a patient for a lumbar puncture, read the cues. Signs of high intracranial pressure without imaging mean stop and call.
questions.strategy: Three options prepare for the procedure. Ask whether the procedure is safe before choosing how to prepare.

steps.detail: Headache, projectile vomiting and drowsiness point to high intracranial pressure.
No imaging has ruled out a mass.
Three move toward the procedure. One stops it.

elimination.verdict: Hold and call the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Severe brain injury with arms extended and turned inward, unchanged for 3 days
options.rationale: The most alarming picture of the four, and it is unchanged. Unchanged late findings do not outrank a new change.

options.text: Stroke 5 days ago with a limp left arm, crying and refusing breakfast
options.rationale: Needs support and the weakness is stable. Nothing here is new.

options.text: Diabetic neuropathy reporting burning pain and numbness in both feet
options.rationale: Uncomfortable and chronic. It is a safety teaching need, not an emergency.

options.text: Fall yesterday, oriented, now asking the same question for the third time
options.rationale: A subtle new change in mental status after a fall. It is the earliest sign of neuro decline and the only finding that is new.

questions.takeaway: New beats dramatic. A quiet change in thinking after a head injury outranks severe findings that have not changed.
questions.strategy: Sort each patient as changed or unchanged before you look at how severe the finding sounds.

steps.detail: Posturing for 3 days and a limp arm for 5 days are stable.
Neuropathy pain is long standing.
Repeating a question is a new thinking change in an oriented patient.

elimination.verdict: See the patient who fell and is now repeating questions.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old is seen for a routine visit. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Both pupils are equal and constrict slowly to light
options.rationale: Tempting because a slow pupil is a warning sign in a head injury. Equal, slower pupils are an expected change with age.

options.text: Loses track of conversations, new this week per daughter
options.rationale: A change in attention over days is not normal aging. Any subtle mental status change from baseline needs a cause found.

options.text: Ankle reflexes are weaker and equal on both sides
options.rationale: Weaker reflexes that are the same on both sides are expected with age.

options.text: Takes extra time but recalls a list of three words
options.rationale: Slower recall is expected with age when the patient still gets there.

questions.takeaway: Normal aging is slow and symmetric. A change that is new this week is a cue, however mild it looks.
questions.strategy: Every option sounds like a deficit. Look for the one with a time stamp that makes it new.

steps.detail: Equal pupils and equal reflexes fit aging.
Slower is expected. Lost is not.
New this week, reported by family.

elimination.verdict: Follow up on the new loss of attention.

questions.stem: Four hours after a head injury a drowsy patient's blood pressure has gone from 118/76 to 164/70 and the pulse from 80 to 54. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the prescribed as needed antihypertensive and recheck in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting because the systolic pressure is high. The pressure is the brain's attempt to keep itself perfused, not the problem to treat.

options.text: Complete a full cranial nerve assessment before calling anyone
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives a late sign pattern, and more assessment costs time.

options.text: Call the rapid response team and report the findings now
options.rationale: Rising systolic pressure with a wider pulse pressure and a slow pulse in a drowsy patient is a late sign of high intracranial pressure. It is reported at once.

options.text: Recheck the blood pressure in the other arm in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Reasonable for one odd reading. Here the pressure and pulse changed together in a pattern.

questions.takeaway: Higher systolic pressure, wider pulse pressure and a slower pulse together are the brainstem's late alarm. Do not treat the number and do not keep assessing.
questions.strategy: Read the two vital signs as one pattern instead of two separate problems, then ask which option responds to the pattern.

steps.detail: Pulse pressure widened from 42 to 94 while the pulse slowed.
An antihypertensive and a recheck both treat a reading.
The decisive findings are already in hand.

elimination.verdict: Call the rapid response team now.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with atrial fibrillation was neurologically intact at 1400. Which finding at 1500 requires immediate follow up?

options.text: A mild headache that eased after acetaminophen
options.rationale: A headache that responds to a mild analgesic is not the sudden severe headache of a bleed.

options.text: Briefly unsure of the date after waking from a nap
options.rationale: Tempting because confusion is a stroke sign, but it clears on waking and is not sudden and persistent.

options.text: Sudden double vision and veering to one side
options.rationale: Sudden balance and eye changes are stroke signs from the back of the brain. Atrial fibrillation is an embolic source.

options.text: Hand tremor present since admission
options.rationale: Unchanged from baseline, so it is not a new deficit.

questions.takeaway: Stroke is not only face, arm and speech. Sudden balance or vision change in a patient with an embolic source is a stroke until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Look for the finding that is both new and sudden. Face and arm are not the only places a stroke shows up.

steps.detail: The tremor has not changed.
The headache and the grogginess both cleared.
Double vision plus veering is balance and eyes.

elimination.verdict: Sudden double vision and veering. Call the stroke alert.

questions.stem: A patient with right hemiplegia finished an alteplase infusion 6 hours ago and cannot get out of bed. Which measure to prevent venous thromboembolism should the nurse include?

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices to both lower legs
options.rationale: Mechanical prevention carries no bleeding risk during the 24 hours when anticoagulants are held.

options.text: Request a prescription for subcutaneous enoxaparin
options.rationale: The usual choice for an immobile patient, but no anticoagulants for 24 hours after a clot buster and until a follow up CT.

options.text: Place pillows under both knees
options.rationale: Pressure behind the knee slows venous return and raises clot risk.

options.text: Keep the legs still until the follow up CT
options.rationale: Immobility is the cause of the problem, so position changes continue.

questions.takeaway: For 24 hours after a clot buster, prevent clots mechanically. Anticoagulants and antiplatelets wait for the follow up CT.
questions.strategy: Two options prevent clots. The 6 hour mark decides which one is safe right now.

steps.detail: Knee pillows and keeping still both slow venous flow.
Enoxaparin and compression devices both work.

steps.action: Use the time in the stem
steps.detail: 6 hours is inside the 24 hour no anticoagulant window.

elimination.verdict: Sequential compression devices.

questions.stem: Two days after a left hemisphere stroke, a patient cannot name objects, coughs when drinking water, cries without warning and has a flaccid right arm. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: Inability to name common objects
options.rationale: A real communication need, but it does not threaten the airway.

options.text: Coughing when drinking water
options.rationale: Coughing with thin liquids signals aspiration, which threatens the airway.

options.text: Crying without warning
options.rationale: Emotional lability is expected after stroke and needs explanation, not urgent action.

options.text: Flaccid right arm
options.rationale: Needs support on a pillow to protect the shoulder, which can follow airway protection.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke, the swallow problem outranks the language, mood and mobility problems because it threatens the airway.
questions.strategy: All four are real stroke problems. Rank them with airway, breathing and circulation.

steps.detail: Language, mood and limb function are not airway.
Coughing on water means the airway is not protected.

elimination.verdict: Coughing with water. Stop oral intake and rescreen the swallow.

questions.stem: A patient with increased ICP has gurgling secretions in the upper airway and an SpO2 of 90%. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Suction right away until the airway sounds clear
options.rationale: Tempting because airway is first, but prolonged suctioning without oxygen deepens hypoxia and raises ICP.

options.text: Hold suctioning and reposition to avoid raising the ICP
options.rationale: Suction only when needed is the rule. Gurgling with an SpO2 of 90% is when it is needed.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed so the secretions can drain out
options.rationale: A flat or head down position blocks venous drainage and raises ICP.

options.text: Give oxygen, suction briefly, then give oxygen again
options.rationale: The airway must be cleared. Oxygen before and after limits the hypoxia and ICP spike that suctioning causes.

questions.takeaway: With high ICP, suction only when needed, keep it brief and give oxygen before and after. Hypoxia itself raises ICP.
questions.strategy: Two options both clear the airway. Choose the one that also protects the brain from low oxygen.

steps.detail: Gurgling with a low SpO2 means yes.

steps.action: Cut the position that raises ICP
steps.detail: Head of bed stays up.

steps.action: Pick the safer way to suction
steps.detail: Brief, with oxygen on both sides.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen, brief suction, oxygen.

questions.stem: Six days after a subarachnoid hemorrhage, a patient who was alert becomes confused with a new left arm drift. The headache is unchanged. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Vasospasm reducing blood flow to brain tissue
options.rationale: New ischemic deficits between days 4 and 14 without a new headache fit arteries clamping down after the bleed.

options.text: Rebleeding from the aneurysm into the subarachnoid space
options.rationale: A rebleed would bring a sudden severe headache. This headache is unchanged.

options.text: Hypoglycemia mimicking a stroke
options.rationale: Can cause confusion, but a one sided drift on day 6 after a bleed points to the vessel.

options.text: Expected recovery pattern after the hemorrhage
options.rationale: A new deficit is never expected recovery and needs to be reported now.

questions.takeaway: After a subarachnoid hemorrhage, new confusion or weakness on days 4 to 14 means vasospasm until proven otherwise. Report it immediately.
questions.strategy: Use the day and the headache. Day 6 with no new headache separates spasm from a rebleed.

steps.action: Cut the option that calls a new deficit normal
steps.detail: New drift is a change.
Rebleed brings sudden worst headache. Spasm brings new ischemia.
Day 6 sits inside days 4 to 14.

elimination.verdict: Vasospasm.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke had a BP of 192/114 and received IV labetalol. Which finding indicates the patient is now ready for alteplase?

options.rationale: The diastolic is under the limit but the systolic is still above 185.
Both numbers are below 185/110, the limit before a clot buster.
The systolic is under the limit but the diastolic is still above 110.
The systolic has fallen the most, which makes it tempting. The diastolic is still above 110.

questions.takeaway: Before a clot buster both numbers must be below 185/110. One number in range is not enough.
questions.strategy: Check each option against both halves of 185/110.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 186 is not below 185.
112 and 114 are not below 110.
178 is below 185 and 100 is below 110.

questions.stem: The nurse taught a patient with left homonymous hemianopsia to scan. Which observation at lunch indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: The patient eats what the family moved to the right side
options.rationale: Tempting because the meal is eaten, but the family compensated and the patient did not scan.

options.text: The patient says the vision seems better today
options.rationale: A report of feeling better does not show the skill being used.

options.text: The patient asks staff to describe what is on the tray
options.rationale: Relies on others instead of scanning.

options.text: The patient turns the head left and finishes the whole tray
options.rationale: Turning toward the lost field and finding the food there shows the patient is scanning independently.

questions.takeaway: Scanning is effective when the patient turns the head toward the lost field without being set up by someone else.
questions.strategy: The goal was a patient behavior. Pick the option where the patient does the work.

steps.detail: Saying the vision is better is not a demonstration.
In one the family moved the food. In the other the patient turned the head.

steps.action: Match the outcome to the teaching
steps.detail: The teaching was scanning.

elimination.verdict: Turns the head left and finishes the tray.

questions.stem: A patient with an ischemic stroke was not a candidate for a clot buster. BP is 196/98 and the neuro status is unchanged. Labetalol is prescribed PRN for systolic pressure above 220. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the labetalol to bring the pressure below 180/105
options.rationale: 180/105 is the limit after a clot buster, which makes this tempting. This patient did not receive one.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat to reduce the pressure
options.rationale: Lying flat does not treat the BP and reduces venous drainage from the head.

options.text: Hold the labetalol and continue the neuro checks
options.rationale: Without a clot buster, BP is allowed to run high to keep the injured brain perfused. 196 is under the prescribed limit.

options.text: Call the provider to request a lower labetalol threshold
options.rationale: The threshold is deliberate. A sudden drop in pressure can starve the tissue around the stroke.

questions.takeaway: After an ischemic stroke with no clot buster, a high BP is tolerated to protect perfusion. The strict 180/105 limit belongs to the 24 hours after a clot buster.
questions.strategy: Three options try to lower the pressure. Check the stem for whether a clot buster was given and what the prescription says.

steps.detail: No clot buster means the 180/105 limit does not apply.
Labetalol is for systolic above 220. This is 196.

steps.action: Ask what the pressure is doing
steps.detail: It is pushing blood to tissue that can still be saved.

elimination.verdict: Hold the labetalol and keep monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient with a left hemisphere stroke stares at the sink when told, "Wash your face, brush your teeth and comb your hair." Which change does the nurse make?

options.text: Give one step at a time and wait for each to be finished
options.rationale: Left hemisphere damage affects language, so one idea per sentence and one step commands work best.

options.text: Repeat the full instruction more slowly and loudly
options.rationale: The problem is processing language, not hearing. The same three ideas will still overload him.

options.text: Write the three steps on a card by the sink
options.rationale: Tempting as a memory aid. Reading is also a left hemisphere function, so a written list has the same problem.

options.text: Have the assistive worker complete the morning care
options.rationale: Gets the care done and takes away his chance to regain function.

questions.takeaway: After a left hemisphere stroke, give one step commands in simple sentences and allow time. Speak slowly, not loudly.
questions.strategy: Name what the left hemisphere does, then pick the option that asks the least of that function.

steps.detail: Left hemisphere means language, including reading.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep three steps
steps.detail: Repeating the sentence or writing it down still gives three ideas at once.

steps.action: Keep the patient doing the task
steps.detail: Having staff do it skips the goal of function.

elimination.verdict: One step at a time.

questions.stem: Thirty hours after a stroke, a previously calm patient becomes restless and pulls at the IV line. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed PRN sedative for agitation
options.rationale: Sedation hides the LOC changes the nurse needs to track.

options.text: Assess LOC, pupils and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: New restlessness is the earliest sign of rising ICP and can also mean hypoxia, so the cause must be found first.

options.text: Apply hand mitts to protect the IV line
options.rationale: Tempting for safety, but it restrains a symptom without finding its cause and is not the least restrictive step.

options.text: Dim the lights and reduce noise in the room
options.rationale: A good measure for ICP, but it comes after finding out why the patient changed.

questions.takeaway: New restlessness in the first 72 hours after a stroke is a neurologic change. Assess before you sedate, restrain or settle.
questions.strategy: Nothing in the stem has been assessed yet. The behavior is a cue, not a diagnosis.

steps.detail: Calm to restless is a change in LOC.
Sedatives and mitts treat the behavior only.
Dimming the lights can wait a minute.

elimination.verdict: Assess LOC, pupils and oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: The nurse observes assistive personnel caring for a patient with a flaccid left arm and left sided neglect. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Approaching the patient from the right side
options.rationale: Looks wrong because the left is neglected, but approaching from the unaffected side is what the patient can attend to.

options.text: Putting the left arm into the sleeve first
options.rationale: Dressing the affected side first is correct.

options.text: Pulling the patient up by the left arm
options.rationale: Pulling on a flaccid arm can injure the shoulder.

options.text: Resting the left arm on a pillow
options.rationale: Supporting a flaccid arm protects the joint.

questions.takeaway: Never pull on a flaccid arm. Support it on a pillow and teach assistive personnel to do the same.
questions.strategy: You are looking for the unsafe action. One correct action is written to look wrong.

steps.detail: Find the one action that harms.
Affected sleeve first and a pillow under the arm are right.
Approaching from the unaffected side is taught practice.

elimination.verdict: Pulling by the flaccid arm.

questions.stem: A wife is upset that her husband, 4 days after a right hemisphere stroke, burst into laughter when told sad family news. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Request a depression screening because his mood is changing
options.rationale: Tempting because poststroke depression is real, but abrupt mismatched laughter is lability, not low mood.

options.text: Advise the family to hold back upsetting news until he recovers
options.rationale: Isolates the patient and does not explain the behavior.

options.text: Tell her the laughter shows he is coping well with the news
options.rationale: Kind, and wrong. The laughter is not a sign of coping. It is a stroke effect he cannot control.

options.text: Explain that stroke can cause emotions that do not match his mood
options.rationale: Sudden laughing that does not fit the situation is emotional lability. The family needs it explained.

questions.takeaway: Emotional lability is sudden laughing or crying that does not match the mood. Explain it to the family so they do not take it personally.
questions.strategy: Mismatched and sudden are the tipping words. Depression is sustained, not a burst.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: The laughter is not coping. He cannot control it.
Withholding news does not help the family understand.
A burst that does not fit is lability.

elimination.verdict: Explain emotional lability to the wife.

questions.stem: A patient with facial droop and arm drift had a glucose of 54 mg/dL and received IV dextrose. The glucose is now 118 mg/dL and both deficits persist. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before doing anything further
options.rationale: Tempting after treating hypoglycemia, but 118 is corrected and waiting costs brain tissue.

options.text: Give a snack to keep the glucose up
options.rationale: The patient has a facial droop and has not had a swallow screen.

options.text: Continue the stroke alert and prepare for CT
options.rationale: The mimic is corrected and the deficits remain, so this is treated as a stroke and the clock is running.

options.text: Cancel the stroke alert because the glucose was the cause
options.rationale: If glucose were the cause, the deficits would have cleared.

questions.takeaway: Treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess. Deficits that outlast a normal glucose are a stroke until imaging says otherwise.
questions.strategy: The reassessment is already done. The glucose is normal and the deficits are not.

steps.detail: 118 is corrected.
Droop and drift did not clear.

steps.action: Cut the delays and the oral intake
steps.detail: Waiting loses time and a snack risks aspiration.

elimination.verdict: Continue the stroke alert and go to CT.

questions.stem: A patient arrives 1 hour after sudden aphasia began. Which history finding does the nurse report to the stroke team first?

options.text: Takes aspirin 81 mg every day with breakfast
options.rationale: Tempting because it affects bleeding, but daily aspirin does not decide eligibility the way an anticoagulant does.

options.text: Took a dose of apixaban this morning
options.rationale: A recent anticoagulant dose raises bleeding risk and can rule out a clot buster.

options.text: Has had hypertension for 10 years
options.rationale: A risk factor that explains the stroke but does not change the next decision.

options.text: Stopped smoking 2 years ago
options.rationale: Background history that can wait.

questions.takeaway: With last known well already inside the window, the next urgent history is medications, especially anticoagulants.
questions.strategy: The time is already known. Ask which remaining fact could stop the treatment.

steps.detail: Hypertension and smoking do not change the next hour.
Aspirin is an antiplatelet. Apixaban is an anticoagulant.
A same day anticoagulant dose decides candidacy.

elimination.verdict: The apixaban dose this morning.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient going home after a TIA. Which statement indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "If the numbness returns, I will take an extra aspirin and rest."
options.rationale: Returning symptoms mean call 911. Aspirin could worsen a bleed.

options.text: "If symptoms come back and clear, I will tell my provider at my next visit."
options.rationale: Symptoms that clear are still an emergency.

options.text: "I can stop the clopidogrel once my BP is normal."
options.rationale: The antiplatelet and the BP drug do different jobs.

options.text: "I will take my clopidogrel and BP pills even though I feel normal."
options.rationale: A TIA is a warning. Prevention continues when symptoms are gone.

questions.takeaway: After a TIA, feeling normal is not the end of treatment. Antiplatelets and BP control continue. Any return of symptoms means 911.
questions.strategy: Three statements treat the TIA as finished. One treats it as a warning.

steps.action: Cut the statements that delay care
steps.detail: Resting and waiting for the next visit both delay.

steps.action: Cut the one that stops a drug
steps.detail: A normal BP does not replace an antiplatelet.

steps.action: Keep the one that continues prevention
steps.detail: Feeling normal does not change the plan.

elimination.verdict: Keeps taking clopidogrel and BP pills.

questions.stem: Thirty five minutes into an alteplase infusion, a patient reports a new severe headache and nausea. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the alteplase infusion
options.rationale: A new severe headache with nausea during a clot buster suggests bleeding in the brain. Stopping the drug is the one action that limits the harm.

options.text: Give the PRN antiemetic and analgesic
options.rationale: Treats the symptoms as discomfort and lets the drug keep running.

options.text: Repeat the neuro check and BP
options.rationale: Assessment is usually first, which makes this tempting. The cue is already enough to act on, and the check follows within the minute.

options.text: Call the provider and await orders
options.rationale: The call is required and comes right after the infusion is stopped. Waiting for orders leaves the drug running.

questions.takeaway: During a clot buster, a new severe headache, nausea or vomiting means stop the infusion, then notify and expect a head CT.
questions.strategy: Three options are things the nurse will do. Ask which one stops the harm while the others happen.

steps.detail: New severe headache and nausea during alteplase point to bleeding.
The cue is already in hand. More assessment while the drug infuses adds harm.
Stop, then call, then reassess and prepare for CT.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion first.

questions.stem: A patient reports seeing two of everything since a stroke and misjudges the cup when reaching for it. Which intervention should the nurse include?

options.text: Place all items on the patient's right side
options.rationale: This fits a patient who has lost the left half of the visual field. This patient sees the whole field, doubled.

options.text: Teach turning the head side to side to scan
options.rationale: Scanning helps with hemianopsia and is tempting as the usual vision teaching. It does not remove a double image.

options.text: Patch one eye and alternate it every 2 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Covering one eye removes the second image. Alternating the patch keeps both eyes in use.

options.text: Keep the room dim and limit visual stimulation
options.rationale: Light is not the problem, and a dim room adds a fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Match the aid to the vision problem. Double vision gets an alternating eye patch. A lost half field gets scanning and items placed in the intact field.
questions.strategy: Two options treat a lost visual field. Decide whether this patient has lost part of the view or sees it twice.

steps.detail: Two of everything is double vision, not a missing field.
Items to one side and head scanning both treat hemianopsia.

steps.action: Pick what removes the second image
steps.detail: One eye covered gives one image.

elimination.verdict: Alternating eye patch.

questions.stem: A patient with increased ICP had a GCS of 11 and was restless. The nurse raised the head of the bed, kept the head midline and spaced care. Which findings 1 hour later indicate the interventions are effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: GCS of 14
options.rationale: A rising GCS shows LOC is improving, the best sign that ICP is coming down.

options.text: Resting quietly and waking easily to voice
options.rationale: The restlessness is gone and the patient still arouses easily, so this is calm and not stupor.

options.text: Pupils equal and briskly reactive
options.rationale: Brisk equal pupils show the brainstem is not being compressed.

options.text: Heart rate 52 with BP 182/68
options.rationale: A slow pulse with a wide pulse pressure is part of the Cushing triad, a late sign of worsening.

options.text: Quiet and responding only to pain
options.rationale: Quiet because of a deeper LOC is deterioration.

options.text: New vomiting without nausea
options.rationale: Vomiting is a sign of rising ICP.

questions.takeaway: Judge ICP care by the neuro status. Quiet is only good news when the patient still wakes easily.
questions.strategy: Two options describe a quiet patient. Check how easily each one wakes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: GCS 14 and easy to wake are better. Responding only to pain is worse.

steps.action: Read the vital signs as a pattern
steps.detail: Slow pulse with a wide pulse pressure is a late warning.
Brisk pupils are good. New vomiting is not.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old finished an alteplase infusion 3 hours ago. BP is 188/106. She failed the bedside swallow screen. Neuro status is unchanged from baseline.
questions.stem: For each prescription or action, indicate whether the nurse should implement it or question it at this time.

rows.text: Aspirin 81 mg by mouth now
rows.rationale: No antiplatelets for 24 hours after a clot buster and until a follow up CT shows no bleeding.

rows.text: Insert a urinary catheter to measure output
rows.rationale: Catheters are avoided until the patient is stable because of bleeding risk.

rows.text: Neuro checks and vital signs every 30 minutes
rows.rationale: After the first 2 hours, checks are every 30 minutes for the next 6 hours.

rows.text: Notify the provider about the BP
rows.rationale: 188/106 is above the 180/105 limit after a clot buster.

rows.text: Insert a nasogastric tube for medications
rows.rationale: She failed the swallow screen, but tubes wait until she is stable. Other routes are used.

rows.text: Keep NPO
rows.rationale: A failed swallow screen means nothing by mouth.

questions.takeaway: For 24 hours after a clot buster: frequent neuro checks, BP below 180/105, no tubes, no catheters and no antiplatelets.
questions.strategy: Ask of each row whether it could cause bleeding. If it punctures, scrapes or thins the blood, question it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aspirin, a catheter and a nasogastric tube.

steps.action: Check the BP against the limit
Match the check frequency to the hour
steps.detail: Hour 3 falls in the every 30 minutes period.

elimination.verdict: Question aspirin, catheter and tube. Implement the checks, the BP report and NPO.

questions.scenario: A 54-year-old with hypertension and cocaine use arrives 50 minutes after a sudden severe headache. He has vomited twice and had a brief seizure in triage. He is drowsy but follows commands. BP 212/118.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Prepare the patient for an immediate noncontrast CT
options.rationale: CT detects bleeding fast and must come before any treatment decision.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and keep the head midline
options.rationale: Helps venous blood drain from the skull while ICP is at risk.

options.text: Prepare the alteplase infusion
options.rationale: He is inside the time window, which makes this tempting, but a clot buster in a bleed is harmful.

options.text: Give aspirin by mouth
options.rationale: Worsens bleeding. He has had no swallow screen.

options.text: Hemorrhagic stroke
options.rationale: Sudden headache, vomiting, a seizure, falling LOC, hypertension and cocaine use all point to a bleed.

options.text: Embolic ischemic stroke
options.rationale: Sudden onset fits, but LOC is usually preserved and seizures and headache are not typical.

options.text: Transient ischemic attack
options.rationale: He is getting worse, not resolving.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: A mimic worth checking, but it does not explain a sudden severe headache.

options.text: Level of consciousness
options.rationale: The earliest sign that ICP is rising.

options.text: Pupil size and reaction
options.rationale: Sluggish pupils are an early ICP sign and fixed pupils a late one.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Not affected by this problem.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Useful for fluid balance over days, not for a bleed in the first hour.

questions.takeaway: Headache, vomiting, seizure and falling LOC point to a bleed. Being inside the time window never replaces the CT.
questions.strategy: The 50 minutes is there to pull you toward a clot buster. Decide the type of stroke before you decide the treatment.

steps.action: Name the problem from the cues
steps.detail: Headache, vomiting, seizure, drowsy, cocaine.
Alteplase and aspirin.
LOC and pupils show rising ICP.

elimination.verdict: Hemorrhagic stroke; CT and head of bed up; LOC and pupils.

questions.stem: A restless patient with increased ICP has the head of the bed at 30 degrees, the head turned sharply right and clear lungs. A bath, a turn and suctioning are due. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Do the bath and turn together so the patient can then rest
options.rationale: Clustering care is the usual way to protect rest, which makes this tempting. With high ICP, back to back care raises the pressure.

options.text: Suction now to keep the airway clear, then let the patient rest
options.rationale: Airway sounds like the priority, but the lungs are clear. Suctioning without need spikes ICP.

options.text: Place the head midline and space the care activities apart
options.rationale: A turned neck blocks venous drainage from the skull, and spacing care keeps the pressure from climbing. Both fit the cues given.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to improve blood flow to the brain
options.rationale: Tempting as a perfusion fix. Lying flat reduces venous drainage and raises ICP.

questions.takeaway: High ICP reverses the clustering rule. Keep the head midline, suction only when needed and space care out.
questions.strategy: Two usual rules, cluster care and airway first, both point to wrong options here. Check each against a stem detail.

steps.detail: Clear lungs mean there is nothing to suction.
Clustering is the rule that flips with high ICP.
A sharply turned head is a fixable cause of restlessness and pressure.

elimination.verdict: Head midline and space the care.

questions.stem: A man went to bed well at 2200 and spoke normally to his wife at 0500. At 0700 she found him unable to speak. They arrived at 0740. Which time is reported as last known well?

options.text: 0500, when he last spoke normally to his wife
options.rationale: Last known well is the last time someone saw him at baseline. That sets the treatment clock.

options.text: 0700, when his wife found him unable to speak
options.rationale: Tempting because it is when the stroke was noticed. Found time is not onset time and would overstate the window.

options.text: 2200, when he went to bed feeling well
options.rationale: The safe answer when a patient wakes with symptoms and nobody saw him overnight. Here the wife saw him normal at 0500.

options.text: 0740, when he arrived in the emergency department
options.rationale: Arrival starts the door to needle clock, not the treatment window.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen normal. Not when he was found and not always bedtime.
questions.strategy: Three times are defensible. Walk the timeline and stop at the last moment a witness saw him at baseline.

steps.detail: It measures the hospital, not the stroke.
Symptoms began at some point before 0700.
The 0500 conversation is a witnessed normal.

elimination.verdict: Report 0500 as last known well.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients on a stroke unit. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Hemorrhagic stroke with a headache rated 6, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: A headache is expected with a bleed and it has not changed.

options.text: Left hemisphere stroke, unable to speak and crying in frustration
options.rationale: Aphasia is expected with left hemisphere damage. The patient needs support soon, not first.

options.text: Right hemisphere stroke, ignoring the left side, bed alarm sounding twice
options.rationale: A real safety risk and very tempting. Impulsivity and neglect are expected, and the alarm is doing its job while the nurse sees the new deficit.

options.text: TIA awaiting discharge, trouble finding words again for 10 minutes
options.rationale: Returning symptoms after a TIA may be a stroke in progress, and treatment is time limited. This is the only new deficit.

questions.takeaway: A TIA is a warning. When the symptoms come back, the clock has started and that patient goes first.
questions.strategy: Safety and a new deficit compete here. Ask which problem gets worse by the minute if the nurse is elsewhere.

steps.detail: Headache with a bleed and aphasia with a left stroke are expected.
It is a potential harm with an alarm already in place.
New, sudden and time limited.

elimination.verdict: See the TIA patient whose symptoms returned.

questions.stem: A patient passed a swallow screen yesterday. At breakfast the assistive worker reports a wet, gurgly voice and a cough after each sip of juice. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have the assistive worker thicken the juice and continue the meal
options.rationale: Thickened liquids may be the eventual plan, which tempts. That decision follows a new swallow evaluation, not a guess during a meal.

options.text: Stop the meal, keep NPO and request a swallow evaluation
options.rationale: A wet voice and coughing with sips are signs of aspiration now. Yesterday's passed screen no longer describes this patient.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees and feed more slowly
options.rationale: Upright positioning lowers risk in a patient who can swallow safely. It does not fix a swallow that is failing.

options.text: Suction the mouth, then resume with the chin tucked down
options.rationale: Clears what is in the mouth and treats a technique that has not been prescribed as safe.

questions.takeaway: A passed screen is a snapshot. Wet voice or coughing with intake means stop, nothing by mouth and a new evaluation.
questions.strategy: Three options keep feeding with an adjustment. The deciding detail is that the cues are happening now, whatever yesterday's result was.

steps.action: Weigh the old result against today's cues
steps.detail: Today's wet voice and cough win.
Three continue oral intake and one stops it.
Aspiration is an airway problem.

elimination.verdict: Stop the meal, NPO and request a swallow evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient arrives 40 minutes after sudden right arm weakness began. The airway is clear, glucose is 110 mg/dL and the neuro check is charted. Alteplase is being considered. Which action is next?

options.text: Obtain an actual weight to calculate the alteplase dose
options.rationale: Needed before the drug is given and quick to do. It is not what decides whether the drug can be given at all.

options.text: Perform the swallow screen so aspirin can be given
options.rationale: The screen is required before anything by mouth. No antiplatelet or clot buster is given until bleeding is ruled out.

options.text: Take the patient for the noncontrast CT scan
options.rationale: Airway, glucose and the neuro check are done. Imaging to rule out a bleed is the step that every treatment decision waits on.

options.text: Repeat the full neuro assessment to confirm the deficit
options.rationale: Tempting as assess first. The assessment is already charted and repeating it spends treatment time.

questions.takeaway: Once airway, glucose and the neuro check are done, the scan is next. Nothing that dissolves or prevents clots is given before a bleed is ruled out.
questions.strategy: List what the stem says is already done, then pick the step everything else waits on.

steps.detail: Airway, glucose and neuro check.
It adds no new information.
Weight and swallow screen matter only after the scan shows no bleed.

elimination.verdict: Go to CT now.

questions.stem: A client on a Venturi mask at 35% had an SpO2 at goal until being tucked in. It now reads 88% and the blanket covers the mask adapter. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the flowmeter
options.rationale: Tempting because the saturation fell, but the device is blocked. More flow through covered ports does not restore the set concentration.

options.text: Pull the blanket away from the air entrainment ports
options.rationale: The ports must stay open for a Venturi mask to deliver its exact concentration. Fixing the device is the fastest correction.

options.text: Change to a nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: A step up in device is not needed when the ordered device has a fixable problem.

options.text: Notify the provider of the drop in saturation
options.rationale: Reasonable if the saturation stays low after the device is corrected. The nurse fixes the obvious cause first.

questions.takeaway: When saturation drops on oxygen, check the device before you change the dose. Venturi ports must stay uncovered.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you the cause: the blanket over the adapter. The answer removes that cause.

steps.detail: The drop followed the blanket covering the adapter.
More flow, a new device and a call all skip the simple fix.
Uncover the ports, then recheck the client.

elimination.verdict: Uncover the entrainment ports.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with pneumonia was started on high flow nasal cannula for a respiratory rate of 34 with accessory muscle use. Which finding one hour later best indicates the therapy is effective?

options.text: SpO2 rose from 89% to 95% with continued neck muscle use
options.rationale: Tempting because the number improved. Continued accessory muscle use means the work of breathing has not eased.

options.text: He says the warm humidified air feels more comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort helps him tolerate the device. It does not show better breathing.

options.text: Respiratory rate is 22 and he speaks in full sentences
options.rationale: Slower breathing and full sentences show less work of breathing, which is the reason the device was started.

options.text: He is sleeping and hard to wake for vital signs
options.rationale: A hard to wake client after respiratory distress may be tiring or retaining CO2. This needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: Judge oxygen therapy by the patient, not only the number. Lower rate, easier effort and full sentences mean it is working.
questions.strategy: Two options show improvement. Ask which one answers the problem that started the therapy: the work of breathing.

steps.detail: Rate 34 with accessory muscles.
One is not an outcome. The other is a warning.
A better number with the same effort loses to a slower rate with full sentences.

elimination.verdict: Rate 22 and full sentences.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old at a clinic visit describes several changes in his breathing. Which report requires follow up?

options.text: He needs several hard coughs to clear mucus that one cough used to clear
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds like trouble clearing the airway. A less effective cough is an expected change with aging. Teach him to stay hydrated and keep moving.

options.text: He slows down on hills that he walked easily ten years ago
options.rationale: Weaker respiratory muscles and a stiffer chest wall lower endurance gradually. A change over ten years fits aging.

options.text: He had three colds this winter and one in most earlier winters
options.rationale: Tempting because the number went up. More infections are expected with aging. Teach vaccination and hand hygiene.

options.text: He added a second pillow this month because lying flat feels stuffy
options.rationale: He describes it mildly, but needing to prop up to breathe is new shortness of breath. New shortness of breath is not normal aging.

questions.takeaway: New or severe shortness of breath is never normal aging. A client may describe it as a small change in habit, such as an extra pillow.
questions.strategy: Do not rank the reports by how bad they sound. Ask which one is recent and which ones built up over years.

steps.action: Match each report to an aging change
steps.detail: Weaker cough, less endurance and more infections are all expected.
Ten years and most winters are gradual. This month is new.
A second pillow because lying flat feels stuffy is shortness of breath when flat.

elimination.verdict: The second pillow. New dyspnea lying flat needs follow up.

questions.stem: A client admitted after 36 hours of vomiting and diarrhea is restless, with cool mottled legs, a blood pressure of 84/50 and an SpO2 of 98% on room air. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Tissue oxygen delivery is low because of poor perfusion
options.rationale: Low volume means less blood reaches the tissues. Saturation can be normal while the tissues go without oxygen.

options.text: Air movement into the alveoli is inadequate
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a ventilation problem. The saturation is normal and no breathing difficulty is described.

options.text: Gas exchange across the alveolar membrane is impaired
options.rationale: A diffusion problem lowers the saturation. This client's is 98%.

options.text: The pulse oximeter reading is falsely high
options.rationale: Tempting with cool legs, but poor circulation makes readings low or unreadable. The low pressure explains the picture.

questions.takeaway: A normal SpO2 does not prove the tissues are oxygenated. Hypovolemia cuts perfusion, so oxygen never reaches them.
questions.strategy: Match each finding to ventilation, diffusion or perfusion. Low pressure and mottled skin are blood flow findings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 98% rules out a ventilation or diffusion problem.

steps.action: Use the fluid loss and pressure
