steps.detail: A day and a half of losses with 84/50 means low volume.
Poor circulation does not make a reading falsely high.

elimination.verdict: Poor perfusion from hypovolemia.

questions.stem: A client who received a first dose of an IV antibiotic 5 minutes ago has a harsh high pitched sound on inspiration with retractions above the collarbones. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Auscultate all lung fields from apex to base
options.rationale: The sound and retractions already show upper airway obstruction. A full exam delays help.

options.text: Give the prescribed as needed bronchodilator inhaler
options.rationale: Tempting because the breathing is noisy. A bronchodilator treats wheezes from narrowed lower airways. This harsh inspiratory sound is stridor from the upper airway.

options.text: Stay with the client and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Stridor with retractions means the airway is closing. The nurse stays, gets help and supports the airway.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula and reassess in 5 minutes
options.rationale: Tempting as a breathing action. Oxygen cannot pass a closing airway, and 5 minutes is too long to wait.

questions.takeaway: Stridor and retractions are findings that need immediate intervention. The assessment is done. Get help and protect the airway.
questions.strategy: Two options act and two assess or wait. The stem already gave you the finding that matters, so ask which action deals with a closing airway.

steps.detail: Harsh inspiratory sound plus retractions is an obstructing upper airway.
The assessment that matters is done.
An inhaler and a cannula work below the blockage. Neither opens it.
Stay and call for help.

elimination.verdict: Stay and call rapid response.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old who smokes a pack a day says he is ready to quit and has set a date two weeks away. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Start a nicotine patch today and review progress at his annual visit
options.rationale: Tempting because medication helps. It leaves out counseling, and follow up a year away is far too late.

options.text: Set up counseling now and add medication only if he relapses
options.rationale: Tempting because counseling is half of the plan. The two work best together from the start.

options.text: Give written quit materials and ask him to call with questions
options.rationale: This fits a client who is not ready. He has a quit date.

options.text: Pair counseling with medication and book a visit near the quit date
options.rationale: He is willing, so the nurse assists with medication plus counseling and arranges follow up within the first week after the quit date.

questions.takeaway: For a client who is ready: assist with counseling plus medication, then arrange follow up within the first week after the quit date.
questions.strategy: He has passed Ask, Advise and Assess. The answer should cover Assist and Arrange.

steps.detail: Ready with a date means Assist and Arrange.

steps.action: Cut the plan for an unready client
steps.detail: Written materials only.
One has medication alone, one has counseling alone, one has both with early follow up.

elimination.verdict: Counseling plus medication with a visit near the quit date.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old office clerk has a dry cough and dyspnea that have worsened over a year. He has never smoked and reports no irritants at home or at his current job. Which question is most useful next?

options.text: What kinds of work did you do in earlier years?
options.rationale: Past work is the part of the exposure history still missing. Lung damage can show up decades after a job ended.

options.text: Which tasks at your office make you short of breath?
options.rationale: Tempting because work exposure matters. He has already reported no irritants at his current job.

options.text: Does anyone smoke inside your home?
options.rationale: Secondhand smoke is a real exposure. He has already reported no irritants at home.

options.text: Did you get an influenza vaccine this season?
options.rationale: Worth asking for health promotion. It does not explain symptoms that built over a year.

questions.takeaway: An exposure history covers present work, residence, environment and past work. Past work is the piece most often skipped.
questions.strategy: List what the stem has already cleared: smoking, home and current job. The answer asks about what is left.

steps.detail: No smoking, no irritants at home or at the current job.
Office tasks and smoke in the home repeat cleared ground.

steps.action: Cut the question that cannot explain a year of symptoms
steps.detail: Vaccine status.
Earlier jobs.

elimination.verdict: Ask about past work.

questions.stem: A client wearing dark nail polish has an SpO2 reading of 87% but is breathing easily at 16 with pink lips. The nurse moves the sensor. Which finding indicates the new reading can be trusted?

options.text: The new number is higher than the first reading
options.rationale: A higher number alone does not prove accuracy.

options.text: The displayed pulse rate matches the apical pulse
options.rationale: A pulse rate that matches the heart rate shows the sensor is picking up a real pulse, so the saturation beside it can be trusted.

options.text: The client says the new site feels comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort does not confirm signal quality.

options.text: The low saturation alarm has stopped sounding
options.rationale: An alarm silences at any value above its limit, accurate or not.

questions.takeaway: Correlate the oximeter with the patient. Trust a reading only when the pulse rate on the monitor matches the client's pulse.
questions.strategy: Ask which option checks the signal itself instead of the number or the alarm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Easy breathing and pink lips do not fit 87%.

steps.action: Cut options about the number, comfort or alarm
steps.detail: None tests signal quality.
Monitor pulse matches apical pulse.

elimination.verdict: Displayed pulse rate matching the apical pulse.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with pneumonia on 4 L/min has a steady SpO2 of 93%. Her blood pressure fell from 130/78 to 92/54 and her lactate is 3.4 mmol/L. Which problem is the priority?

options.text: Impaired gas exchange
options.rationale: Tempting because pneumonia is a lung problem. Her saturation is steady on low oxygen, so it is controlled for now.

options.text: Activity intolerance
options.rationale: Real, but it does not threaten her life.

options.text: Developing sepsis
options.rationale: A falling pressure with a raised lactate shows infection is affecting perfusion. Preventing sepsis is part of the pneumonia plan.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about pneumonia vaccination
options.rationale: Teaching waits until she is stable.

questions.takeaway: In pneumonia, watch for sepsis as closely as for gas exchange. The problem that is changing outranks the one that is steady.
questions.strategy: Two problems are serious. One is stable on treatment. The other is new and worsening.

steps.detail: Activity and teaching can wait.
93% and steady on 4 L/min.
Pressure falling, lactate up.

elimination.verdict: Developing sepsis.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel reports that a sleeping client's SpO2 reads 86%. The reading was normal two hours ago. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Go to the client and assess breathing and responsiveness
options.rationale: The nurse has only a number. Looking at the client shows whether it is real and how urgent it is.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel raise the head of the bed and recheck
options.rationale: Tempting because sitting up helps most breathing problems. The nurse still has not seen the client, and assessment cannot be delegated.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel move the sensor to another finger
options.rationale: Tempting because a sleeping client's sensor may have slipped. If the reading is real, this spends time the client may not have.

options.text: Call the provider to report the change in the reading
options.rationale: The provider will ask for an assessment the nurse does not have yet.

questions.takeaway: A single reported number is not an assessment. Go to the patient, then act on what you find.
questions.strategy: No assessment data is in the stem. That is the cue that assessment comes first.

steps.detail: Only a reported number.
There is nothing to report yet.
Each could help, but both leave the nurse without an assessment.
The nurse goes to the client.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client now.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches an older adult about seasonal influenza before winter. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I had the vaccine, so I do not need to wash my hands as often."
options.rationale: Vaccination reduces risk and severity. Handwashing stays critical.

options.text: "If I get sick, I will rest for three days and call if I am no better."
options.rationale: Antivirals work best within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms. Three days is too late.

options.text: "Influenza comes on slowly, so I will have time to plan."
options.rationale: Influenza has a rapid onset with severe headache, muscle aches and fever.

options.text: "I will call the day symptoms start to ask about antiviral medicine."
options.rationale: Early contact lets treatment start inside the 24 to 48 hour window.

questions.takeaway: Influenza starts fast. Vaccinate, wash hands and call early because antivirals help only if started within 24 to 48 hours.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against one fact: timing. Only one gets the timing right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A vaccine does not replace handwashing.
Waiting three days misses the window. Calling day one fits it.
Influenza is sudden.

elimination.verdict: Call the day symptoms start.

questions.stem: The nurse auscultates the chest of a client admitted with a productive cough. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Soft, low pitched sounds at both lung bases
options.rationale: Vesicular sounds are expected at the bases.

options.text: Loud, high pitched sounds over the right lower lobe
options.rationale: Bronchial sounds belong over the trachea. Heard over a lung field, they suggest consolidation such as pneumonia.

options.text: Medium pitched sounds beside the sternum
options.rationale: Bronchovesicular sounds are expected near the sternum.

options.text: Loud, high pitched sounds over the trachea
options.rationale: Bronchial sounds are expected over the trachea.

questions.takeaway: Location decides whether a breath sound is normal. A tracheal sound heard out over the lung is abnormal.
questions.strategy: Two options describe the same sound in different places. Look closely at the pair.

steps.detail: Soft at bases and medium near the sternum are expected.
Over the trachea is normal. Over a lower lobe is not.

elimination.verdict: Loud, high pitched sounds over the right lower lobe.

questions.stem: A client with COVID 19 on oxygen drops to 90% and becomes breathless whenever bathing, linen change and meals happen back to back. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Cluster care into short blocks with rest periods between them
options.rationale: Spacing activity with rest lowers oxygen demand while keeping her moving.

options.text: Keep her on strict bed rest until discharge
options.rationale: Tempting because activity drops her saturation. Full bed rest removes the mobility she needs and adds risks.

options.text: Schedule three hallway walks a day to build endurance
options.rationale: Mobility matters, but adding exertion now ignores the drop to 90%.

options.text: Complete all care early so she can rest all afternoon
options.rationale: Doing everything at once is what causes the drop.

questions.takeaway: For activity intolerance, balance rest and mobility. Group care, then protect rest between groups to lower oxygen demand.
questions.strategy: The stem says the trouble comes from activities done back to back. The answer changes the spacing, not the amount.

steps.detail: Care done back to back.
Strict bed rest and extra walks.

steps.action: Cut the plan that repeats the trigger
steps.detail: All care at once.

elimination.verdict: Cluster care with rest periods.

questions.stem: A client on a nasal cannula for 4 days has reddened, intact skin over the tops of both ears. The oxygen saturation is at goal. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Remove the cannula for one hour each shift
options.rationale: Stopping prescribed oxygen risks hypoxemia.

options.text: Apply petroleum jelly under the tubing
options.rationale: Petroleum based products are not used with oxygen.

options.text: Pad the tubing over the ears and reposition it
options.rationale: Padding relieves pressure while the ordered oxygen continues.

options.text: Change to a simple face mask
options.rationale: Tempting because it moves the tubing off the ears. It changes the ordered device and adds mask pressure points.

questions.takeaway: Inspect skin under oxygen tubing. Relieve pressure without interrupting the oxygen or changing the order.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that fixes the skin problem and keeps the therapy the same.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No petroleum with oxygen.

steps.action: Cut options that change the therapy
steps.detail: Removing the cannula or switching devices.
Pad and reposition.

elimination.verdict: Pad and reposition the tubing.

questions.stem: A client prescribed a simple face mask at 8 L/min returns from x-ray drowsy. The flowmeter reads 3 L/min. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Change to a nasal cannula at the same 3 L/min
options.rationale: Tempting because 3 L/min suits a cannula. It changes the ordered device and gives less oxygen than prescribed.

options.text: Turn the flow back up to the prescribed 8 L/min
options.rationale: A simple mask needs at least its minimum flow, about 5 L/min, to flush exhaled carbon dioxide out of the mask. Restoring the ordered setting fixes the cause.

options.text: Check the saturation and keep this flow if it is at goal
options.rationale: Tempting as an assessment. Pulse oximetry does not show carbon dioxide, so a good number would not make this flow safe.

options.text: Ask the provider about lowering the oxygen concentration
options.rationale: Drowsiness here comes from rebreathed carbon dioxide at a low flow, not from too much oxygen.

questions.takeaway: A simple mask needs its minimum flow so exhaled carbon dioxide is not rebreathed. Use the ordered device at the ordered setting.
questions.strategy: The stem gives two numbers that disagree: the order and the flowmeter. Fix the mismatch before anything else.

steps.detail: 8 L/min ordered, 3 L/min running.
Drowsiness fits carbon dioxide rebreathed inside the mask.

steps.action: Cut the options that leave the flow low
steps.detail: A cannula, a saturation check and a lower concentration all keep him at 3 L/min or less.
Restore the prescribed flow, then reassess.

elimination.verdict: Return the flow to 8 L/min.

questions.stem: A client with right lower lobe pneumonia has had IV antibiotics and oxygen for 48 hours. Which finding best indicates the gas exchange goal is met?

options.text: Temperature has been normal for 24 hours
options.rationale: Tempting because it shows the infection is responding. It does not measure oxygenation.

options.text: The white blood cell count is trending down
options.rationale: An infection marker, not a gas exchange measure.

options.text: She coughs up less sputum than yesterday
options.rationale: Less sputum can mean improvement or a weaker cough.

options.text: SpO2 stays at 97% on room air while she walks
options.rationale: Holding saturation without oxygen during activity shows adequate gas exchange.

questions.takeaway: Match the evidence to the goal. Gas exchange is judged by oxygenation and breathing, not by infection markers.
questions.strategy: Three options show the infection improving. Only one measures the goal named in the stem.

steps.detail: Gas exchange.
Temperature, white cells and sputum.
Saturation on room air with activity.

elimination.verdict: 97% on room air while walking.

questions.stem: A client is about to have a thoracentesis. Consent is signed and baseline breath sounds are charted. The client mentions taking warfarin last night. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the warfarin dose to the provider now
options.rationale: Bleeding risk must be reviewed before a needle enters the chest. The provider needs this now.

options.text: Auscultate the lungs again for a second baseline
options.rationale: Tempting because baseline findings matter. The stem says they are already charted.

options.text: Position the client upright leaning over the bedside table
options.rationale: Correct positioning, but it comes after the bleeding risk is cleared.

options.text: Remind the client not to cough during the procedure
options.rationale: Good teaching that does not address the new risk.

questions.takeaway: Before thoracentesis: verify preparation and consent, review allergies and bleeding risk, get baseline respiratory findings. A new bleeding risk stops the line.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you what is already done. The answer deals with the one item that is not.

steps.detail: Consent and baseline.
An anticoagulant.

steps.action: Cut the steps that proceed anyway
steps.detail: Positioning and teaching assume the procedure goes ahead.

elimination.verdict: Report the warfarin first.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old with pneumonia had an SpO2 of 84% and a respiratory rate of 30. The nurse applied a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and raised the head of the bed. Thirty minutes later the nurse reassesses.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is reassuring or requires follow up.

rows.text: Respiratory rate went from 30 to 20
rows.rationale: Slower breathing shows less distress.

rows.text: She now speaks only 2 or 3 words at a time
rows.rationale: Short phrases mean the work of breathing is rising.

rows.text: SpO2 went from 84% to 94%
rows.rationale: The saturation is back above 90%.

rows.text: She was oriented and is now pulling at the mask and confused
rows.rationale: New confusion is a concerning sign of poor oxygenation.

rows.text: The reservoir bag collapses fully with each breath
rows.rationale: A collapsed bag means the device is not delivering high concentration oxygen. Check the flow and the valves.

questions.takeaway: Monitor the response to oxygen with the whole patient: rate, speech, mental status, saturation and the device itself.
questions.strategy: Judge each row alone. One good number does not cancel new confusion or a collapsed reservoir.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 84% and a rate of 30.
Rate and saturation better. Speech and mental status worse.
A nonrebreather bag must stay inflated.

elimination.verdict: Reassuring, follow up, reassuring, follow up, follow up.

questions.stem: A long term care resident whose roommate has COVID 19 has had diarrhea for 2 days and now has a fever, cough and dry mucous membranes. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client on the facility's COVID 19 precautions
options.rationale: Preventing transmission is a priority hypothesis, and roommates are exposed.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Upright positioning supports ventilation.

options.text: Offer fluids often and track intake
options.rationale: Fever, diarrhea and dry mucous membranes put her at risk for fluid volume deficit.

options.text: Monitor the SpO2 trend and breathing effort
options.rationale: Trends catch deterioration early.

options.text: Wait for a positive test before starting precautions
options.rationale: Tempting because the test confirms the diagnosis. Exposure plus symptoms is enough to start precautions, and waiting exposes others.

options.text: Seat her at her own table in the dining room for meals
options.rationale: Isolation is a real concern, but a shared room spreads infection even at a separate table. Use other ways to connect.

questions.takeaway: GI symptoms can come before respiratory ones in COVID 19. Act on exposure plus symptoms: precautions, positioning, hydration, monitoring.
questions.strategy: Tie each option to a cue in the stem: the exposed roommate, the cough, the fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Exposure needs precautions. Cough needs positioning and monitoring. Diarrhea and fever need fluids.
Precautions start on suspicion, before the result.
A shared dining room.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old has been on 60% oxygen by mask for 3 days. SpO2 has stayed at 99% to 100%. Today the nurse hears new crackles with decreased breath sounds at both bases. The prescribed goal is an SpO2 of 92% or higher.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Report the findings and ask about lowering the oxygen concentration
options.rationale: The goal is met with room to spare. The lowest effective concentration limits further harm.

options.text: Help the client deep breathe, cough and change position
options.rationale: Deep breaths and movement reopen collapsed alveoli.

options.text: Increase the oxygen to keep the SpO2 at 100%
options.rationale: More oxygen worsens a complication caused by high oxygen.

options.text: Remove the oxygen until the next provider rounds
options.rationale: Stopping oxygen abruptly without an order risks hypoxemia.

options.text: A complication of high concentration oxygen
options.rationale: High oxygen for days washes out the nitrogen that holds alveoli open. New crackles and decreased sounds fit absorption atelectasis.

options.text: Upper airway obstruction
options.rationale: That causes stridor, not crackles at the bases.

options.text: An inaccurate pulse oximeter reading
options.rationale: The reading has been steady, and the lung sounds are the new finding.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario points to fluid loss.

options.text: Breath sounds at the bases
options.rationale: Shows whether the alveoli are reopening.

options.text: SpO2 against the prescribed goal as oxygen is lowered
options.rationale: Confirms the lower concentration still meets 92% or higher.

options.text: Skin turgor
options.rationale: A hydration check that does not track this problem.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Not related to the oxygen complication.

questions.takeaway: A saturation of 100% on high oxygen is not a goal. Use the lowest effective concentration and listen for new crackles.
questions.strategy: Opposite actions are offered: lower the oxygen or raise it. The goal of 92% tells you which way to go.

steps.action: Read the goal against the reading
steps.detail: 92% wanted, 100% delivered for 3 days.

steps.action: Link the new lung findings to the therapy
steps.detail: High oxygen can collapse alveoli.

steps.action: Choose monitoring that tracks the fix
steps.detail: Breath sounds and saturation at the lower dose.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen complication; ask to lower oxygen and deep breathe; breath sounds and SpO2 against goal.

questions.stem: A client given an IV opioid an hour ago is on oxygen by nasal cannula with an SpO2 of 96%. The respiratory rate is 8 and the client is hard to wake. Which action is first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and coach deep breathing
options.rationale: Tempting because both help ventilation. A client who is hard to wake cannot follow coaching, so this does not get breaths moving.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow to give the client a safety margin
options.rationale: Oxygen is not the missing piece. The client is not moving enough air to clear carbon dioxide, and extra oxygen can hide slow shallow breathing.

options.text: Check the oximeter waveform to confirm the reading
options.rationale: A good step when a reading does not match the client. Here the reading is not the concern. Pulse oximetry shows saturation, not ventilation.

options.text: Stimulate the client to breathe and call for help
options.rationale: A rate of 8 with poor arousal is failing ventilation. The nurse acts on the client, not on the number.

questions.takeaway: A normal SpO2 on oxygen does not prove the client is breathing enough. Rate, depth and alertness tell you about ventilation.
questions.strategy: The dramatic number is the reassuring one. Find the quieter findings that disagree with it.

steps.action: Compare the number with the client
steps.detail: 96% does not fit a rate of 8 and poor arousal.

steps.action: Cut the option about the reading
steps.detail: Confirming the waveform tests the oximeter, not the breathing.
The problem is ventilation.
Coaching needs an awake client. Stimulation does not.

elimination.verdict: Stimulate the client and get help.

questions.stem: One hour after a right thoracentesis a client says breathing feels easier. Which finding does the nurse report now?

options.text: Fainter right sided breath sounds, rate up from 18 to 26
options.rationale: Breath sounds should be the same or better after fluid is removed. Fainter sounds with a rising rate suggest a pneumothorax despite the client feeling better.

options.text: A coughing spell lasting several minutes after the procedure
options.rationale: Coughing is common as the lung expands again. It settled, so it is watched.

options.text: Soreness at the needle site rated 3 on a 0 to 10 scale
options.rationale: Expected after a needle through the chest wall.

options.text: A small spot of clear yellow drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Tempting as a bleeding concern. A small amount of serous drainage is expected.

questions.takeaway: After a thoracentesis, compare breath sounds with the baseline. Feeling better does not rule out a pneumothorax.
questions.strategy: The client's own report points to improvement. Look for the finding that only means something when compared with the baseline.

steps.detail: Mild soreness and a small serous spot.
Common with lung expansion.
Fainter sounds and a climbing rate.

elimination.verdict: Report the fainter right breath sounds and rising rate.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Pneumonia with a fever of 38.6 C, crackles and rust colored sputum
options.rationale: All three findings are expected with pneumonia.

options.text: COPD with an SpO2 of 91% who is breathing through pursed lips
options.rationale: Looks unstable, and this is a usual picture for a client with chronic lung disease.

options.text: Admitted with loud wheezing that is now quiet, speaking in single words
options.rationale: Wheezing that goes quiet while the client can barely speak means little air is moving. Silent breath sounds are a danger sign, not improvement.

options.text: COVID 19 on 2 L/min with a steady saturation, fatigue and loss of taste
options.rationale: Expected cues with a stable saturation.

questions.takeaway: Quiet is not always better. When wheezing stops and speech shortens, air has stopped moving.
questions.strategy: One client sounds improved. Check that against a second detail before you believe it.

steps.action: Cut findings expected for the condition
steps.detail: Pneumonia and COVID 19 findings fit their diagnoses.
91% with pursed lips is a chronic picture.
Single word speech says the quiet chest is worse.

elimination.verdict: See the client whose wheezing went quiet.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia who was calm at 0800 is now restless, keeps pulling off the nasal cannula and insists on going home. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed as needed medication for anxiety
options.rationale: Tempting because the client looks anxious. A sedative could slow breathing in a client who may be hypoxic.

options.text: Check the SpO2 and assess the client's breathing
options.rationale: New restlessness in a client with a lung problem is an early sign of low oxygen until proven otherwise. No assessment has been done yet.

options.text: Stay with the client and reorient to place and situation
options.rationale: A good safety response to confusion. It addresses the behavior and misses the likely cause.

options.text: Ask a family member to sit with the client for safety
options.rationale: Protects the client from a fall and leaves the cause unexamined.

questions.takeaway: New restlessness or confusion in a respiratory client is hypoxia first. Assess oxygenation before you treat behavior.
questions.strategy: Safety and assessment compete. The stem gives a behavior change and no assessment, so find the cause first.

steps.detail: Restlessness plus a removed cannula points to low oxygen.
It treats a symptom and can worsen breathing.
They follow the oxygen check.

elimination.verdict: Check SpO2 and assess breathing.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia and thick sputum has heart failure and new swelling in both ankles. The client asks how much to drink. Which response is best?

options.text: Aim for 3 liters of water a day to thin the sputum
options.rationale: The usual pneumonia teaching, which makes it tempting. It applies unless fluids are contraindicated, and heart failure with new edema may be that case.

options.text: Limit yourself to 1 liter a day because of the swelling
options.rationale: Recognizes the heart failure, but a restriction is a prescription the nurse does not set.

options.text: Drink whenever you feel thirsty and that will be enough
options.rationale: Gives no goal and ignores both the thick sputum and the edema.

options.text: I will confirm your fluid goal with the provider first
options.rationale: Two conditions pull in opposite directions and the edema is new. The nurse clarifies the goal before teaching a number.

questions.takeaway: Three liters a day for pneumonia comes with a condition: unless contraindicated. Heart failure with new edema means clarify first.
questions.strategy: Two options state opposite amounts with equal confidence. A detail in the stem makes both numbers unsafe to give.

steps.detail: Thick sputum calls for fluids. Heart failure with edema calls for caution.
The nurse cannot pick 3 liters or 1 liter here.
Thirst is not a plan.

elimination.verdict: Confirm the fluid goal with the provider.

chapters.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone has a platelet count of 18,000/mm3. Which assessment best detects new petechiae in this client?

options.text: Inspect the shins and forearms under bright light
options.rationale: Tempting because petechiae often start on the legs, but they are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin even in good light.

options.text: Palpate the lower legs for raised spots
options.rationale: Petechiae are flat, so there is nothing to feel.

options.text: Inspect the oral mucosa and conjunctiva
options.rationale: These areas carry little pigment, so pinpoint bleeding shows there when the skin hides it.

options.text: Press a glass slide over the lower legs
options.rationale: Diascopy checks blanching of a lesion you can already see. It does not find hidden petechiae.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, look for petechiae inside the mouth and on the conjunctiva.
questions.strategy: Two options are inspection. The skin tone in the stem decides which site will actually show the finding.

steps.detail: Low platelets mean you are hunting for bleeding into the skin.
Petechiae are flat, and a slide needs a visible lesion.
Dark pigment hides petechiae on the legs. Mucosa does not.

elimination.verdict: Oral mucosa and conjunctiva.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old in a skilled nursing unit has hard, thick, overhanging toenails and asks the nurse to trim them today. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Soak both feet in warm water to soften the nails
options.rationale: Correct preparation for hard, thick nails, which makes it tempting. It is a step in trimming, and the nurse does not yet know that trimming is allowed.

options.text: Find out whether agency policy lets nurses trim them
options.rationale: Many agencies reserve thick toenails in older adults for a podiatrist. Scope is settled before any step of the procedure begins.

options.text: Cut the nails straight across at the toe tips
options.rationale: The right technique once trimming is approved. It is not the first step.

options.text: Request an antifungal for the thickened toenails
options.rationale: Thick, layered toenails are common with aging. Nail appearance alone does not establish a fungal infection.

questions.takeaway: Thick toenails in an older adult: agency policy decides who trims them. If approved, soak hard nails and cut straight across.
questions.strategy: Three options start the job or treat the nails. One asks whether the job is the nurse's to do.

steps.detail: Thick nails alone do not prove fungus.

steps.action: Notice the soak and the cut belong together
steps.detail: Both are steps of trimming.

steps.action: Ask what must be true before trimming
steps.detail: The agency has to allow it.

elimination.verdict: Confirm the policy first.

questions.stem: A client had a punch biopsy on the forearm this morning and plans to swim laps tonight. Which statement indicates the discharge teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will cover it with a waterproof bandage before I swim laps tonight."
options.rationale: The dressing stays in place and dry for at least 8 hours, so swimming tonight is out either way.

options.text: "Redness that spreads this week is part of normal healing."
options.rationale: Spreading redness or heavy drainage is reported, not expected.

options.text: "I will scrub off any crust with soap so it stays clean."
options.rationale: Crusts are loosened gently with tap water or saline after the dressing comes off.

options.text: "I will skip the pool and keep the dressing dry until tomorrow."
options.rationale: The dressing stays dry and in place for at least 8 hours, then the site is cleaned daily.

questions.takeaway: After a biopsy, keep the dressing dry and in place for at least 8 hours, then clean daily and report redness or drainage.
questions.strategy: The swim plan is the cue. Look for the statement that changes that plan.

steps.detail: Swimming tonight would wet the dressing inside 8 hours.
Spreading redness is reported. Scrubbing a crust harms new tissue.
A waterproof bandage still means removing the dressing early.

elimination.verdict: Skips the pool and keeps the dressing dry.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client with gel nail enhancements on every finger has a pulse oximeter that will not read reliably. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove the enhancement from one nail for assessment
options.rationale: One bare nail gives a place to check color, capillary refill and the oximeter with the least loss to the client.

options.text: Ask the client to have all enhancements removed today
options.rationale: It would work, which makes it tempting. One nail is enough, so removing all of them is more than the assessment needs.

options.text: Estimate capillary refill through the enhancement
options.rationale: The coating hides the nail bed, so the result means nothing.

options.text: Record the nails as unable to assess
options.rationale: The nurse still needs perfusion data and has a simple way to get it.

questions.takeaway: For a hospitalized client with nail enhancements, remove the enhancement from one nail so the nail bed can be assessed.
questions.strategy: Two options solve the problem. Pick the one that solves it with the least cost to the client.

steps.action: Cut the options that give up the data
steps.detail: Guessing through gel and skipping the assessment both leave you blind.

steps.action: Compare one nail with all nails
steps.detail: Both give access to a nail bed.
One nail meets the need.

elimination.verdict: Remove one enhancement.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old reports an itchy rash since yesterday that began on the trunk and is spreading to the arms. The client first saw a cardiologist 12 days ago. Which question does the nurse ask first?

options.text: "Have you changed your soap or laundry detergent lately?"
options.rationale: A fair question, and a contact rash would be the runner up. Contact rashes stay where the product touched. This one started on the trunk and is spreading.

options.text: "Does anyone in your family have a skin condition?"
options.rationale: Part of a full history. It does not explain a rash that began yesterday.

options.text: "Have you started any new medicine or supplement recently?"
options.rationale: A new specialist visit often means a new drug, and a rash that starts on the trunk and spreads outward fits a drug reaction. This is the question that can change today's plan.

options.text: "How much time have you spent in the sun this week?"
options.rationale: Sun related rashes follow exposed skin. The trunk is usually covered.

questions.takeaway: When a new rash appears, ask what drug was started. A rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward points to a drug, not a product on the skin.
questions.strategy: Soap and medicine are both reasonable questions. The pattern of the rash and the recent specialist visit pick between them.

steps.detail: Family history and sun do not fit a one day course on the trunk.
Contact rashes sit where the product touched.
A cardiology visit 12 days ago suggests a new prescription.

elimination.verdict: Ask about a new medicine or supplement.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old found in a hot apartment has a temperature of 104 F (40 C), new confusion and dry skin. A coworker says the dry skin rules out overheating. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the temperature in one hour
options.rationale: A temperature this high with confusion cannot wait an hour.

options.text: Begin cooling measures and notify the provider
options.rationale: The temperature and confusion already show hyperthermia. Older adults sweat less, so dry skin does not argue against it.

options.text: Inspect the axillae and skinfolds for moisture
options.rationale: Looking for sweat feels like careful assessment, but sweating is not a reliable sign in older adults and the data needed are already in hand.

options.text: Offer oral fluids and reassess after the client drinks
options.rationale: A confused client may not swallow safely, and fluids alone do not cool.

questions.takeaway: Aging reduces sweat gland activity. Do not use sweating to decide whether an older adult is overheated.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already done. More looking only delays cooling.

steps.detail: High temperature, hot room, new confusion.
Less sweating is an aging change, so dry skin proves nothing.
Rechecking later, hunting for sweat and waiting on fluids all postpone treatment.

elimination.verdict: Cool the client and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman reports coarse, dark hair on her chin and chest that appeared over 3 months. The nurse also notes several bruises and a rounder face than in her last photograph. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Document the hair growth as an expected change of aging
options.rationale: Facial hair can increase with aging, which makes this tempting. A 3 month onset at 44 with bruising and a rounder face is not an aging pattern.

options.text: Teach safe hair removal methods for the face
options.rationale: Treats the appearance and leaves the cause unexamined.

options.text: Ask how the hair growth affects her self-image
options.rationale: Body image matters and belongs in her care. It comes after the findings that suggest a hormone problem are reported.

options.text: Report the hair growth with the bruising and facial change
options.rationale: New hirsutism with easy bruising and a change in fat distribution suggests a hormone disorder and needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: Hirsutism is a cue, not a diagnosis. Look for what travels with it: bruising, fat redistribution, voice change, acne. Then report the cluster.
questions.strategy: Aging and self-image are both real considerations. The speed of onset and the two extra findings push this past either one.

steps.detail: Hair removal does not address why it grew.
Three months, age 44, plus bruising and a rounder face.
A possible hormone disorder is evaluated first.

elimination.verdict: Report the cluster of findings.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with reduced sensation in the hands and feet had a scald burn last winter. Which statement shows the safety teaching was effective?

options.text: "I check the bath with a thermometer before I get in."
options.rationale: A thermometer does not depend on the client's sensation. Lowering the water heater setting is the other half of the plan.

options.text: "I dip one foot in first to feel how hot the water is."
options.rationale: The feet have reduced sensation, so they cannot judge the water.

options.text: "I test the water with my hand before I step in."
options.rationale: The usual advice for most adults, which makes it tempting. This client's hands have reduced sensation too.

options.text: "I add the hot water once I am sitting in the tub."
options.rationale: The client would be sitting in water that is heating up without being able to feel it.

questions.takeaway: When sensation is reduced, the client cannot be the thermometer. Measure the water and lower the water heater setting.
questions.strategy: Three statements rely on the client feeling the water. Reread the stem for which body parts can still feel.

steps.detail: Foot, hand and sitting in the tub all depend on sensation.
Sensation is reduced in the hands and the feet.
A thermometer reads the same for everyone.

elimination.verdict: The thermometer statement.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with a long smoking history reports feeling well. Which nail finding requires follow up?

options.text: Longitudinal ridges on several fingernails
options.rationale: An expected aging change.

options.text: A 160 degree angle between nail plate and nail fold
options.rationale: This is the normal angle with a firm nail base.

options.text: A 180 degree nail angle with a spongy nail base
options.rationale: Early clubbing. It points to hypoxia, and with this smoking history lung disease has to be ruled out.

options.text: Thick, yellowish gray toenails
options.rationale: Common with aging. Worth watching for fungal infection, but not the finding tied to this client's risk.

questions.takeaway: A nail angle that straightens to 180 degrees with a spongy base is early clubbing, a sign of chronic hypoxia.
questions.strategy: Sort expected aging from the one change that fits the smoking history.

steps.action: Link the history to the nails
steps.detail: Smoking raises the risk of chronic hypoxia and lung cancer.
Ridges and thick yellow gray toenails are expected.
160 degrees is normal. 180 degrees with a spongy base is not.

elimination.verdict: The 180 degree angle with a spongy base.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old on bed rest has paper thin skin, moist skinfolds under the breasts and reduced sensation in the feet. Which interventions does the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Position the client so air reaches the skinfolds
options.rationale: Air circulation keeps moisture from breaking down skin in the folds.

options.text: Assist with position changes at least every 2 hours
options.rationale: Thin subcutaneous tissue gives little padding over bone.

options.text: Secure dressings without adhesive tape when possible
options.rationale: Tape tears thin epidermis when it is removed.

options.text: Measure bath water temperature before bathing
options.rationale: Reduced sensation means the client will not feel water that is too hot.

options.text: Use warm water and limit soap to soiled areas
options.rationale: Hot water and full body soap dry aging skin. Warm water and less soap protect it.

options.text: Slide the client up in bed using the draw sheet edge
options.rationale: Sliding causes shear. A lift sheet is used to lift, not drag.

questions.takeaway: Aging skin: reposition at least every 2 hours, lift without sliding, let air reach skinfolds, avoid tape, bathe gently and measure water temperature when sensation is reduced.
questions.strategy: Judge each option on its own against the three cues in the stem. Only the option that drags the skin fails.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each cue to an action
steps.detail: Thin skin: turn, avoid tape, gentle bathing. Moist folds: air. Reduced sensation: measure water temperature.

steps.action: Test the one about moving her
steps.detail: Sliding on the sheet edge drags skin over linen and causes shear.

steps.action: Do not expect a fixed number
steps.detail: Five of six are supported here.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A client with thick, greasy scalp scales has been rubbing coconut oil into the scalp each night for "dryness." Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will wash my hair less often so that my scalp can recover."
options.rationale: Less washing leaves more oil on the scalp, which feeds the problem.

options.text: "I will stop the oil and see my provider about treatment."
options.rationale: Dandruff comes from excess oil, not dryness. Severe dandruff needs treatment because it can lead to hair loss.

options.text: "I will switch to a heavier moisturizing scalp cream."
options.rationale: Still treating dryness that is not there.

options.text: "I will pick the scales off gently before I shampoo."
options.rationale: Picking irritates an already inflamed scalp and treats nothing.

questions.takeaway: Dandruff is caused by excess oil. Untreated severe dandruff can cause hair loss, so it is treated with the provider.
questions.strategy: The client's own word, dryness, is the misunderstanding. Find the statement that drops it.

steps.detail: The client is adding oil to an oily scalp.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the belief
steps.detail: Less washing and heavier cream both add oil.
Picking scales inflames the scalp.

elimination.verdict: Stop the oil and see the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse cleans a client's leg ulcer as prescribed. A foul odor is still present after cleaning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the persistent odor as possible bioburden
options.rationale: Odor that remains after cleaning suggests organisms in the wound itself, so the provider needs to know.

options.text: Document the odor and reassess at the next dressing change
options.rationale: Documenting is correct and feels complete. The odor outlasting the cleaning makes this an unexpected finding that should not wait.

options.text: Apply an odor absorbing dressing over the ulcer
options.rationale: Covers the sign without addressing its cause.

options.text: Clean the ulcer a second time with more saline
options.rationale: The wound was already cleaned as prescribed. Repeating it delays reporting.

questions.takeaway: Odor that persists after a wound is cleaned suggests bioburden. Describe it and report it.
questions.strategy: The timing tips it. Odor before cleaning may be old drainage. Odor after cleaning belongs to the wound.

steps.detail: The odor is still there after cleaning.

steps.action: Cut the cover up and the repeat
steps.detail: A dressing hides it and more saline stalls.
An unexpected finding is reported now, not watched.

elimination.verdict: Report possible bioburden.

questions.stem: A client's nail beds look bluish. The nurse squeezes a fingertip, presses the nail bed and releases. The blue color does not change. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Cyanosis from poor oxygenation
options.rationale: Color carried by blood fades with pressure and returns on release.

options.text: Venous stasis in the fingers
options.rationale: Also a blood flow color, so it would blanch.

options.text: Pigment in the nail bed
options.rationale: Pigment does not move with pressure, so the color stays the same through the blanch test.

options.text: Slow capillary refill from poor perfusion
options.rationale: Refill describes how fast color returns after blanching. Here nothing blanched.

questions.takeaway: Blanch test: color from blood changes with pressure and returns. Color from pigment does not change.
questions.strategy: Three options are blood flow problems and would all blanch. The unchanged color rules out all three together.

steps.detail: No change with pressure or release.
Cyanosis, stasis and slow refill all depend on blood in the nail bed.

steps.action: Keep the one that is not blood
steps.detail: Pigment stays put.

elimination.verdict: Pigment in the nail bed.

questions.scenario: A 78-year-old is seen for a yearly visit. The nurse notes: small cherry red papules on the trunk. Lengthwise ridges on the fingernails. Sparse hair on both lower legs for years. A round bald patch on the scalp that appeared this month. Soft, thin fingernails that bend easily. A brown spot on the forearm that the client says is larger than last year.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected aging change or requires follow up.

rows.text: Cherry red papules on the trunk
rows.rationale: Cherry hemangiomas are benign. Reassure the client.

rows.text: Lengthwise ridges on the fingernails
rows.rationale: Reduced nail bed blood flow causes longitudinal ridges.

rows.text: Sparse hair on both lower legs for years
rows.rationale: Gradual, even hair loss on the lower legs is expected with aging.

rows.text: Round bald scalp patch that appeared this month
rows.rationale: Sudden patchy hair loss at any age is reported.

rows.text: Soft, thin fingernails that bend easily
rows.rationale: Soft, bending nails can mean malnutrition or other systemic disease.

rows.text: Brown forearm spot larger than last year
rows.rationale: A pigmented lesion that is changing needs evaluation for malignancy.

questions.takeaway: Gradual and symmetric is usually aging. Sudden, patchy or changing gets reported.
questions.strategy: For each row ask two things: did it come on slowly, and is it the same on both sides?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cherry papules, nail ridges and thin leg hair.

steps.action: Mark the sudden or changing ones
steps.detail: A new bald patch and a growing pigmented spot.
Ridges are aging. Soft nails that bend are not.

elimination.verdict: Expected, expected, expected, follow up, follow up, follow up.

questions.stem: A new nurse collects fluid from an intact vesicle for a viral culture. Pickup by the lab courier is delayed. Which action by the new nurse shows the orientation was effective?

options.text: Places the swab in formalin until the courier arrives
options.rationale: Formalin is for pathology specimens and would ruin a culture.

options.text: Leaves the swab in a dry tube at the nurses' station
options.rationale: Without transport medium and cooling the virus will not survive.

options.text: Discards the swab and collects from a crusted lesion later
options.rationale: Intact vesicles give the best viral sample. Crusted lesions do not.

options.text: Keeps the swab in viral transport medium on ice
options.rationale: Viral specimens go in viral transport medium and stay cold until they reach the lab.

questions.takeaway: Viral culture: fluid from an intact vesicle, viral transport medium, kept cold, sent promptly.
questions.strategy: The delay is the cue. Ask which choice keeps the specimen usable while it waits.

steps.detail: The specimen has to survive the wait.
Formalin fixes tissue for pathology.

steps.action: Cut the options that lose the sample
steps.detail: Room temperature and a crusted lesion both lower the yield.

elimination.verdict: Viral transport medium on ice.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old who was always well groomed arrives at the clinic with matted hair, body odor and soiled clothing. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Teach a daily bathing and hair care routine
options.rationale: Teaching assumes the client can learn and carry it out, which is not yet known.

options.text: Assess cognition and ability to perform self-care
options.rationale: A change from the client's usual grooming is a cue. The nurse needs to know why before choosing a response.

options.text: Arrange a home health aide to help with bathing
options.rationale: May turn out to be the right solution, which makes it tempting. It skips finding out whether the cause is cognitive, physical or something else.

options.text: Ask the family to supervise the client's hygiene
options.rationale: Hands the problem to others before the nurse knows what it is.

questions.takeaway: Poor hygiene that is new for an older adult calls for assessing cognition and self-care ability before teaching or referral.
questions.strategy: The words always well groomed make this a change. A change is assessed before it is fixed.

steps.detail: Well groomed before, neglected now.
Three are interventions and one is assessment.
The stem gives the appearance only, not the cause.

elimination.verdict: Assess cognition and self-care ability.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a shave biopsy on the back, blood is soaking steadily through the gauze. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Tape a second gauze pad over the first
options.rationale: Adds padding without stopping the bleeding.

options.text: Notify the provider that sutures may be needed
options.rationale: May be needed if bleeding continues, so it is tempting. The nurse controls the bleeding before making the call.

options.text: Apply direct pressure to the site
options.rationale: Pressure is the first measure for biopsy site bleeding. Topical agents and sutures follow only if it fails.

options.text: Remove the gauze to measure the wound
options.rationale: Measuring delays control of active bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding after a biopsy: direct pressure first, then a topical hemostatic agent or sutures if it continues.
questions.strategy: The bleeding is already seen, so more assessment is not the answer. Pick the fastest action that is in the nurse's own hands.

steps.detail: Active bleeding, already observed.

steps.action: Cut what does not stop it
steps.detail: More gauze and measuring leave it bleeding.
Pressure works now. The call comes next if it fails.

elimination.verdict: Apply direct pressure.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone is on day 3 of antibiotics for cellulitis of the lower leg. Which finding best indicates the treatment is effective?

options.text: The darkened area is smaller and cooler than on day 1
options.rationale: In dark skin inflammation shows as a darker area. Shrinking size and less warmth mean it is resolving.

options.text: No redness is visible on the lower leg
options.rationale: Sounds like improvement, but erythema is often not visible in dark skin, so its absence tells you nothing.

options.text: The client rates pain lower after the scheduled analgesic
options.rationale: The analgesic explains the relief, not the antibiotic.

options.text: The leg feels warm with firm edges at the border
options.rationale: Warmth and firmness are signs of ongoing inflammation.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, inflammation looks darker than the surrounding skin. Track the size of the darkened area and its warmth, not redness.
questions.strategy: Two options sound like less inflammation. Only one uses a sign that shows in this client's skin.

steps.detail: Redness may never have been visible.

steps.action: Cut the finding with another cause
steps.detail: Pain relief follows the analgesic.
Cooler and smaller is improving. Warm and firm is not.

elimination.verdict: Smaller, cooler darkened area.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a punch biopsy of a pigmented lesion on the shoulder. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Confirm that informed consent was obtained
options.rationale: First. Nothing is opened or injected until consent is confirmed.

options.text: Set up the sterile field and supplies
options.rationale: The field is prepared once the procedure is cleared to go ahead.

options.text: Tell the client the anesthetic will sting briefly
options.rationale: The warning comes just before the provider injects the local anesthetic.

options.text: Place the specimen in 10% formalin
options.rationale: A pathology specimen goes into formalin as soon as it is removed.

options.text: Teach the client to keep the dressing dry for 8 hours
options.rationale: Aftercare teaching follows once the site is dressed.

questions.takeaway: Biopsy sequence: consent, sterile setup, prepare the client for the sting, specimen into formalin, aftercare teaching.
questions.strategy: Anchor the two ends first. Consent opens the sequence and discharge teaching closes it.

steps.detail: Consent is confirmed before anything else.
Dressing teaching happens after the procedure.
Setup, then the anesthetic warning, then the specimen.

elimination.verdict: Consent, setup, warn, formalin, teach.

questions.stem: A nursing student is asked to establish a baseline skin tone for a client who works outdoors. Which action by the student shows the instruction was understood?

options.text: Inspects the face and neck in natural daylight
options.rationale: Good lighting, but these areas are darkened by sun exposure.

options.text: Compares the backs of both hands
options.rationale: Symmetry is checked, but the backs of the hands are among the most sun exposed skin.

options.text: Inspects the forearms after removing the client's watch
options.rationale: Removing the watch is a good thought, but the forearm is still sun exposed.

options.text: Inspects the inner upper arm
options.rationale: Skin less exposed to UV shows the genetically determined tone, which is the most accurate baseline.

questions.takeaway: Assess baseline skin tone in areas with little UV exposure, where sun has not changed the pigment.
questions.strategy: The outdoor job is the cue. Three sites tan and one does not.

steps.detail: Sun adds pigment to exposed skin.
Face, hands and forearms are all exposed.
The inner upper arm sees little sun.

elimination.verdict: Inner upper arm.

questions.stem: Four clients with dark skin tones are on bed rest. Which finding does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: Yellow callused soles with white sclera next to the cornea
options.rationale: Calluses can look yellow without jaundice, and the clear sclera confirms it. Expected.

options.text: Gray lips and tongue in a client who is newly restless
options.rationale: Gray lips and tongue are cyanosis in dark skin, and new restlessness fits low oxygen. Breathing comes first.

options.text: One heel that is painful and cooler than the other heel
options.rationale: Tempting because it is real tissue damage, likely a deep tissue injury. It is offloaded and reported right after the client who may be short of oxygen.

options.text: A darker, warm patch on the forearm at an old IV site
options.rationale: Darker and warm is inflammation in dark skin. It is local and gets reported, after the oxygen problem.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, cyanosis shows as gray lips and tongue. Gray lips with new restlessness is an oxygen problem and outranks local skin damage.
questions.strategy: Three options are real problems. Ask which one is a whole body problem and which are local.

steps.detail: Yellow calluses with clear sclera are a normal variant.
The heel and the forearm are local tissue problems.
Gray lips and tongue plus new restlessness means low oxygen.

elimination.verdict: The gray lips and tongue with new restlessness. Breathing before skin.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old is receiving IV fluids for dehydration. Forearm skin still tents, abdominal skin returns at once, and the lung bases have new crackles. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the provider to increase the fluid rate
options.rationale: Tempting because the forearm still tents. Forearm tenting in an older adult is lost elasticity, so it does not show dehydration.

options.text: Continue the current rate and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Tempting because the abdominal turgor shows the fluids worked. The new crackles mean the fluid is now too much, so waiting is unsafe.

options.text: Recheck turgor over the radial wrist before deciding
options.rationale: The abdomen already gave a reliable turgor result. Another turgor check adds nothing and delays acting on the lungs.

options.text: Slow the infusion and report the new crackles
options.rationale: Abdominal turgor shows the dehydration is corrected, and new crackles show fluid moving into the lungs. Breathing decides it.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, read turgor on the abdomen or radial wrist. Once turgor is normal there, new crackles mean the fluids have gone too far.
questions.strategy: Decide which turgor site counts in an 85-year-old, then ask which finding is new.

steps.detail: Forearm tenting is aging skin.
Abdominal skin returns at once, so hydration is restored.
Crackles are a breathing problem and were not there before.

elimination.verdict: Slow the infusion and report the crackles.

questions.stem: A client with a dark skin tone has had brown vertical bands on every nail for years. Today the band on one thumbnail is wider and darker than last month. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the changed thumbnail band for evaluation
options.rationale: The bands are a common variant, and this one has changed. A changing pigmented band is treated as a new finding and evaluated for melanoma.

options.text: Document the bands as an expected normal variant
options.rationale: Tempting because about 75% of people with dark skin have these bands. That covers the stable ones and does not cover a band that is changing.

options.text: Press the thumbnail to see whether the color blanches
options.rationale: The blanch test separates blood from pigment. This is already known to be pigment, so the test does not answer the question of change.

options.text: Ask about thumb injury and recheck in one month
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. The change is already documented against last month, so waiting only delays the evaluation.

questions.takeaway: Pigmented nail bands are common and normal in dark skin when they are long standing and stable. A band that widens or darkens is evolving and gets reported.
questions.strategy: The normal variant rule tempts you to stop. Look for the one word that says something changed.

steps.detail: Wider and darker than last month.

steps.action: Cut the test that answers a different question
steps.detail: Blanching separates blood from pigment only.
The comparison is already made, so more watching adds nothing.

elimination.verdict: Report the changed band. Stable is a variant. Changing is not.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old is 48 hours into antibiotics for forearm cellulitis. The redness is fainter than at admission. The warm area now extends past yesterday's marked border and is more tender. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Continue the plan and recheck the arm tomorrow
options.rationale: Tempting because the redness has faded. In older adults redness does not track severity, and the warm area has grown.

options.text: Elevate the arm and recheck the border in 2 hours
options.rationale: Elevation is reasonable comfort care. The border has already been crossed, so another check only repeats what is known.

options.text: Report that the infection appears to be extending
options.rationale: Warmth past the marked border and more tenderness show the infection is spreading even though the color looks better.

options.text: Ask the provider to order a culture of the skin
options.rationale: A culture may follow. The provider first needs to hear that the infection is spreading on the current drug.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, do not judge infection by how red it looks. Track the border, the warmth and the pain.
questions.strategy: One finding looks better and two look worse. Decide which findings can be trusted in a 67-year-old.

steps.detail: Faint redness underestimates infection in older adults.
Warmth past the mark and more tenderness.
The assessment is complete, so the next step is to tell the provider.

elimination.verdict: Report the spreading infection.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old whose skin tears easily has slid down in bed. She is comfortable and breathing easily. The AP is alone, and a second staff member will be free in 5 minutes. Which direction does the nurse give?

options.text: Pull her up now with a hand under each arm
options.rationale: Tempting because it fixes the position at once. Pulling under the arms drags thin skin across the sheet and tears it.

options.text: Wait for the second person and use the lift sheet
options.rationale: She is comfortable and breathing easily, so nothing is urgent. Five minutes costs nothing and a two person lift avoids shear.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed until the helper arrives
options.rationale: Raising the head makes her slide farther and adds shear over the sacrum.

options.text: Have her push with her heels while the AP helps
options.rationale: Tempting because it uses her own mobility. Digging the heels in adds friction to fragile heel skin, and one person still ends up dragging her.

questions.takeaway: Aging skin tears with shear. When the client is not in distress, wait for help and lift with a sheet.
questions.strategy: Ask whether anything in the stem makes this urgent. If not, the safest method wins over the fastest.

steps.detail: Comfortable and breathing easily, so no reason to rush.

steps.action: Cut the moves that add shear
steps.detail: Pulling, raising the head and pushing with the heels all drag skin.
Two people and a lift sheet.

elimination.verdict: Wait 5 minutes and lift with the sheet.

chapters.title: Care of Clients with Conditions of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: A client with a reddened sacrum and a Braden score of 12 receives continuous tube feeding. Which positioning plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat between turns
options.rationale: Tempting because flat removes shear. The continuous feeding tips it away, since lying flat risks aspiration.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees with side tilts
options.rationale: Thirty degrees is the lowest safe angle for the feeding and the highest angle that limits shear. The side tilt takes weight off the sacrum.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees during the feeding
options.rationale: Protects the airway but the client slides, and shear builds on a sacrum that is already red.

options.text: Turn the client fully onto the side at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Moves the pressure from the sacrum to the hip bone.

questions.takeaway: Two risks, one angle. Thirty degrees protects the airway during feeding and limits shear, and a 30 degree tilt offloads the sacrum.
questions.strategy: Two options protect one thing and harm another. Pick the option that covers both the airway and the skin.

steps.detail: Aspiration from the feeding and shear on the sacrum.
Flat fails the airway. 45 degrees fails the skin.
It loads the trochanter.

elimination.verdict: 30 degrees up and 30 degrees tilted.

questions.stem: Five days after abdominal surgery, a client's dressing is suddenly soaked with pink, watery drainage. The incision edges are closed without redness. Which complication does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Wound infection
options.rationale: Tempting because any new drainage suggests infection. The drainage is pink and watery, not purulent, and there is no redness.

options.text: Hemorrhage from the incision
options.rationale: Bleeding would be frank red blood, not blood tinged serum.

options.text: Wound dehiscence
options.rationale: A sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage in a closed incision often comes just before the edges separate.

options.text: Delayed inflammatory phase
options.rationale: Serosanguineous drainage is expected in the first 48 hours. A sudden increase on day 5 is a change.

questions.takeaway: A sudden rise in serosanguineous drainage from a closed incision warns of dehiscence, even when the edges still look closed.
questions.strategy: Read the drainage color and the timing. Pink and watery plus sudden on day 5 points away from infection and toward separation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pink and watery is serosanguineous, not purulent and not frank blood.
Normal for 48 hours. A sudden increase on day 5 is new.
Sudden serosanguineous increase comes before dehiscence.

elimination.verdict: Dehiscence.

questions.stem: A client with toxic epidermal necrolysis had the causative drug stopped yesterday. The client now has a hoarse voice and is drooling. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Call the rapid response team for airway evaluation
options.rationale: Hoarseness and drooling mean the airway mucosa is sloughing. Airway comes before everything else.

options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate as prescribed
options.rationale: Tempting because detached skin loses fluid like a burn. Circulation comes after an airway that is closing.

options.text: Apply lubricant to both eyes
options.rationale: Eye care prevents scarring and belongs in the plan after the airway is secured.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV analgesic
options.rationale: Pain control matters and it does not come before the airway.

questions.takeaway: In SJS or TEN, stop the drug first. Once that is done, the airway leads the supportive care, ahead of fluids, pain and eyes.
questions.strategy: The stem says the drug is already stopped, so the usual first step is gone. Rank what is left with the ABCs.

steps.detail: The drug was stopped yesterday.
Hoarse voice and drooling are airway cues.
Fluids are circulation. Pain and eyes follow.

elimination.verdict: Airway evaluation now.

questions.stem: The day after surgery, the AP reports a red heel. The nurse finds intact maroon skin that feels boggy and does not blanch. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document a stage 1 injury and recheck next shift
options.rationale: Tempting because the skin is intact and does not blanch. The maroon color and boggy feel tip it to deeper damage.

options.text: Cover the heel with a hydrocolloid and continue the turning schedule
options.rationale: A dressing does not remove the pressure, and the turning schedule alone leaves the heel on the bed.

options.text: Ask the AP to recheck the heel after the next turn
options.rationale: Assessment of a changing area stays with the nurse.

options.text: Float the heel and report a suspected deep tissue injury
options.rationale: Maroon, boggy, nonblanchable intact skin is deep tissue damage that can open quickly. Offload it and report.

questions.takeaway: Stage 1 is red. Purple or maroon intact skin is a deep tissue injury, so offload it at once and report.
questions.strategy: Intact skin does not mean minor. Color is the detail that separates stage 1 from deep tissue injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maroon and boggy means deep damage, not stage 1.
Only floating the heel takes weight off it.
The AP reports. The nurse assesses.

elimination.verdict: Float the heel and report.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old reports 36 hours of deep, burning pain on the left side of the chest. Today the nurse sees grouped vesicles in a band that stops at the midline. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply calamine lotion and recheck the rash next week
options.rationale: Calamine is a real comfort measure for these lesions. Used alone, it lets the window for antiviral treatment close.

options.text: Arrange provider evaluation today for antiviral treatment
options.rationale: One sided vesicles in a band after deep pain fit herpes zoster. Antivirals work best within 72 hours of the rash, and these vesicles appeared today.

options.text: Teach that the blisters will crust and clear without treatment
options.rationale: The lesions do crust in time. Early treatment is what limits the course and lasting nerve pain in older adults.

options.text: Schedule the shingles vaccine for later this week
options.rationale: The vaccine prevents zoster. It does not treat an active outbreak.

questions.takeaway: Pain first, then one sided vesicles along a dermatome: think herpes zoster and get antivirals started within 72 hours of the rash.
questions.strategy: Calamine and antivirals are both part of zoster care. The rash is new today, which makes one of them time sensitive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Deep pain, then grouped vesicles in a band on one side.
A vaccine is not treatment.
Antivirals work best within 72 hours of the rash. Calamine can be added.

elimination.verdict: Same day evaluation for antiviral treatment.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 2 coccyx injury rates pain 7 of 10 with movement and refuses to turn. The dressing change is due. Which action comes first?

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic before repositioning
options.rationale: Pain is treated before repositioning and dressing changes. Once it is controlled, the turn and the dressing change can go ahead.

options.text: Ask the client to describe the pain location and quality
options.rationale: Tempting because assessment usually comes first. The stem already gives the rating and the trigger, so action is due.

options.text: Explain that turning is needed to heal the wound
options.rationale: True, and teaching does not work on a client in pain.

options.text: Postpone the dressing change until the next shift
options.rationale: Leaves the pain untreated and the client on the wound.

questions.takeaway: Give pain medication before repositioning and dressing changes. Controlled pain is what lets the client move.
questions.strategy: Check whether the stem already assessed. When it has, the assessment option is a stall.

steps.action: Find the assessment in the stem
steps.detail: Pain 7 with movement, refusing to turn.
Turning and wound care.
Medicate, then do the care.

elimination.verdict: Analgesic first, then turn and dress.

questions.nursesNote: 1000: 82-year-old with dark skin, bed rest day 4 after a stroke. Sacral skin same color as surrounding skin but warmer and firm, and client winces when it is touched. Weight down 6% in one month. Hair sparse and nails dull. Oxygen tubing in place with red grooves behind both ears. Heels same temperature and firmness as surrounding skin, nontender. Voiding by scheduled toileting, skin dry.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up for tissue integrity.

segments.text: bed rest day 4 after a stroke
segments.rationale: Immobility is the leading risk factor and calls for a pressure reduction plan.

segments.text: Sacral skin same color as surrounding skin but warmer and firm, and client winces when it is touched
segments.rationale: In dark skin, warmth, firmness and pain signal early damage before any color change.

segments.text: Weight down 6% in one month
segments.rationale: More than 5% weight loss is a nutrition cue. Request a dietitian consult.

segments.text: Hair sparse and nails dull
segments.rationale: Both suggest undernutrition, which slows healing.

segments.text: Oxygen tubing in place with red grooves behind both ears
segments.rationale: A device related injury is starting. Pad or reposition the tubing.

segments.text: Heels same temperature and firmness as surrounding skin, nontender
segments.rationale: No temperature change, firmness change or pain. Keep floating the heels.

segments.text: Voiding by scheduled toileting, skin dry
segments.rationale: Moisture is controlled. Nothing to act on.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, use your hands: warmth, firmness and pain come before color. Check under every device and read the nutrition cues.
questions.strategy: The sacrum is the trap because the color is normal. Normal color does not clear dark skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm, firm and painful means early damage.
Grooves behind the ears are pressure.
Weight loss, sparse hair, dull nails.

questions.stem: A long term care resident has intense itching at night and thin raised lines between the fingers. The roommate has begun itching too. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply moisturizer after bathing and add a room humidifier
options.rationale: Tempting because dry skin is the usual cause of itching in older adults. The burrows and the roommate tip it away.

options.text: Request a bedtime antihistamine for the resident
options.rationale: Eases the itch and leaves the mites and the spread untreated.

options.text: Start contact precautions and have the roommate examined
options.rationale: Burrows in the finger webs with night itching and an itching contact point to scabies, which spreads by contact and bedding.

options.text: Inspect the hair shafts near the scalp for nits
options.rationale: Nits fit lice. The finger web lines fit mite burrows.

questions.takeaway: Night itching, finger web burrows and an itching contact mean scabies: contact precautions, examine and treat contacts, hot water laundry.
questions.strategy: Two cues separate this from simple dry skin: the lines between the fingers and the second person itching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Raised lines in the finger webs are burrows.
A second itching person means spread.
Precautions and contact examination come before comfort care.

elimination.verdict: Contact precautions and check the roommate.

questions.stem: Two days after sharp debridement, a stage 3 injury measures larger than last week. The bed is moist and red with no odor, and the surrounding skin is unchanged. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The wound is deteriorating, so the provider needs a report today
options.rationale: Tempting because a larger wound is normally reported. The recent debridement and the healthy bed tip it away.

options.text: The wound is infected, so an antimicrobial dressing is needed
options.rationale: No purulent drainage, odor or spreading redness supports infection.

options.text: The debridement failed, so mechanical debridement should be added
options.rationale: Mechanical debridement is avoided when the bed is mostly granulation.

options.text: The change is expected, so continue the current plan
options.rationale: Wound size increases after dead tissue is removed. A red moist bed, no odor and calm margins show a healthy wound.

questions.takeaway: Wounds measure larger right after debridement. Judge the bed, the drainage and the margins before calling it deterioration.
